In the CM frame the projectile moves at speed $v_1' = \dfrac{m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v$ before and after; only its direction changes. Its final lab velocity is $\vec v_{1f} = \vec v_{\text{cm}} + \vec v_1'$, where $\vec v_{\text{cm}}$ has length $\dfrac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v$. As $\theta^*$ ranges over every possible value, the tip of $\vec v_{1f}$ traces a circle of radius $v_1'$ centered at the tip of $\vec v_{\text{cm}}$.

The diagram is drawn for $m_1 = 2m_2$, so the circle's radius is half the distance $OC$.

![Velocity diagram: the CM velocity runs from the origin O to the circle's center C, the circle's radius is the projectile's CM-frame speed, and the final lab velocity runs from O to a point on the circle; the largest lab angle occurs where that line is tangent to the circle](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- If $m_1 > m_2$, the circle's radius is smaller than the distance to its center, so the origin lies outside it. The lab velocity can tilt only until it is tangent to the circle, at angle $\theta_{\max}$ with $\sin\theta_{\max} = \dfrac{v_1'}{v_{\text{cm}}} = \dfrac{m_2}{m_1}$.
- If $m_1 = m_2$, the circle passes through the origin. Combined with the target's velocity, this is the collisions lesson's right-angle rule.
- If $m_1 < m_2$, the origin is inside the circle, and every direction, including straight back, is possible.

### Example 3

An alpha particle (mass about 4 u) collides elastically with a proton (about 1 u) at rest. What is the largest angle through which the alpha can be deflected? And by an electron at rest ($m_\alpha/m_e \approx 7300$)?

Proton: $\sin\theta_{\max} = \tfrac14$, so $\theta_{\max} = 14.5°$. Electron: $\sin\theta_{\max} = 1/7300$, so $\theta_{\max} \approx 0.008°$.

That second number is history. In 1909 Geiger and Marsden, working in Rutherford's laboratory, found that about 1 alpha particle in 8000 striking a platinum sheet was turned back through more than 90°, and that even very thin gold foil turned some back. Collisions with electrons can't do that: each one deflects an alpha by at most 0.008°, and a thin foil gives far too few of them for random tiny deflections to add up to a reversal. Only a target much heavier than the alpha could turn it back. Rutherford concluded that the atom's positive charge and almost all its mass sit in a tiny nucleus.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting that the CM part of the kinetic energy, $\tfrac12Mv_{\text{cm}}^2$, can never be lost; only $\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$ can.
- Using the total mass or one of the masses where the reduced mass belongs.
- Changing the speeds in the CM frame for an elastic collision. Elastic means same speeds there, only new directions.
- Forgetting to add $\vec v_{\text{cm}}$ back at the end.
- Expecting a heavy projectile to bounce back off a light target. Its deflection can't exceed $\sin^{-1}(m_2/m_1)$.

## Key points

- CM frame: $\vec v' = \vec v - \vec v_{\text{cm}}$; momenta are $\pm\mu\vec v_{\text{rel}}$ with $\mu = m_1m_2/(m_1 + m_2)$.
- $K = \tfrac12Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$; only the second part can be lost: $K_{\text{lost}} = (1 - e^2)\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$.
- An elastic collision keeps CM-frame speeds and only turns the momenta.
- Head-on elastic, target at rest: fraction transferred $4m_1m_2/(m_1 + m_2)^2$, largest for equal masses.
- Heavy on light: largest lab deflection $\sin\theta_{\max} = m_2/m_1$.

lessons.title: Rotational kinematics and moment of inertia
lessons.body:
## Spinning instead of sliding

So far objects have been treated as points. Real objects also rotate: wheels, turbines, planets, figure skaters. The good news is that rotation about a fixed axis mirrors one-dimensional motion almost exactly, with angles in place of positions. This lesson builds that dictionary and introduces the rotational version of mass, the moment of inertia, which leads to rotational kinetic energy.

## Angular position, velocity and acceleration

Measure a rotating object's orientation by the angle $\theta$ that a reference line on it makes with a fixed direction. Physics uses **[[radians]]**: an angle in radians is arc length divided by radius, $\theta = s/r$, so a full turn is $2\pi$ rad ($= 360^\circ$). Radians are dimensionless, which is why they can quietly disappear from units.

- **[[Angular displacement]]**: $\Delta\theta$ (rad). Counterclockwise is usually positive.
- **[[Angular velocity]]**: $\omega = \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$ (rad/s).
- **[[Angular acceleration]]**: $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta t}$ (rad/s²).

Every point on a rigid object shares the same $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$, which is what makes them useful. Rotation rates are often quoted in revolutions per minute: $1\text{ rpm} = \dfrac{2\pi\text{ rad}}{60\text{ s}} = 0.1047$ rad/s. And $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$.

## Linking rotation to linear motion

A point at distance $r$ from the axis moves along a circle. Because $s = r\theta$,

$$v = r\omega, \qquad a_t = r\alpha, \qquad a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = r\omega^2.$$

Here $v$ is the point's speed (tangential), $a_t$ its tangential acceleration (speeding up or slowing) and $a_c$ its centripetal acceleration. Points farther from the axis move faster. These relations need $\omega$ in rad/s; plugging in rpm or degrees per second gives nonsense.

The picture puts all of these on one point of a disk that is turning counterclockwise and slowing down, so its tangential acceleration points backward along the rim.

![A disk turning counterclockwise about its axis. A radius r runs from the axis to a point on the rim at angle theta from a dashed reference line; the arc from the reference line to the point is the arc length s = r theta. At the point, the velocity v is tangent to the rim in the direction of rotation, the tangential acceleration points the opposite way along the rim because the disk is slowing, and the centripetal acceleration points along the radius toward the axis.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Constant angular acceleration

With $\alpha$ constant, the kinematic equations carry over symbol by symbol:

| Linear | Rotational |
|---|---|
| $v = v_0 + at$ | $\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$ |
| $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$ | $\Delta\theta = \omega_0t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2$ |
| $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$ | $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta$ |
| $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t$ | $\Delta\theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0 + \omega)t$ |

Each equation leaves out one of the five quantities, so pick the one that leaves out the quantity you neither know nor need:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  accTitle: Choosing a constant angular acceleration equation
  accDescr: Among the five quantities omega zero, omega, alpha, delta theta and t, find the one that is neither given nor asked for, and use the equation that leaves it out. If time is missing, use omega squared equals omega zero squared plus two alpha delta theta. If the final angular velocity is missing, use delta theta equals omega zero t plus one half alpha t squared. If the angle is missing, use omega equals omega zero plus alpha t. If alpha is missing, use delta theta equals one half of omega zero plus omega, times t.
  B["Which of ω₀, ω, α, Δθ, t is neither given nor asked for?"] -->|"t"| C["ω² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ"]
  B -->|"ω"| D["Δθ = ω₀t + ½αt²"]
  B -->|"Δθ"| E["ω = ω₀ + αt"]
  B -->|"α"| F["Δθ = ½(ω₀ + ω)t"]
```

### Example 1

A ceiling fan spinning at 240 rpm is switched off and slows uniformly to rest in 12 s. Find its angular acceleration and how many revolutions it makes while stopping.

$\omega_0 = 240 \times 0.1047 = 25.13$ rad/s; $\omega = 0$.

$\alpha = \dfrac{0 - 25.13}{12} = -2.09$ rad/s².

$\Delta\theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0 + \omega)t = \tfrac12(25.13)(12) = 150.8$ rad, which is $150.8/2\pi = 24$ revolutions. (Shortcut in rev units: average 120 rpm $= 2$ rev/s for 12 s gives 24 rev.)

On a graph of $\omega$ against $t$, the angle turned is the area under the line, here a triangle: $\tfrac12(12)(25.13) = 150.8$ rad.

```plot
{"x": [0, 14], "y": [0, 28], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "ω (rad/s)", "functions": [{"f": "25.13 - 2.094*x", "from": 0, "to": 12}], "labels": [{"at": [7.5, 13], "text": "ω(t)"}], "shade": [{"f": "25.13 - 2.094*x", "from": 0, "to": 12}], "caption": "The fan slowing down: the shaded area is the 150.8 rad it turns through"}
```

### Example 2

The fan's blade tips are 0.60 m from the axis. At the moment the fan is switched off, what are a tip's speed, tangential acceleration and centripetal acceleration?

$v = r\omega = 0.60(25.13) = 15.1$ m/s. $a_t = r\alpha = 0.60(-2.09) = -1.26$ m/s². $a_c = r\omega^2 = 0.60(25.13)^2 = 379$ m/s². The centripetal part dominates; it's what would fling a loose blade off.

## Rotational kinetic energy and moment of inertia

A spinning wheel has kinetic energy even though its center doesn't move. Add up $\tfrac12mv^2$ for every particle, using $v_i = r_i\omega$:

$$K = \sum\tfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2 = \tfrac12\left(\sum m_ir_i^2\right)\omega^2 = \tfrac12I\omega^2.$$

The quantity

$$I = \sum m_ir_i^2$$

is the **[[moment of inertia]]** about the chosen axis (kg·m²). It plays the role of mass for rotation: it measures how hard it is to change an object's rotation. Crucially, it depends not just on the mass but on *how far the mass is from the axis*, and so on which axis you choose.

Standard results for uniform objects of mass $M$:

| Object | Axis | $I$ |
|---|---|---|
| Point mass at distance $R$ | — | $MR^2$ |
| Thin hoop or ring, radius $R$ | through center, perpendicular to the plane | $MR^2$ |
| Solid disk or cylinder, radius $R$ | through center, along the axis | $\tfrac12MR^2$ |
| Solid sphere, radius $R$ | through center | $\tfrac25MR^2$ |
| Thin spherical shell, radius $R$ | through center | $\tfrac23MR^2$ |
| Thin rod, length $L$ | through center, perpendicular | $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$ |
| Thin rod, length $L$ | through one end, perpendicular | $\tfrac13ML^2$ |

A hoop has all its mass at distance $R$, so $I = MR^2$; a disk has much of its mass closer in, so less. A flywheel designer who wants to store energy puts the mass in the rim.

### Example 3

Three small 0.50 kg masses sit at the ends and middle of a light 1.2 m rod. Find $I$ about (a) an axis through the middle mass, perpendicular to the rod, and (b) an axis through one end.

(a) Distances 0.6, 0, 0.6 m: $I = 0.50(0.36) + 0 + 0.50(0.36) = 0.36$ kg·m².

(b) Distances 0, 0.6, 1.2 m: $I = 0 + 0.50(0.36) + 0.50(1.44) = 0.90$ kg·m². Same object, different axis, two and a half times the moment of inertia.

*Parallel-axis theorem.* If $I_{\text{cm}}$ is the moment of inertia about an axis through the center of mass, then about any parallel axis a distance $d$ away,

$$I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2.$$

For a rod about one end: $\tfrac1{12}ML^2 + M\left(\tfrac L2\right)^2 = \tfrac13ML^2$, matching the table. The CM axis always gives the smallest $I$ among parallel axes.

### Example 4

A 2.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.25 m spins at 300 rpm. What is its rotational kinetic energy?

$I = \tfrac12(2.0)(0.25)^2 = 0.0625$ kg·m². $\omega = 300(0.1047) = 31.4$ rad/s. $K = \tfrac12(0.0625)(31.4)^2 = 30.8$ J.

## Derivatives and integrals in rotation

Angular velocity and acceleration are derivatives: $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $\alpha = d\omega/dt$, exactly paralleling $v$ and $a$, and non-constant $\alpha$ is handled by integration.

For a continuous body, the sum becomes an integral over mass elements:

$$I = \int r^2\,dm.$$

*Thin uniform rod about its center.* Linear density $\lambda = M/L$, $dm = \lambda\,dx$, $x$ from $-L/2$ to $L/2$:

$$I = \int_{-L/2}^{L/2}\frac{M}{L}x^2\,dx = \frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{x^3}{3}\Big|_{-L/2}^{L/2} = \frac{M}{L}\cdot\frac{L^3}{12} = \frac1{12}ML^2.$$

*Uniform disk about its axis.* Split it into thin rings of radius $r$ and width $dr$, area $2\pi r\,dr$, mass $dm = \dfrac{M}{\pi R^2}2\pi r\,dr$:

$$I = \int_0^R r^2\frac{2M}{R^2}r\,dr = \frac{2M}{R^2}\cdot\frac{R^4}{4} = \frac12MR^2.$$

## Common mistakes

- Using rpm or degrees in $v = r\omega$ or $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ (convert to rad/s).
- Treating moment of inertia as a property of the object alone; it depends on the axis.
- Using $MR^2$ for every round object.
- Applying the parallel-axis theorem between two axes neither of which passes through the CM.

## Key points

- $\theta$ in radians; $\omega = d\theta/dt$, $\alpha = d\omega/dt$; constant-$\alpha$ equations mirror linear ones.
- $v = r\omega$, $a_t = r\alpha$, $a_c = r\omega^2$.
- $I = \sum m_ir_i^2 = \int r^2\,dm$; rotational KE $= \tfrac12I\omega^2$.
- Parallel-axis theorem: $I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$.

lessons.title: Torque and rotational dynamics
lessons.body:
## What makes things rotate

Last lesson described rotation; now we ask what causes it. Push a door near its hinges and it barely moves; push at the handle with the same force and it swings easily. Push straight toward the hinges and nothing happens at all. The rotational effect of a force depends on where and in what direction it's applied, and that effect is called torque. With torque in hand, Newton's second law gets a rotational twin.

## Torque

The **[[torque]]** $\tau$ of a force about an axis is

$$\tau = rF\sin\theta,$$

where $r$ is the distance from the axis to the point where the force is applied and $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec r$ (pointing from the axis to that point) and $\vec F$. Units: N·m (not called joules, even though the units match, because torque isn't energy).

Two equivalent ways to see it:

- $F\sin\theta$ is the component of the force perpendicular to $\vec r$; only that component turns the object. So $\tau = rF_\perp$.
- $r\sin\theta$ is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force's line of action, called the **[[lever arm]]** (moment arm) $\ell$. So $\tau = \ell F$.

The drawing shows both pictures at once: the lever arm is the perpendicular dropped from the axis to the force's line of action.

![Top view of a bar turning about an axis at its left end. The position vector r runs along the bar from the axis to the point where the force F is applied at angle theta to the bar. The force's line of action is extended as a dashed line, and the lever arm, ell equals r sine theta, is the perpendicular from the axis to that line, with a right-angle mark.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A force aimed straight at or away from the axis ($\theta = 0$ or $180^\circ$) has zero torque. Torque has a sign: by convention, counterclockwise is positive and clockwise negative. A wrench with a longer handle gives more torque for the same push, which is the whole point of a wrench.

```shape
{"segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, 0], "label": "r = 0.30 m"}, {"from": [3, 0], "to": [4, 1.732], "arrow": true, "label": "F"}, {"from": [3, 0], "to": [4.5, 0], "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0], "label": "axis"}], "labels": [{"at": [3.55, 0.25], "text": "60°"}], "caption": "Torque = rF sin θ: only the part of F perpendicular to the wrench turns the bolt"}
```

### Example 1

A mechanic pulls on a 0.30 m wrench with 80 N at $60^\circ$ to the handle. What torque does she apply? What if she pulls perpendicular to the handle?

$\tau = 0.30(80)\sin 60^\circ = 20.8$ N·m. Perpendicular: $\tau = 0.30(80) = 24$ N·m, the maximum for that force.

## Newton's second law for rotation

Consider a particle of mass $m$ on a light rod of length $r$, pushed by a force with tangential component $F_t$. Newton's second law tangentially: $F_t = ma_t = mr\alpha$. Multiply by $r$: $rF_t = mr^2\alpha$, i.e. $\tau = I\alpha$. Summing over all the particles of a rigid body (internal forces' torques cancel in pairs) gives

$$\sum\tau = I\alpha.$$

This is the rotational form of $\sum F = ma$: net torque causes angular acceleration, and the moment of inertia resists it. Like $\sum F = ma$, it's an equation you write for a chosen axis, with consistent sign conventions.

### Example 2

A 4.0 kg solid disk of radius 0.20 m is mounted on a frictionless axle. A string wrapped around its rim is pulled with a constant 6.0 N. Find the angular acceleration and the length of string unwound in 2.0 s, starting from rest.

$I = \tfrac12(4.0)(0.20)^2 = 0.080$ kg·m². $\tau = 0.20(6.0) = 1.2$ N·m. $\alpha = 1.2/0.080 = 15$ rad/s².

In 2.0 s: $\Delta\theta = \tfrac12(15)(2.0)^2 = 30$ rad, so string unwound $= r\Delta\theta = 0.20(30) = 6.0$ m.

## Pulleys with mass

Earlier we treated pulleys as massless, so the tension was the same on both sides. A real pulley has a moment of inertia, and to give it angular acceleration the tensions on its two sides must differ. Solve these problems by combining $\sum F = ma$ for each hanging or sliding object with $\sum\tau = I\alpha$ for the pulley, linked by the no-slip condition $a = R\alpha$.

If the question only asks for a speed after some distance, energy is quicker (as Example 4 below shows). The two routes:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Two routes through a problem with a massive pulley
  accDescr: First ask what the problem wants. For an acceleration, a tension or a force, draw a free-body diagram for each object, write sum of forces equals m a for each moving mass and sum of torques equals I alpha for the pulley, and link them with a equals R alpha. For a speed after a distance, use energy, setting the lost potential energy equal to the translational plus rotational kinetic energy, and link them with v equals R omega. Both routes end by solving and checking a limit such as a massless pulley.
  A["What does the problem ask for?"] --> B["Acceleration, tension or force"]
  A --> C["Speed after a distance"]
  B --> D["Free-body diagram for each object"]
  D --> E["Sum of F = ma for each moving mass"]
  E --> F["Sum of torques = Iα for the pulley"]
  F --> G["Link them: a = Rα"]
  C --> H["Energy: lost PE = translational KE + rotational KE"]
  H --> I["Link them: v = Rω"]
  G --> J["Solve, then check a limit such as a massless pulley"]
  I --> J
```

### Example 3

A 2.0 kg bucket hangs from a rope wrapped around a 3.0 kg solid-cylinder windlass of radius 0.10 m that turns without friction. The bucket is released. Find its acceleration and the rope tension.

Bucket (down positive): $mg - T = ma$.

Cylinder: $TR = I\alpha = \tfrac12MR^2\cdot\dfrac{a}{R}$, so $T = \tfrac12Ma$.

Substitute: $mg - \tfrac12Ma = ma$, so

$$a = \frac{mg}{m + \tfrac12M} = \frac{2.0(9.8)}{2.0 + 1.5} = 5.6\text{ m/s}^2.$$

$T = \tfrac12(3.0)(5.6) = 8.4$ N, less than the bucket's 19.6 N weight. The cylinder acts like an extra $\tfrac12M$ of inertia that the bucket must also accelerate. As $M\to 0$, $a\to g$.

The same method handles an Atwood machine with a massive pulley: $a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2 + I/R^2}$.

## Work and power in rotation

A torque acting through an angle does work, $W = \tau\Delta\theta$ (for constant torque), and the rotational work–energy theorem says $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta\left(\tfrac12I\omega^2\right)$. Power is $P = \tau\omega$, the rotational version of $Fv$. A car engine's power curve comes from its torque and rpm: 300 N·m at 4000 rpm ($419$ rad/s) is 126 kW.

### Example 4

The windlass in Example 3 starts from rest. Using energy, find the bucket's speed after falling 1.5 m.

Gravity's lost potential energy goes into the bucket's translational and the cylinder's rotational kinetic energy, with $\omega = v/R$:

$$mgh = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac12\left(\tfrac12MR^2\right)\left(\frac{v}{R}\right)^2 = \tfrac12\left(m + \tfrac12M\right)v^2.$$

$2.0(9.8)(1.5) = 29.4 = \tfrac12(3.5)v^2$, so $v = 4.10$ m/s. Check with kinematics: $v = \sqrt{2(5.6)(1.5)} = 4.10$ m/s ✓.

## Torque as a vector

In three dimensions torque is a cross product:

$$\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F,$$

with magnitude $rF\sin\theta$ and direction along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule (curl your fingers in the sense of rotation; your thumb gives $\vec\tau$). Counterclockwise rotation in the $xy$ plane corresponds to $\vec\tau$ along $+\hat k$, which is where the "counterclockwise is positive" convention comes from. In components, $\tau_z = xF_y - yF_x$.

For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, $\tau = I\,\dfrac{d\omega}{dt}$, and if the torque varies with time, $\omega(t) = \omega_0 + \dfrac1I\int\tau\,dt$. Work by a variable torque is $W = \int\tau\,d\theta$.

For instance, a force $\vec F = (3\hat\imath + 4\hat\jmath)$ N applied at $\vec r = (2\hat\imath + 1\hat\jmath)$ m gives $\tau_z = 2(4) - 1(3) = 5$ N·m, counterclockwise.

## Common mistakes

- Using the distance along the object instead of the perpendicular lever arm when the force is at an angle.
- Using the same tension on both sides of a pulley that has mass.
- Mixing sign conventions between the linear and rotational equations (choose them so $a = R\alpha$ with both positive).
- Forgetting rotational kinetic energy in energy problems with spinning parts.

## Key points

- $\tau = rF\sin\theta = rF_\perp = \ell F$; counterclockwise positive; $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$.
- $\sum\tau = I\alpha$ (rotational second law).
- Massive pulley: combine $\sum F = ma$, $\sum\tau = I\alpha$ and $a = R\alpha$.
- $W = \tau\Delta\theta$, $P = \tau\omega$; include $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ in energy conservation.

lessons.title: Rolling and angular momentum
lessons.body:
## Two ideas that complete rotational mechanics

A wheel rolling down a road both translates and rotates, and the two motions are locked together. And a spinning skater who pulls in her arms speeds up without anyone pushing her. This lesson explains both: rolling without slipping, which combines the last two lessons, and angular momentum, whose conservation is as fundamental as that of linear momentum.

## Rolling without slipping

When a wheel of radius $R$ rolls without slipping, the point touching the ground is momentarily at rest (no skidding). In one revolution the center moves forward one circumference, $2\pi R$, so

$$v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega, \qquad a_{\text{cm}} = R\alpha.$$

The motion is a translation of the center plus a rotation about it. The top of the wheel moves at $v_{\text{cm}} + R\omega = 2v_{\text{cm}}$, the bottom at $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega = 0$. That's why the top of a bicycle wheel's spokes look blurred in photos while the bottom ones look sharp.

Adding the two motions point by point gives the rolling velocities:

![Three wheels side by side. The first, in pure translation, has velocity v at the top, center and bottom. The second, in pure rotation about its center, has v forward at the top, zero at the center and v backward at the bottom. Their sum, the rolling wheel, has 2v at the top, v at the center and zero at the contact point.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The kinetic energy has both parts:

$$K = \tfrac12Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \tfrac12I_{\text{cm}}\omega^2.$$

Writing $I_{\text{cm}} = cMR^2$ (with $c = 1$ for a hoop, $\tfrac12$ for a disk, $\tfrac25$ for a solid sphere, $\tfrac23$ for a hollow sphere) and $\omega = v/R$:

$$K = \tfrac12(1 + c)Mv^2.$$

## Rolling down an incline

Release a rolling object from rest at height $h$. Static friction at the contact point makes it roll, but does no work, because the contact point doesn't move. So mechanical energy is conserved:

$$Mgh = \tfrac12(1 + c)Mv^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + c}}.$$

Mass and radius cancel; only the shape factor $c$ matters. Objects with mass concentrated near the center (small $c$) win a race: solid sphere ($c = 0.4$) beats solid cylinder ($0.5$) beats hollow sphere ($0.667$) beats hoop ($1$). A frictionless sliding block ($c = 0$, no rotation) beats them all, because none of its energy is tied up in spinning.

The acceleration down a slope of angle $\theta$ follows the same pattern: $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + c}$.

### Example 1

A solid ball and a hoop are released from rest at the top of a ramp 1.5 m high. Find each one's speed at the bottom.

Ball: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(9.8)(1.5)}{1.4}} = \sqrt{21.0} = 4.58$ m/s.

Hoop: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(9.8)(1.5)}{2}} = \sqrt{14.7} = 3.83$ m/s.

The ball arrives first. The hoop puts half its kinetic energy into rotation; the ball only $\tfrac{0.4}{1.4} = 29\%$.

## Angular momentum

The rotational analog of momentum is **[[angular momentum]]**. For a rigid object rotating about a fixed axis,

$$L = I\omega$$

(kg·m²/s). For a single particle moving past a point, $L = mvr_\perp$, where $r_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the point to the particle's line of motion: even a particle moving in a straight line has angular momentum about a point not on that line.

Just as net force changes linear momentum, net torque changes angular momentum:

$$\sum\tau = \frac{\Delta L}{\Delta t}.$$

## Conservation of angular momentum

If the net external torque on a system is zero, its angular momentum is constant:

$$I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f.$$

This is **[[conservation of angular momentum]]**. The striking consequence: if a system changes shape and its moment of inertia changes, its rotation rate adjusts in the opposite direction. A skater pulling in her arms reduces $I$, so $\omega$ increases. A diver tucks to spin faster and opens out to slow down before entering the water. A collapsing star can shrink to a neutron star spinning hundreds of times per second.

Before using it, check the condition, about a definite axis:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Deciding whether angular momentum is conserved
  accDescr: Choose a system and an axis. If the net external torque about that axis is zero, angular momentum about it is conserved, so the initial I omega equals the final I omega; kinetic energy may still change, so do not assume it is conserved. If the net external torque is not zero, use torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum, or torque equals I alpha for a fixed axis.
  A["Choose a system and an axis"] --> B{"Net external torque zero?"}
  B -->|"yes"| C["L is conserved: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂"]
  B -->|"no"| D["Use τ = dL/dt, or τ = Iα"]
  C --> E["Kinetic energy may still change: check it separately"]
```

### Example 2

A skater spins at 2.0 rev/s with her arms out, where $I = 4.5$ kg·m². She pulls her arms in, reducing $I$ to 1.8 kg·m². (a) What is her new spin rate? (b) What happens to her kinetic energy?

(a) $\omega_f = \dfrac{I_i}{I_f}\omega_i = \dfrac{4.5}{1.8}(2.0) = 5.0$ rev/s. (Units of $\omega$ cancel in the ratio, so rev/s is fine here.)

(b) In rad/s, $\omega_i = 12.57$ and $\omega_f = 31.42$. $K_i = \tfrac12(4.5)(12.57)^2 = 355$ J; $K_f = \tfrac12(1.8)(31.42)^2 = 888$ J. Kinetic energy increases by a factor of 2.5: her arm muscles do work pulling the mass inward. Angular momentum is conserved, kinetic energy is not.

### Example 3: a rotational collision

A 2.0 kg disk spins at 30 rad/s on a frictionless axle; $I_1 = 0.040$ kg·m². A second, non-rotating disk with $I_2 = 0.060$ kg·m² is dropped onto it and they spin together. Find the final angular speed.

No external torque about the axle: $I_1\omega_1 = (I_1 + I_2)\omega_f$, so $\omega_f = \dfrac{0.040(30)}{0.100} = 12$ rad/s. Like a perfectly inelastic collision, kinetic energy drops (from 18 J to 7.2 J), lost to friction between the disks.

## Angular momentum as a vector

In general, angular momentum about a point is the cross product

$$\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p,$$

and differentiating, $\dfrac{d\vec L}{dt} = \dfrac{d\vec r}{dt}\times\vec p + \vec r\times\dfrac{d\vec p}{dt} = \vec v\times m\vec v + \vec r\times\vec F = \vec\tau$, since $\vec v\times\vec v = 0$. So

$$\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec L}{dt}.$$

For a rigid body spinning about a symmetry axis, $\vec L = I\vec\omega$, with $\vec\omega$ along the axis by the right-hand rule.

The vector form explains a **[[gyroscope]]**'s **[[precession]]**. A spinning top tilted from vertical has $\vec L$ along its axis. Gravity's torque about the pivot is horizontal, perpendicular to $\vec L$. A torque perpendicular to $\vec L$ changes its direction, not its size, so instead of falling over, the axis swings slowly around the vertical. The precession rate is $\Omega = \dfrac{\tau}{L} = \dfrac{Mgr}{I\omega}$: the faster the spin, the slower the precession.

Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) is also angular momentum conservation: gravity points toward the Sun, so its torque about the Sun is zero, $\vec L$ of the planet is constant, and the area swept per unit time, $\dfrac{L}{2m}$, is constant.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting rotational kinetic energy for rolling objects (getting $\sqrt{2gh}$).
- Thinking static friction does work on a rolling object.
- Assuming kinetic energy is conserved when angular momentum is.
- Using rev/s in an energy formula (fine in a ratio, not in $\tfrac12I\omega^2$).

## Key points

- Rolling without slipping: $v = R\omega$; $K = \tfrac12Mv^2 + \tfrac12I\omega^2 = \tfrac12(1 + c)Mv^2$.
- Down an incline from rest: $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1 + c)}$; smaller $c$ wins.
- $L = I\omega$ (or $\vec r\times\vec p$); $\vec\tau = d\vec L/dt$.
- No external torque: $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$.

lessons.title: Static equilibrium
lessons.body:
## Structures that stay put

Bridges, shelves, ladders and your own skeleton are designed not to move. Engineers need to know the forces in each support and cable to make sure nothing breaks or tips over. For a point particle, staying at rest just needs zero net force. An extended object can have zero net force and still start spinning (think of two equal, opposite forces at opposite ends of a ruler), so it needs a second condition. This lesson puts torque to work on objects that don't move at all.

## The two conditions

A rigid object is in **[[static equilibrium]]** when it is at rest and stays at rest. That requires

$$\sum\vec F = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum\tau = 0 \text{ about any axis}.$$

The first prevents translation, the second rotation. In two dimensions this gives three equations: $\sum F_x = 0$, $\sum F_y = 0$, $\sum\tau = 0$. So you can solve for up to three unknown forces or distances.

*Freedom to choose the axis.* If the net force is zero, the net torque is the same about every point. So you may compute torques about whatever point is most convenient. The best choice is a point where an unknown force acts: that force then has zero lever arm and drops out of the torque equation, leaving fewer unknowns.

## Center of gravity

Gravity acts on every bit of an object, but for torque purposes its total effect is as if the whole weight $Mg$ acted at one point, the **[[center of gravity]]**. In a uniform gravitational field (any object on Earth smaller than a mountain), the center of gravity is the center of mass. A uniform beam's weight acts at its midpoint.

This explains tipping. An object resting on a base is stable as long as its center of gravity lies above the base. Lean it until the center of gravity passes beyond the edge of the base, and gravity's torque about that edge tips it over. Wide bases and low centers of gravity make objects harder to tip, which is why racing cars are low and wide.

![Two identical tall boxes resting on one bottom edge. The box tilted 20 degrees has its center of gravity to the left of the pivot edge, inside the base, so it falls back. The box tilted 45 degrees has its center of gravity to the right of the pivot edge, outside the base, so it tips over.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For this box (90 by 150 units), the center of gravity is directly above the edge at a tilt of $\arctan(45/75) = 31^\circ$: tilted less, it falls back; tilted more, it tips.

## Solving equilibrium problems

1. Draw a free-body diagram of the object, showing each force *at the point where it acts*.
2. Choose a pivot point for torques, ideally where an unknown force acts.
3. Write $\sum\tau = 0$ about that point (counterclockwise positive).
4. Write $\sum F_x = 0$ and $\sum F_y = 0$.
5. Solve. If a force comes out negative, it points opposite to the way you drew it.

As a flowchart, with a final check that catches most slips:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Solving a static equilibrium problem
  accDescr: Draw a free-body diagram with each force at the point where it acts. Choose the pivot at a point where an unknown force acts. Write the torque balance about that pivot with counterclockwise positive. Write the force balances in x and y. Solve. If a force comes out negative, it points opposite to the way it was drawn. Finally check with a torque balance about a second point.
  A["Free-body diagram: each force at its point of action"] --> B["Choose the pivot where an unknown force acts"]
  B --> C["Torque balance about the pivot, counterclockwise positive"]
  C --> D["Force balances: sum Fx = 0 and sum Fy = 0"]
  D --> E["Solve for the unknowns"]
  E --> F["Negative answer: that force points the other way"]
  F --> G["Check: torques about a second point also sum to zero"]
```

### Example 1: a seesaw

A 30 kg child sits 1.8 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 45 kg child sit on the other side to balance it? (The seesaw is uniform and pivoted at its center.)

Torques about the pivot (the pivot's force and the board's weight act there, so they contribute nothing):

$$30g(1.8) = 45g\,x \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{30(1.8)}{45} = 1.2\text{ m}.$$

The heavier child sits closer. Balance is about equal torques, not equal weights.

### Example 2: a beam on two supports

A uniform 6.0 m plank of mass 20 kg rests on supports at its two ends, A (left) and B (right). A 60 kg painter stands 1.5 m from end A. Find the force each support exerts.

Weights: plank $20(9.8) = 196$ N at 3.0 m from A; painter $60(9.8) = 588$ N at 1.5 m from A.

Torques about A (eliminates $F_A$):

$$F_B(6.0) - 196(3.0) - 588(1.5) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_B = \frac{588 + 882}{6.0} = 245\text{ N}.$$

Vertical forces: $F_A + F_B = 196 + 588 = 784$ N, so $F_A = 539$ N.

Check with torques about B: $-F_A(6.0) + 196(3.0) + 588(4.5) = -3234 + 588 + 2646 = 0$ ✓. The support nearer the painter carries more of the load.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[0, 0], [6, 0], [6, 0.2], [0, 0.2]]}, {"points": [[-0.2, -0.6], [0.2, -0.6], [0, 0]]}, {"points": [[5.8, -0.6], [6.2, -0.6], [6, 0]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, -1.6], "to": [0, -0.7], "arrow": true}, {"from": [6, -1.6], "to": [6, -0.7], "arrow": true}, {"from": [3, 0.1], "to": [3, -0.9], "arrow": true}, {"from": [1.5, 1.4], "to": [1.5, 0.25], "arrow": true}], "labels": [{"at": [0.45, -1.3], "text": "F_A"}, {"at": [5.55, -1.3], "text": "F_B"}, {"at": [3.6, -0.6], "text": "196 N"}, {"at": [2.1, 0.9], "text": "588 N"}], "caption": "Plank on two supports with a painter 1.5 m from the left end"}
```

### Example 3: a hinged beam held by a cable

A uniform 4.0 m horizontal beam of mass 25 kg is hinged to a wall at its left end. A cable from its right end to the wall makes $30^\circ$ with the beam. A 40 kg sign hangs from the right end. Find the cable tension and the hinge force.

Weights: beam 245 N at 2.0 m; sign 392 N at 4.0 m.

Torques about the hinge (removes both unknown hinge components). The cable's perpendicular component is $T\sin 30^\circ$ at 4.0 m:

$$T\sin 30^\circ(4.0) - 245(2.0) - 392(4.0) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T = \frac{490 + 1568}{2.0} = 1029\text{ N}.$$

Horizontal: hinge pushes outward, $H = T\cos 30^\circ = 891$ N. Vertical: $V + T\sin 30^\circ = 245 + 392$, so $V = 637 - 514.5 = 122.5$ N upward. A shallow cable angle makes the tension much larger than the weights it holds, a recurring theme.

![Free-body diagram of the beam in Example 3. A horizontal beam is hinged to a wall on the left; a cable runs from its right end up to the wall at 30 degrees. Forces on the beam: the cable tension T along the cable toward the wall, the beam's 245 N weight at its middle, the sign's 392 N weight at the right end, and the hinge force split into a horizontal part H pointing away from the wall and a vertical part V pointing up.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Ladders

A ladder leaning on a smooth wall is held by the floor's normal force, floor friction, the wall's normal force, and gravity. Taking torques about the foot of the ladder eliminates the two floor forces and gives the wall force; horizontal balance then gives the friction needed. If friction would need to exceed $\mu_s n$, the ladder slips. Steeper ladders need less friction, which is why the usual safety rule is a 4:1 ratio of height to base distance (about $76^\circ$).

## Distributed loads and stability

Torque balance for continuous loads uses integrals. A beam carrying a distributed load $w(x)$ (newtons per meter) experiences a total load $W = \int w(x)\,dx$, acting at $\bar x = \dfrac{\int x\,w(x)\,dx}{\int w(x)\,dx}$, the load's "center of mass." For a load increasing linearly from 0 to $w_0$ along a beam of length $L$, $W = \tfrac12w_0L$ and $\bar x = \tfrac23L$: replace it by a single force there and proceed as before.

Equilibrium can also be stable or unstable, which ties back to potential energy: an object resting where its gravitational $U = Mgy_{\text{cg}}$ is at a minimum (any small tilt raises its center of gravity) is stable; at a maximum, unstable.

## Elasticity: supports that stretch

Equilibrium problems treat beams and cables as rigid, but every real support deforms a little. For small deformations the **[[stress]]** (force per unit area, $F/A$, in pascals) is proportional to the **[[strain]]** (the fractional change in length, $\Delta L/L$, a pure number):

$$\frac{F}{A} = Y\,\frac{\Delta L}{L},$$

where $Y$ is **[[Young's modulus]]**, a property of the material (roughly $2\times10^{11}$ Pa for steel, $7\times10^{10}$ Pa for aluminum). This is Hooke's law written for materials: comparing with $F = k\,\Delta L$, a rod or cable acts as a spring of stiffness $k = YA/L$. The same stress works for compression (squeezing a metal column shortens it by the same rule, with essentially the same $Y$). Past the material's **[[elastic limit]]** it no longer springs back when the load is removed, and beyond that it breaks. Two more moduli describe other deformations. A force $F$ applied parallel to a face of area $A$ (a shear) slides that face sideways by $\Delta x$ relative to the opposite face a distance $L$ away: $F/A = S\,\Delta x/L$, where $S$ is the **[[shear modulus]]**. Squeezing from all sides with an added pressure $\Delta P$ shrinks the volume: $\Delta P = -B\,\Delta V/V$, where $B$ is the **[[bulk modulus]]** (it sets the speed of sound in a fluid, and fluids have a bulk modulus but no shear modulus). For instance, the cable in Example 3 is $4.0/\cos 30^\circ = 4.6$ m long; if it is steel with a 1.0 cm² cross-section, the 1029 N tension stretches it by $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} = \dfrac{1029(4.6)}{(1.0\times10^{-4})(2\times10^{11})} \approx 0.24$ mm, small enough that treating it as rigid was fine.

## Common mistakes

- Taking torques about a point but then including forces acting at that point (they have zero lever arm).
- Placing a beam's weight at its end instead of its center of gravity.
- Using the distance along the beam instead of the perpendicular lever arm for a slanted force.
- Forgetting that a hinge can exert both horizontal and vertical components.
- In $F/A = Y\,\Delta L/L$, using the diameter instead of the cross-sectional area $\pi d^2/4$, or forgetting to convert mm² or cm² to m².

## Key points

- Static equilibrium: $\sum\vec F = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$.
- Choose the torque pivot where an unknown force acts.
- A uniform object's weight acts at its center (center of gravity).
- An object tips when its center of gravity moves outside its base.
- Elasticity: stress $F/A = Y \times$ strain $\Delta L/L$, so $\Delta L = FL/(AY)$; shear $F/A = S\,\Delta x/L$; bulk $\Delta P = -B\,\Delta V/V$.

lessons.title: Gravitation and orbits
lessons.body:
## One law for apples and planets

Until now, gravity has been the constant $g = 9.8$ m/s² near Earth's surface. Newton's great insight was that the force pulling an apple down is the same one holding the Moon in orbit, and that it weakens with distance in a precise way. This lesson states his law of universal gravitation and uses it, with circular-motion ideas, to explain orbits and Kepler's laws.

## Newton's law of universal gravitation

Every two masses attract each other with a force along the line joining them:

$$F = \frac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2},$$

where $r$ is the distance between their centers and $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg² is the **[[gravitational constant]]**. This is **[[Newton's law of gravitation]]**. Each mass feels the same magnitude of force (third law). The force is an **[[inverse-square law]]**: double the distance and the force drops to a quarter.

$G$ is tiny, so gravity between everyday objects is negligible: two 70 kg people 1 m apart attract with about $3\times10^{-7}$ N. It dominates astronomy only because planets and stars are enormous. For spherical bodies, the force acts as if all the mass were at the center (a result Newton proved with calculus).

## Surface gravity

At Earth's surface, an object's weight is the gravitational force from Earth: $mg = \dfrac{GM_Em}{R_E^2}$, so

$$g = \frac{GM}{R^2}.$$

With $M_E = 5.97\times10^{24}$ kg and $R_E = 6.37\times10^6$ m, this gives 9.8 m/s². At height $h$ above the surface, replace $R$ with $R + h$: $g$ decreases, but slowly at first. At the International Space Station's altitude (about 400 km), $g$ is still about 8.7 m/s², 89% of its surface value. Astronauts float not because gravity is absent but because they and the station are in free fall together.

### Example 1

Find the acceleration due to gravity on Mars ($M = 6.42\times10^{23}$ kg, $R = 3.39\times10^6$ m).

$$g = \frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(6.42\times10^{23})}{(3.39\times10^6)^2} = \frac{4.28\times10^{13}}{1.149\times10^{13}} = 3.73\text{ m/s}^2,$$

about 38% of Earth's.

## Circular orbits

A satellite in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a planet of mass $M$ is in uniform circular motion, with gravity supplying the centripetal force:

$$\frac{GMm}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}.$$

The satellite's mass cancels, and lower orbits are faster. The period is the circumference over the speed, $T = 2\pi r/v$, and squaring:

$$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3.$$

### Example 2

Find the speed and period of a satellite orbiting 400 km above Earth's surface.

$r = 6.37\times10^6 + 4.0\times10^5 = 6.77\times10^6$ m.

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(5.97\times10^{24})}{6.77\times10^6}} = \sqrt{5.88\times10^7} = 7.67\times10^3\text{ m/s}.$$

$T = \dfrac{2\pi(6.77\times10^6)}{7670} = 5.55\times10^3$ s $= 92$ min. The ISS circles Earth about 16 times a day.

A **[[geostationary]]** satellite has a 24 h period, so it stays above one spot on the equator. Solving $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$ with $T = 86\,400$ s gives $r = 4.22\times10^7$ m, about 36 000 km above the surface.

## Kepler's laws

Decades before Newton, Johannes Kepler distilled Tycho Brahe's observations into three laws of planetary motion. Newton's gravitation explains all three.

1. *Orbits are ellipses* with the Sun at one focus. (A circle is the special case of zero eccentricity. Inverse-square forces produce conic-section orbits.)
2. *Equal areas in equal times*: the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest at its closest point (perihelion). This is conservation of angular momentum, because gravity points toward the Sun and exerts no torque about it.
3. *$T^2 \propto a^3$*: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's semimajor axis $a$ (its radius, for a circle), with the same constant $\dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM_{\text{Sun}}}$ for every planet.

```shape
{"x": [-4.6, 2.8], "y": [-1.8, 1.8], "curves": [{"x": "-1 + 2*cos(t)", "y": "1.6*sin(t)", "t": [0, "2pi"]}], "points": [[0.2, 0], [1, 0], [-3, 0]], "labels": [{"at": [0.2, -0.35], "text": "Sun (focus)"}, {"at": [1.85, -0.07], "text": "perihelion"}, {"at": [-3.8, -0.07], "text": "aphelion"}], "caption": "An elliptical orbit: the planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion"}
```

The second drawing, to scale for an orbit of eccentricity 0.6, marks the semimajor axis and shades the areas swept in two equal time intervals: a short, wide wedge near perihelion and a long, thin one near aphelion.

![An ellipse of eccentricity 0.6 with the Sun at the right-hand focus and an empty focus on the left. Perihelion is the point of the orbit nearest the Sun, at the right end of the long axis, and aphelion the farthest, at the left end. A bracket above marks the semimajor axis a, half the long axis. Two shaded wedges from the Sun, a short wide one at perihelion and a long thin one at aphelion, have equal areas.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 3

Mars orbits the Sun at 1.52 times Earth's orbital radius. How long is a Martian year?

Kepler's third law as a ratio: $\dfrac{T_M^2}{T_E^2} = \dfrac{a_M^3}{a_E^3}$, so $T_M = (1.52)^{3/2}(1\text{ yr}) = 1.87$ yr. No constants needed when comparing orbits around the same body.

## Gravitational potential energy and escape speed

The formula $U = mgy$ assumes constant $g$. Far from the surface we need the general form:

$$U = -\frac{GMm}{r},$$

with $U = 0$ at infinite separation. It's negative because work must be done to pull the masses apart. For small height changes near the surface, $\Delta U \approx mg\Delta y$.

The minimum launch speed that lets an object coast to infinity (arriving with zero speed) is the **[[escape speed]]**. Set the total energy to zero: $\tfrac12mv^2 - \dfrac{GMm}{R} = 0$, so

$$v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}.$$

For Earth, $v_{\text{esc}} = 11.2$ km/s, exactly $\sqrt2$ times the speed of a low circular orbit. In a circular orbit the total energy is $E = K + U = \tfrac12\dfrac{GMm}{r} - \dfrac{GMm}{r} = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$: negative, meaning bound.

Plotted against orbit radius (in units where $GMm = 1$), the kinetic energy is always half the size of the potential energy and the total is the negative of the kinetic energy: moving to a higher orbit raises the total energy (it becomes less negative) even though the satellite slows down.

```plot
{"x": [0, 2.2], "y": [-2.2, 1.2], "xLabel": "r", "yLabel": "energy", "functions": [{"f": "1/(2*x)"}, {"f": "-1/x"}, {"f": "-1/(2*x)", "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [1.5, 0.55], "text": "K"}, {"at": [1.3, -1.2], "text": "U"}, {"at": [0.22, -0.9], "text": "E"}], "caption": "Circular orbits: K = GMm/2r, U = −GMm/r, E = −GMm/2r"}
```

## Potential energy from the force law

Gravitational potential energy comes from integrating the force. The work needed to move $m$ from $r$ out to infinity against $F = GMm/r^2$ is

$$\int_r^\infty\frac{GMm}{r'^2}\,dr' = \frac{GMm}{r},$$

so $U(r) = -GMm/r$, and conversely $F = -\dfrac{dU}{dr} = -\dfrac{GMm}{r^2}$ (attractive). Integration also proves the shell theorem: a uniform spherical shell attracts outside masses as if its mass were at its center and exerts no net force on a mass inside it. Consequently, inside a uniform solid planet only the mass closer to the center counts, and $g(r) = \dfrac{GM}{R^3}r$ grows linearly from zero at the center.

## Common mistakes

- Measuring $r$ from the surface instead of the center.
- Forgetting to square $r$ (or squaring it twice).
- Thinking astronauts in orbit are weightless because there's no gravity.
- Using $U = mgh$ for orbits or escape problems.
- Converting km to m incorrectly in $r$.

## Key points

- $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$, $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²; $g = GM/R^2$.
- Circular orbit: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$.
- Kepler: ellipses, equal areas (angular momentum conservation), $T^2 \propto a^3$.
- $U = -GMm/r$; $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$; orbital energy $-GMm/(2r)$.

lessons.title: Skidding, rolling and the sweet spot
lessons.body:
## When the no-slip condition fails

The rolling lesson assumed that the wheel or ball never skids: the contact point is at rest and $v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega$ at every instant. That is true once an object has settled into rolling, but not at the start. A bowling ball leaves the bowler's hand sliding, with little spin. A cue ball struck low slides with backspin. A car that brakes too hard locks its wheels and skids. In each case $v_{\text{cm}} \ne R\omega$, the contact point slides, and **[[kinetic friction]]** acts until the motion settles into rolling.

This lesson works out what happens during that sliding phase using only the tools of this module: $\sum F = Ma$ for the center of mass, $\sum\tau = I\alpha$ about the center, and angular momentum about a well-chosen point. It ends with the reverse problem: where to strike an object so that it starts rolling (or swinging) cleanly, with no jolt at all. That point is the **[[center of percussion]]**, the physicist's version of a bat's sweet spot.

Throughout, the surface is level, $I_{\text{cm}} = cMR^2$ as in the rolling lesson, and "forward spin" means spin in the rolling sense (clockwise for an object moving to the right).

## The slip velocity decides the friction

The velocity of the contact point is the velocity of the center plus the velocity due to rotation about the center. At the bottom of the ball, forward spin carries the surface backward, so

$$v_{\text{contact}} = v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega.$$

This is the **[[slip velocity]]** (zero exactly when the object rolls without slipping). Kinetic friction always opposes sliding, so it points opposite to the slip velocity:

- $v_{\text{cm}} > R\omega$ (too little spin, the bowling-ball case): the contact point slides forward, friction points backward.
- $v_{\text{cm}} < R\omega$ (more forward spin than rolling needs, as for a cue ball struck high): the contact point slides backward, friction points forward.
- Backspin ($\omega < 0$) always belongs to the first case, because then $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$ is larger than $v_{\text{cm}}$. The safe rule is to compute $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$ with signs and let friction oppose it.
- $v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega$: no sliding, no kinetic friction. On a level surface with no other horizontal force, nothing changes after that: the object rolls on at constant speed (ignoring rolling resistance).

![A ball sliding to the right with no spin. Its velocity arrow points right from the center, its spin is in the rolling sense, and kinetic friction at the contact point points left, opposite to the sliding of the contact point. Weight acts down at the center and the normal force up at the contact point.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Friction does two jobs at once. Pointing backward at the bottom of the ball, it slows the center ($a_{\text{cm}} = -\mu_k g$) and, because it acts a distance $R$ below the center, it exerts a torque $\mu_kMgR$ in the forward-spin sense, so it spins the ball up ($\alpha = \mu_kMgR/I_{\text{cm}} = \mu_kg/(cR)$). The speed falls and the spin rises until they match.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: What friction does to a ball launched on a level floor
  accDescr: Start by comparing the center's speed with R times omega. If the center's speed is larger, the contact point slides forward, friction points backward, the center slows and the spin increases. If it is smaller, the contact point slides backward, friction points forward, the center speeds up and the spin decreases. If they are equal there is no sliding and no kinetic friction. Both sliding branches end when the speed equals R times omega, after which the ball rolls at constant speed.
  A["Compare v and R times omega"] --> B["v greater: contact slides forward"]
  A --> C["v smaller: contact slides backward"]
  A --> D["Equal: no sliding"]
  B --> E["Friction backward: v falls, spin rises"]
  C --> F["Friction forward: v rises, spin falls"]
  E --> G["Until v = R times omega"]
  F --> G
  G --> H["Rolls at constant speed"]
  D --> H
```

## Sliding to rolling with forces and torques

Launch a ball with speed $v_0$ and no spin. While it slides,

$$v(t) = v_0 - \mu_kgt, \qquad R\omega(t) = \frac{\mu_kg}{c}\,t.$$

Rolling begins when these are equal: $v_0 - \mu_kgt^* = \mu_kgt^*/c$, so

$$t^* = \frac{c\,v_0}{(1 + c)\mu_kg}, \qquad v_f = v_0 - \mu_kgt^* = \frac{v_0}{1 + c}.$$

The final speed doesn't depend on the coefficient of friction at all. A slippery lane makes the ball slide longer, a grippy one shorter, but either way a solid sphere ($c = \tfrac25$) ends up rolling at $\tfrac57$ of its launch speed.

## The same answer from angular momentum

That $\mu_k$ dropped out is a hint that a conservation law is at work. Take angular momentum about a fixed point $P$ on the floor, on the line along which the ball touches it. The friction force acts *at* floor level along that line, so its lever arm about $P$ is zero. The normal force and the weight are vertical, equal in size and act along the same vertical line through the center, so their torques about $P$ cancel. The net torque about $P$ is zero, and angular momentum about $P$ is conserved.

The angular momentum of a rolling or sliding ball about $P$ has two parts: the center's motion, $Mv_{\text{cm}}R$ (the center is a height $R$ above the floor), plus the spin about the center, $I_{\text{cm}}\omega$. Initially there is no spin; finally $\omega = v_f/R$:

$$Mv_0R = Mv_fR + cMR^2\cdot\frac{v_f}{R} = (1 + c)Mv_fR \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_f = \frac{v_0}{1 + c}.$$

The same idea handles any starting spin $\omega_0$ (positive for forward spin, negative for backspin):

$$v_f = \frac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c}.$$

If backspin is strong enough that $cR|\omega_0| > v_0$, then $v_f$ is negative: the object stops and rolls back toward you.

### Example 1: a bowling ball

A bowling ball (treat it as a uniform solid sphere, $c = \tfrac25$) of mass 7.0 kg and radius 0.11 m is released at 8.0 m/s with no spin. Take $\mu_k = 0.10$ (a value chosen for round numbers; real lanes are oiled unevenly, so friction varies along the lane). Find the time and distance it slides, its final speed, and the kinetic energy lost.

Time sliding: $t^* = \dfrac{0.4(8.0)}{1.4(0.10)(9.8)} = 2.33$ s.

Final speed: $v_f = 8.0/1.4 = 5.71$ m/s, with $\omega = v_f/R = 51.9$ rad/s.

Distance sliding: $d = v_0t^* - \tfrac12\mu_kg(t^*)^2 = 8.0(2.332) - \tfrac12(0.98)(2.332)^2 = 16.0$ m, most of a 18.3 m lane.

Energy: $K_i = \tfrac12(7.0)(8.0)^2 = 224$ J; $K_f = \tfrac12(1 + c)Mv_f^2 = \tfrac12(1.4)(7.0)(5.714)^2 = 160$ J. So 64 J, exactly $\tfrac{c}{1 + c} = \tfrac27$ of the start, is turned into heat by kinetic friction.

```plot
{"x": [0, 3.5], "y": [0, 9], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "speed (m/s)", "functions": [{"f": "8 - 0.98*x", "from": 0, "to": 2.332}, {"f": "2.45*x", "from": 0, "to": 2.332}, {"f": "5.714", "from": 2.332, "to": 3.5, "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [0.8, 7.9], "text": "v"}, {"at": [1.2, 1.9], "text": "Rω"}], "points": [{"at": [2.332, 5.714], "label": "rolling begins"}], "caption": "Example 1: the center slows and the spin speeds up until v = Rω at 2.33 s"}
```

The lost fraction is general. With no initial spin, $K_f/K_i = \dfrac{(1 + c)v_f^2}{v_0^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 + c}$, so the fraction lost is $\dfrac{c}{1 + c}$, again independent of $\mu_k$: a hoop launched without spin loses half its kinetic energy before it rolls.

### Example 2: a hoop thrown with backspin

A child rolls a hoop of radius 0.40 m along a level path at 3.0 m/s, flicking it so it has 12 rad/s of backspin. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.30. What does the hoop do?

Slip velocity at the start: $v - R\omega = 3.0 - 0.40(-12) = 7.8$ m/s forward, so friction points backward the whole time. Angular momentum about a floor point ($c = 1$):

$$v_f = \frac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c} = \frac{3.0 + 0.40(-12)}{2} = -0.90\text{ m/s}.$$

The hoop ends up rolling *backward* at 0.90 m/s. Timing: friction decelerates the center at $\mu_kg = 2.94$ m/s², so the center stops after $3.0/2.94 = 1.02$ s, 1.53 m out, and the rolling condition is reached at $t^* = \dfrac{c(v_0 - R\omega_0)}{(1 + c)\mu_kg} = \dfrac{7.8}{2(2.94)} = 1.33$ s, by which time the hoop has come back to 1.39 m. Check: $v(1.33) = 3.0 - 2.94(1.327) = -0.90$ m/s ✓.

## Where to hit: the center of percussion

Now reverse the question. Instead of letting friction sort out the motion, can we strike an object so it starts out in exactly the motion we want? A short, hard blow delivers an impulse $J$ that changes both momentum and angular momentum:

$$\Delta(Mv_{\text{cm}}) = J, \qquad \Delta(I_{\text{cm}}\omega) = Jh,$$

where $h$ is the perpendicular distance from the center of mass to the line of the blow.

*A cue ball.* Strike a ball of radius $R$ horizontally at a height $b$ above the table, so $h = b - R$. Then $v = J/M$ and $\omega = J(b - R)/(cMR^2)$. It rolls immediately, with no sliding phase at all, if $v = R\omega$:

$$\frac{J}{M} = \frac{J(b - R)}{cMR} \quad\Rightarrow\quad b = (1 + c)R.$$

For a solid ball, $b = 1.4R$, that is $\tfrac25R$ above the center. Hit higher and the ball starts with extra topspin; hit lower and friction must spin it up, as in Example 1.

*A bat or a hammer swung about a pivot.* Hold a rigid object at a pivot $P$ a distance $d$ from its center of mass, and let a ball strike it a distance $b$ from $P$. In general the pivot (your hands) must also supply an impulse $J_P$, which is the sting you feel. Linear impulse: $J + J_P = Mv_{\text{cm}} = M\omega d$. Angular impulse about $P$ (where $J_P$ has no lever arm): $Jb = I_P\omega$. Setting $J_P = 0$ and dividing,

$$b = \frac{I_P}{Md}.$$

That point is the center of percussion relative to $P$. Strike there and the object starts rotating about $P$ on its own, so the hands feel no jolt.

![A uniform rod pivoted at its top end. The center of mass is at the middle and the center of percussion two thirds of the way down from the pivot. A ball strikes the rod at the center of percussion.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 3: a rod held at one end

Find the center of percussion of a uniform rod of length 0.90 m held at one end.

$I_P = \tfrac13ML^2$ and $d = L/2$, so

$$b = \frac{\tfrac13ML^2}{M(L/2)} = \frac23L = 0.60\text{ m from the hand}.$$

It is below the center of mass, never at it: a blow at the center of mass would push the whole rod sideways, and the hand would have to hold back the handle end. The cue-ball result is the same idea, with the contact point with the table as the pivot: $I_P = cMR^2 + MR^2 = (1 + c)MR^2$ and $d = R$ give $b = (1 + c)R$.

*Simplified model.* A real baseball or cricket bat is not a uniform rod and is not perfectly rigid. Its "sweet spot" is a small region set by both the center of percussion and the bat's vibration modes (where the blow excites the least vibration). The rigid-body result explains the jolt to the hands; the sting from vibration is a separate effect.

## Common mistakes

- Assuming $v = R\omega$ from the start when an object is launched sliding, or "spinning up" with no friction.
- Getting the direction of kinetic friction from the direction of motion instead of from the slip velocity $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$.
- Taking angular momentum about the center of mass and expecting it to be conserved: friction has a lever arm $R$ about the center. Use a point on the floor.
- Forgetting the $MvR$ part of the angular momentum about the floor point.
- Placing the center of percussion at the center of mass.

## Key points

- Slip velocity $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$; kinetic friction opposes it until rolling begins.
- Launched with no spin: $t^* = \dfrac{cv_0}{(1 + c)\mu_kg}$, $v_f = \dfrac{v_0}{1 + c}$, and a fraction $\dfrac{c}{1 + c}$ of the kinetic energy is lost.
- Angular momentum about a point on the floor is conserved during skidding: $v_f = \dfrac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c}$.
- Center of percussion: $b = \dfrac{I_P}{Md}$ from the pivot; $\tfrac23L$ for a uniform rod held at an end; $1.4R$ above the table for a solid ball.

lessons.title: Gyroscopes, precession and unbalanced spin
lessons.body:
## When torque turns the axis instead of tipping it

The rolling lesson ended with the vector law $\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$ and a two-sentence account of why a spinning top doesn't fall over. This lesson takes that sentence seriously. Everything here follows from one fact: a torque changes angular momentum in the *direction of the torque*, and when the torque is perpendicular to $\vec L$, that change swings $\vec L$ around without making it any longer or shorter. We will derive the precession rate, see where the simple formula stops working, meet Earth's own 26,000-year precession, and then look at the other surprise of three-dimensional rotation: a body can spin about a fixed axle while its angular momentum points somewhere else.

## Deriving the precession rate

Take a gyroscope: a disk of moment of inertia $I$ spinning fast at $\omega$ on a light axle. One end of the axle rests on a pivot, the axle is horizontal, and the disk's center of mass is a distance $r$ from the pivot. Its spin angular momentum $L = I\omega$ points along the axle (right-hand rule).

Gravity acts at the center of mass. About the pivot its torque has size $\tau = Mgr$ and, by $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$, points horizontally, perpendicular to the axle. In a short time $dt$ the angular momentum changes by $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$, a small sideways vector added to the tip of $\vec L$. The new $\vec L$ has the same length to first order but points in a slightly different horizontal direction, turned by the angle

$$d\phi = \frac{|d\vec L|}{L} = \frac{\tau\,dt}{L}.$$

The axle therefore swings around the vertical at the **[[precession]]** rate

$$\Omega = \frac{d\phi}{dt} = \frac{\tau}{L} = \frac{Mgr}{I\omega}.$$

![A gyroscope with its axle horizontal on a pivot. The spin angular momentum L points along the axle away from the pivot, the weight Mg acts down at the disk's center, the torque about the pivot points horizontally at right angles to the axle, and a curved arrow shows the axle precessing around the vertical.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If the axle is tilted at angle $\theta$ from the vertical instead of horizontal, the torque becomes $Mgr\sin\theta$ but only the horizontal part of $\vec L$, $L\sin\theta$, swings around, so the rate is the same: $\Omega = Mgr/(I\omega)$, independent of the tilt.

The direction follows from the right-hand rule. With the axle along $+x$ from a pivot at the origin and $\vec L$ along $+x$, gravity at $(r, 0, 0)$ gives $\vec\tau = r\hat\imath\times(-Mg\hat k) = +Mgr\,\hat\jmath$. The tip of $\vec L$ moves toward $+y$: the axle precesses counterclockwise as seen from above. Reverse the spin and the precession reverses.

### Example 1: a toy gyroscope

A toy gyroscope's rotor is a 0.15 kg uniform disk of radius 3.5 cm spinning at 3000 rpm. Its center is 4.0 cm from the pivot. Find the precession rate and period.

$I = \tfrac12(0.15)(0.035)^2 = 9.19\times10^{-5}$ kg·m². $\omega = 3000(2\pi/60) = 314$ rad/s, so $L = I\omega = 0.0289$ kg·m²/s.

$\tau = Mgr = 0.15(9.8)(0.040) = 0.0588$ N·m.

$\Omega = \tau/L = 0.0588/0.0289 = 2.04$ rad/s, a precession period of $2\pi/\Omega = 3.1$ s. As the rotor slows from friction, $L$ drops and the precession speeds up, which is the familiar sign of a toy top about to fall.

## Where the simple formula comes from (and when it fails)

The derivation treated $\vec L$ as pure spin, $I\omega$ along the axle. But a precessing gyroscope also turns slowly about the vertical, and that motion has angular momentum too. The formula is the **[[gyroscopic approximation]]**: it is accurate when the spin is much faster than the precession, $\omega \gg \Omega$. In Example 1, $\omega/\Omega \approx 150$, comfortably in that regime.

The approximation also hides how the precession starts. Release the gyroscope with its axle held still and it cannot instantly be precessing. At first it does begin to fall; the falling motion makes $\vec L$ start to swing; and the axle settles into precession while bobbing slightly up and down around the steady path. That bobbing is **[[nutation]]**. For a fast rotor the bobs are small and quick, and friction at the pivot soon damps them out. This picture is qualitative: the full motion of a top needs the equations of rigid-body dynamics, beyond this course.

Energy is consistent with this. Steady precession has a little extra kinetic energy (the slow turning about the vertical), and it comes from the small dip of the center of mass during the first moments after release.

## Earth is a gyroscope too

Earth spins once a day about an axis tilted $23.4^\circ$ from the perpendicular to its orbit, and its spin makes it bulge at the equator. The Sun and the Moon pull harder on the half of the bulge nearer to them, which produces a torque trying to line the equator up with the orbital plane. Exactly as with the top, the torque doesn't tip the axis; it makes it precess. Earth's axis sweeps out a cone about once every 26,000 years (about 25,800 years), a motion called **[[axial precession]]** or the precession of the equinoxes. The Greek astronomer Hipparchus discovered it around 130 BCE by comparing his star positions with older records.

Its effects are visible on human timescales. Polaris is close to the north celestial pole today but was not in ancient times, and roughly 12,000 years from now the pole will lie near the bright star Vega. The equinoxes also drift slowly westward against the stars, so the year of the seasons (equinox to equinox, the year our calendar follows) is about 20 minutes shorter than the time Earth takes to go once around the Sun measured against the stars.

## Angular momentum need not point along the axle

For a body spinning about a symmetry axis, $\vec L = I\vec\omega$ points along the axle. That is not true in general. Consider a light rod through its center on a vertical axle, with a small mass $m$ at each end, a distance $a$ from the center, but mounted crooked: the rod makes an angle $\beta$ with the axle instead of $90^\circ$.

![A vertical axle turning at angular velocity omega with a crooked dumbbell mounted on it: a rod through the axle's midpoint at angle beta to the axle, with a mass at each end. The angular momentum L points perpendicular to the rod, not along the axle, and so sweeps around a cone as the dumbbell turns.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Each mass moves in a circle of radius $a\sin\beta$ at speed $\omega a\sin\beta$. Its angular momentum about the center, $\vec r\times m\vec v$, has size $ma(\omega a\sin\beta)$ and points perpendicular to the rod, in the plane of the rod and the axle. Both masses give the same vector, so

$$L = 2ma^2\omega\sin\beta, \quad\text{perpendicular to the rod.}$$

Its component along the axle is $L\sin\beta = (2ma^2\sin^2\beta)\,\omega = I_{\text{axle}}\,\omega$, as expected. But it also has a sideways component $L_\perp = 2ma^2\omega\sin\beta\cos\beta$ that turns with the rod. A vector of fixed length $L_\perp$ rotating at rate $\omega$ changes at the rate $\omega L_\perp$, so the bearings must supply a torque

$$\tau = \omega L_\perp = 2ma^2\omega^2\sin\beta\cos\beta,$$

whose direction rotates with the shaft. It vanishes only for $\beta = 90^\circ$ (or $0$).

### Example 2: a crooked rotor

The masses are 0.10 kg each, $a = 0.15$ m, the rod is $10^\circ$ off perpendicular ($\beta = 80^\circ$) and the shaft turns at 50 rad/s. The bearings are 0.20 m apart. Find the torque they must supply and the force on each.

$L_\perp = 2(0.10)(0.15)^2(50)\sin 80^\circ\cos 80^\circ = 0.0385$ kg·m²/s.

$\tau = \omega L_\perp = 50(0.0385) = 1.92$ N·m. Two bearings 0.20 m apart supply it as a couple: $F = 1.92/0.20 = 9.6$ N each, in opposite directions, rotating with the shaft 8 times a second. That is a vibration, even though the center of mass sits exactly on the axle.

For every rigid body there are three perpendicular axes through the center of mass, its **[[principal axes]]**, about which $\vec L$ is parallel to $\vec\omega$; symmetry axes are always principal axes. A car tire is balanced in two senses: static balance puts the center of mass on the axle, and dynamic balance puts a principal axis along the axle. Spinning a tire on a balancing machine detects the rotating torque of Example 2, and small weights clipped to the rim cancel it.

### Example 3: flipping a spinning wheel

A student sits on a stool that turns freely; student and stool have $I = 3.0$ kg·m². She holds a bicycle wheel ($I_w = 0.12$ kg·m²) spinning at 20 rad/s with its axle vertical, angular momentum up. She turns the wheel upside down. What happens?

There is no external torque about the vertical axis, so vertical angular momentum is conserved. Before: $L = 0.12(20) = 2.4$ kg·m²/s up. After, the wheel contributes $2.4$ down, so student and stool must carry $4.8$ up:

$$\omega_{\text{student}} = \frac{4.8}{3.0} = 1.6\text{ rad/s}$$

in the wheel's original sense of rotation. Her hands exerted the torque that flipped the wheel; the wheel exerted the opposite torque on her.

## Gyroscopes at work, and one popular myth

Gyroscopes keep their direction in space unless a torque acts, which makes them useful for sensing and controlling orientation. Ships use gyrocompasses; the International Space Station turns itself using large spinning wheels called control moment gyroscopes, tilting them so the station gets the opposite change in angular momentum, without burning fuel.

A popular claim is that a bicycle stays up because its wheels are gyroscopes. That is *contested and mostly wrong as stated*. The wheels' spin does contribute to steering a moving bicycle, but in 2011 Kooijman and coworkers built a riderless bicycle with the wheels' spin angular momentum canceled by counter-rotating wheels, and it was still self-stable. Stability comes from several interacting design features, such as the steering geometry and how mass is placed on the front assembly.

## Common mistakes

- Expecting a torque to tip a spinning gyroscope in the direction of the force. The axle moves in the direction of the torque vector, at right angles to the force.
- Thinking a faster spin makes precession faster. $\Omega = \tau/(I\omega)$: faster spin, slower precession.
- Assuming $\vec L$ always points along the rotation axis. It does for symmetric bodies spinning about a symmetry axis, not in general.
- Using $\Omega = \tau/L$ when the spin is slow; it is the gyroscopic approximation and needs $\omega \gg \Omega$.

## Key points

- A torque perpendicular to $\vec L$ turns $\vec L$: precession at $\Omega = \tau/L = Mgr/(I\omega)$, independent of tilt.
- Direction: $d\vec L$ is along $\vec\tau$; reversing the spin reverses the precession.
- Release from rest gives nutation around steady precession; the simple formula needs $\omega \gg \Omega$.
- Earth's axis precesses in about 26,000 years because the Sun and Moon pull on its equatorial bulge.
- A crooked rotor has $\vec L$ off the axle; the bearings must supply $\tau = \omega L_\perp$, which rotates with the shaft. Principal axes have $\vec L \parallel \vec\omega$.

lessons.title: The shell theorem, gravity inside a planet, and tides
lessons.body:
## Gravity from bodies that aren't points

The gravitation lesson used $F = GMm/r^2$ for planets as if each were a point at its center, and stated without proof that a spherical shell exerts no force on anything inside it. This lesson proves those statements, uses them to find gravity inside a planet (and how long a fall through a tunnel to the far side would take), and then looks at what happens when the size of a body *does* matter: the stretching that raises the ocean tides, slows Earth's spin, and can tear a moon apart.

## Gravitational potential

Forces from many pieces of mass add as vectors, which is awkward. Potential energies add as plain numbers, which is easy. So work with the **[[gravitational potential]]** $V$, the potential energy per unit mass of a test particle:

$$V = \frac{U}{m}, \qquad V = -\frac{GM}{r}\text{ for a point mass } M.$$

The gravitational field (the acceleration $g$ a test particle feels) follows from $V$ exactly as force follows from potential energy: its component along $r$ is $g_r = -dV/dr$.

## Proving the shell theorem

Take a thin uniform spherical shell of mass $M$ and radius $R$, and a point $P$ a distance $r$ from its center. Slice the shell into rings centered on the line from the center to $P$. The ring at polar angle $\theta$ has radius $R\sin\theta$ and width $R\,d\theta$; its share of the shell's area $4\pi R^2$ is $2\pi R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta$, so its mass is

$$dM = \frac{M}{2}\sin\theta\,d\theta.$$

Every bit of that ring is the same distance $s$ from $P$, with $s^2 = r^2 + R^2 - 2rR\cos\theta$ by the law of cosines.

![A circle representing a spherical shell of radius R with center O. A point P lies outside on a horizontal line through O at distance r. A thin ring on the shell at polar angle theta from the line OP is drawn as a vertical chord, and the distance s from P to the ring is marked.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Differentiating at fixed $r$ and $R$: $2s\,ds = 2rR\sin\theta\,d\theta$, so $\sin\theta\,d\theta = \dfrac{s\,ds}{rR}$. The ring's contribution to the potential at $P$ is

$$dV = -\frac{G\,dM}{s} = -\frac{GM}{2s}\cdot\frac{s\,ds}{rR} = -\frac{GM}{2rR}\,ds.$$

The $s$ cancels, so the integral is just the range of $s$ times a constant.

- *$P$ outside* ($r > R$): $s$ runs from $r - R$ to $r + R$, a range of $2R$. So $V = -\dfrac{GM}{2rR}(2R) = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$, exactly the potential of a point mass at the center.
- *$P$ inside* ($r < R$): $s$ runs from $R - r$ to $R + r$, a range of $2r$. So $V = -\dfrac{GM}{2rR}(2r) = -\dfrac{GM}{R}$, the same everywhere inside. A constant potential has zero slope, so $g = 0$: no net force anywhere inside the shell.

That is the **[[shell theorem]]**. A solid sphere whose density depends only on $r$ is a set of nested shells, so outside it acts like a point mass. Newton proved the result geometrically in the *Principia* (1687), and it was the step that justified treating planets as points.

## Gravity inside a planet

At a distance $r$ from the center of a planet, the shells outside $r$ exert no net force, and the mass inside $r$ acts as if it were at the center: $g(r) = GM(r)/r^2$. For a uniform planet $M(r) = M r^3/R^3$, so

$$g(r) = \frac{GM}{R^3}\,r = g_s\frac{r}{R} \quad (r \le R),$$

rising linearly from zero at the center to the surface value $g_s$, then falling off as $1/r^2$ outside.

```plot
{"x": [0, 3], "y": [0, 1.15], "xLabel": "r / R", "yLabel": "g / g_s", "functions": [{"f": "x", "from": 0, "to": 1}, {"f": "1/x^2", "from": 1, "to": 3}], "labels": [{"at": [0.45, 0.9], "text": "inside: g ∝ r"}, {"at": [2.1, 0.45], "text": "outside: g ∝ 1/r²"}], "points": [{"at": [1, 1], "label": "surface"}], "caption": "Gravity of a uniform planet: linear inside, inverse-square outside"}
```

*Simplified model.* Earth is not uniform: its iron core is much denser than its rocky mantle. Going down, you leave relatively light rock above you while staying close to the dense core, so real $g$ actually *increases* with depth through the mantle, to about 10.7 m/s² near the boundary between the mantle and the outer core (roughly 2,900 km down), before falling to zero at the center.

### Example 1: falling through the Earth

Imagine a straight tunnel through the center of a uniform Earth, with no air and no friction (and ignoring Earth's rotation). A ball is dropped in at the surface. Describe its motion.

At position $x$ from the center (positive on one side, negative on the other), the acceleration points toward the center with size $g_sx/R$:

$$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -\frac{g_s}{R}\,x.$$

This is the equation of simple harmonic motion, met again in the oscillations module. You can check that $x = R\cos(\omega t)$ solves it: two derivatives give $-\omega^2R\cos(\omega t) = -\omega^2x$, which matches if $\omega = \sqrt{g_s/R}$. The ball oscillates from one end of the tunnel to the other with period

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R}{g_s}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{6.37\times10^6}{9.8}} = 5.07\times10^3\text{ s} = 84.4\text{ min}.$$

The trip to the far side takes half of that, 42 minutes, and the ball passes the center at $\omega R = \sqrt{g_sR} = 7.9$ km/s. Those numbers are no coincidence: 84 minutes is the period of an orbit skimming the surface, and 7.9 km/s its speed, because $\sqrt{GM/R} = \sqrt{g_sR}$. (Any straight frictionless tunnel between two surface points, not just one through the center, takes the same 42 minutes.)

## Tidal forces

Now let size matter. The Moon pulls on every part of Earth, but not equally: the near side is closer, so it is pulled harder than Earth's center, and the far side less hard. Earth as a whole falls toward the Moon (more precisely, Earth and Moon orbit their common center of mass) with the acceleration of its center. What remains, the *difference* between the pull at a point and the pull at the center, is the **[[tidal force]]**.

Along the Earth–Moon line, a point a distance $d$ closer to the Moon than Earth's center feels an extra acceleration toward the Moon. With $a(D) = GM/D^2$ at distance $D$,

$$\Delta a \approx -\frac{da}{dD}\,d = \frac{2GM}{D^3}\,d.$$

The far side, at $D + d$, is pulled less than the center, so relative to the center it is pushed *away* from the Moon by the same amount. Points at right angles to the line are pulled slightly toward Earth's center, by $GMd/D^3$, because the Moon's pull there slants inward. The ocean is stretched into two bulges, one facing the Moon and one facing away, and squeezed around the middle.

![Earth with the Moon far to the right. Small arrows show the tidal acceleration at points around Earth: outward toward the Moon on the near side, outward away from the Moon on the far side, and inward at the top and bottom. A dashed oval shows the ocean stretched into two bulges along the Earth-Moon line.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

As Earth turns under the bulges, a coast passes through two high tides and two low tides in a little over a day (24 h 50 min, because the Moon moves along its orbit in the meantime), so high tides come about every 12 h 25 min.

*Simplified model.* This "equilibrium tide" explains why there are two bulges and roughly two tides a day. Real tides also depend on the shapes and resonances of ocean basins: tidal ranges vary from almost nothing in parts of the Mediterranean to more than 15 m in Canada's Bay of Fundy, and high tide is generally not when the Moon is overhead.

### Example 2: the Moon versus the Sun

Compare the tidal accelerations at Earth's surface from the Moon ($M = 7.35\times10^{22}$ kg, $D = 3.84\times10^8$ m) and the Sun ($M = 1.99\times10^{30}$ kg, $D = 1.496\times10^{11}$ m), with $d = R_E = 6.37\times10^6$ m.

Moon: $\dfrac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(7.35\times10^{22})(6.37\times10^6)}{(3.84\times10^8)^3} = 1.10\times10^{-6}$ m/s².

Sun: $\dfrac{2(6.67\times10^{-11})(1.99\times10^{30})(6.37\times10^6)}{(1.496\times10^{11})^3} = 5.05\times10^{-7}$ m/s².

The Sun's *direct* pull on Earth ($GM/D^2 = 5.9\times10^{-3}$ m/s²) is about 180 times the Moon's, yet its tidal effect is only 0.46 times as large, because tides go as $1/D^3$, not $1/D^2$. When Sun, Earth and Moon line up (new and full moon), the effects add: **[[spring tides]]**, with tidal acceleration $1.6\times10^{-6}$ m/s². At first and third quarter they act at right angles and partly cancel: **[[neap tides]]**, about $0.6\times10^{-6}$ m/s². (Check: the exact difference between the Moon's pull at the near side and at the center is $1.13\times10^{-6}$ m/s², within 3% of the approximation.)

## Tidal friction and tidal locking

Earth spins faster (once a day) than the Moon orbits (once a month), and friction drags the tidal bulges slightly ahead of the Earth–Moon line. The Moon's pull on the leading bulge exerts a torque that slows Earth's spin, so the day very slowly lengthens. Angular momentum is conserved for the Earth–Moon system, so what Earth's spin loses, the Moon's orbit gains: the Moon spirals outward.
