questions.stem: A rope makes one full turn around a post ($\mu_s = 0.25$). Holding the free end with 200 N, what is the largest load tension you can resist?
questions.explanation: One turn is $\theta = 2\pi$ rad, so $T_{\text{load}} = 200e^{0.25(2\pi)} = 200e^{1.571} = 200(4.81) = 962$ N. 257 N uses $\theta = 1$ (turns, not radians); 514 N uses $1 + \mu\theta$ instead of $e^{\mu\theta}$; 41.6 N puts the larger tension on the holding side.

questions.stem: In the ideal capstan model, a rope is moved from a thin pole to a bollard with twice the radius, with the same wrap angle and $\mu$. The ratio $T_{\text{load}}/T_{\text{hold}}$
questions.explanation: $T_{\text{load}}/T_{\text{hold}} = e^{\mu\theta}$ has no radius in it. A bigger post spreads the same total normal force over a longer contact, but the derivation only involves angles: $dn = T\,d\theta$ and $dT = \mu T\,d\theta$. (Real ropes, which are stiff, deviate somewhat from this ideal.)

questions.stem: The angle whose tangent equals the coefficient of friction, $\tan\theta = \mu$, is called the angle of ___.
questions.explanation: It is the angle of friction. It is both the best angle to pull a crate and the steepest incline on which an object can rest ($\tan\theta_{\max} = \mu_s$).

questions.stem: A rope wraps one and a half turns around a post. Its wrap angle is ___ radians (3 significant figures).
questions.explanation: Each full turn is $2\pi$ rad, so 1.5 turns is $3\pi = 9.42$ rad. The capstan equation needs the angle in radians.

questions.stem: A block rides on a board that is pulled across a frictionless floor, and the two move together with acceleration $a$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The friction on the block points in the direction of the acceleration
The friction on the block equals $m_{\text{block}}a$
The friction on the block must equal $\mu_s n$
The friction between block and board is an external force on the block-and-board system
questions.explanation: Friction is the only horizontal force on the block, so it points along the acceleration and equals $m_{\text{block}}a$ by the second law. It reaches $\mu_s n$ only on the verge of slipping. The friction pair acts between the two blocks, so it is internal to the two-block system and cancels when you treat them as one.

questions.stem: A rope is wrapped half a turn around a post and is on the verge of slipping toward the load. Name each numbered part.

image.alt: A rope wrapped half a turn around a round post seen from above. Both ends leave to the left, the upper one pulled by a short arrow and the lower one by a long arrow. On a short marked piece of rope at the lower right, one arrow points away from the post and one along the rope toward the top. A dashed curved arrow inside the post spans the wrapped part. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The load end carries the larger tension (2, the long arrow) and the holding end the smaller (1); $T_{\text{load}} = T_{\text{hold}}e^{\mu\theta}$. On the small piece of rope, the post pushes outward (3, the normal force), and friction acts along the rope toward the holding end (4), opposing the rope's tendency to slip toward the load. The dashed arc (5) is the wrap angle. The model treats the rope as massless, so no weight is drawn.

questions.stem: Put the steps for a stacked-block problem (force applied to the bottom block) in order.
choices: Find the common acceleration from the whole system
Find the friction the top block needs, $m_{\text{top}}a$
If it is larger, redo the problem with kinetic friction and separate accelerations
questions.explanation: Each step needs the one before it: the common acceleration only makes sense once you assume they move together; the needed friction uses that acceleration; the comparison with $\mu_s n$ tests the assumption; and only a failed test sends you to the slipping case.

questions.stem: An 800 kg boat coasting at 8.0 m/s feels water drag $cv^2$ with $c = 40$ kg/m and no other horizontal force. How long does it take to slow to 4.0 m/s?
questions.explanation: $v = \dfrac{v_0}{1 + cv_0t/m}$ halves when $cv_0t/m = 1$, so $t = \dfrac{m}{cv_0} = \dfrac{800}{40(8.0)} = 2.5$ s. 1.7 s multiplies by $\ln 2$, treating the decay as exponential in time; 20 s is $m/c$, which has units of meters, not seconds; 0.40 s inverts the fraction.

questions.stem: The same 800 kg boat ($c = 40$ kg/m) coasts from 8.0 m/s. How far does it travel before its speed drops to 2.0 m/s?
questions.explanation: With $v\,dv/dx = -(c/m)v^2$, the speed decays exponentially with distance: $v = v_0e^{-cx/m}$. Slowing to a quarter needs $e^{-cx/m} = \tfrac14$, so $x = \dfrac{m}{c}\ln 4 = 20(1.386) = 27.7$ m. 13.9 m is only one halving (to 4.0 m/s); 41.6 m is three halvings (to 1.0 m/s); 60.0 m uses $(m/c)(v_0/v - 1)$, which is the time formula's form, not the distance's.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg ball falls with quadratic drag $F_D = cv^2$, $c = 0.0050$ kg/m. What is its terminal speed? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: At terminal speed $cv_T^2 = mg$, so $v_T = \sqrt{mg/c} = \sqrt{0.50(9.8)/0.0050} = \sqrt{980} = 31.3$ m/s. 980 forgets the square root; 10.0 m/s leaves out $g$; 0.032 m/s inverts the fraction.

questions.stem: Two balls have the same size and shape, but one has 4 times the mass. With quadratic drag, the heavier ball's terminal speed is
questions.explanation: $v_T = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$ with the same $C$ and $A$, so $v_T \propto \sqrt m$: 4 times the mass gives $\sqrt4 = 2$ times the terminal speed. (With linear drag, $v_T = mg/b$ would be 4 times as large.)

questions.stem: An object falls from rest with quadratic drag. What fraction of its terminal speed does it have at $t = v_T/g$?
questions.explanation: $v = v_T\tanh(gt/v_T)$, so at $t = v_T/g$, $v = v_T\tanh 1 = 0.76v_T$. 63% is the value for linear drag after one time constant ($1 - e^{-1}$). The speed approaches $v_T$ but never quite reaches it.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up and caught at the same height. With air drag, how do the times for the trip up and the trip down compare?
choices: It depends on whether drag is linear or quadratic
questions.explanation: On the way up, drag and gravity both slow the ball, so it stops quickly. On the way down, drag opposes gravity, so the ball gains speed slowly and is moving slower at each height than it was going up. Covering the same distance more slowly takes longer. This holds for any drag that opposes the velocity, linear or quadratic.

questions.stem: A ball with terminal speed 25 m/s is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. With quadratic drag, how high does it rise? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $h = \dfrac{v_T^2}{2g}\ln\!\left(1 + \dfrac{v_0^2}{v_T^2}\right) = \dfrac{625}{19.6}\ln(1.64) = 31.9(0.495) = 15.8$ m. 20.4 m is the no-drag height $v_0^2/2g$; 18.7 m uses $\ln(1 + v_0/v_T)$ without squaring; 6.85 m uses $\log_{10}$ instead of the natural log.

questions.stem: A boat coasting with quadratic drag (and no other horizontal force) slows from 12 m/s to 6.0 m/s in its first 15 m. Its speed after 45 m is ___ m/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: With quadratic drag, $v = v_0e^{-cx/m}$: the speed halves over each equal distance. 45 m is three halvings: $12 \to 6.0 \to 3.0 \to 1.5$ m/s. (Each halving takes twice as long as the one before, so equal distances are not equal times.)

questions.stem: A skydiver's terminal speed is 50 m/s. Her characteristic time $\tau = v_T/g$ is ___ s (3 significant figures, $g = 9.8$ m/s²).
questions.explanation: $\tau = 50/9.8 = 5.10$ s: the time free fall would take to reach 50 m/s. With quadratic drag she has $\tanh 1 = 76\%$ of her terminal speed after one $\tau$.

questions.stem: Match each object to the drag law that describes it best.
left: A 10 μm cloud droplet falling in air
questions.explanation: Tiny, slow objects have Reynolds numbers far below 1 (roughly 0.002 to 0.02 for the droplet, depending on whether 10 μm is its diameter or its radius), so viscosity dominates and drag is linear. A baseball or a skydiver moves fast enough, and is big enough, for $Re$ in the tens of thousands or more, where drag grows as $v^2$.

questions.stem: An object falls from rest with quadratic drag. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: For a fixed size and shape, $v_T$ is proportional to $\sqrt m$
Its acceleration decreases as it speeds up
Its terminal speed doesn't depend on the air's density
questions.explanation: At low speed the drag $cv^2$ is tiny, so the object starts in near free fall. $v_T = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$ grows as $\sqrt m$ and falls with air density $\rho$. As speed rises, drag grows and the net force, and so the acceleration, shrinks toward zero. The speed only approaches $v_T$; at $t = v_T/g$ it is 76% of it.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown straight up and falls back, with air drag. Put these moments in time order.
choices: Just after release, it slows at more than $g$
At the top, it is momentarily at rest and its acceleration is exactly $g$
Falling, it speeds up at less than $g$
It returns to the launch height moving slower than it was thrown
questions.explanation: Going up, drag adds to gravity, so the deceleration exceeds $g$. At the top, $v = 0$ means zero drag, so only gravity acts. Coming down, drag opposes gravity, so the acceleration is less than $g$. Drag has removed energy throughout, so the ball returns slower than it left.

questions.stem: A ball with terminal speed 25 m/s is thrown straight up at 20 m/s and falls back. With quadratic drag, how fast is it moving when it returns to the launch height?
questions.explanation: The return speed is $v = \dfrac{v_0v_T}{\sqrt{v_0^2 + v_T^2}} = \dfrac{20(25)}{\sqrt{1025}} = 15.6$ m/s. 20.0 m/s ignores the energy lost to drag; 11.1 m/s uses $v_0v_T/(v_0 + v_T)$, dropping the squares and root; 25.0 m/s is the terminal speed, which a ball falling from only 15.8 m can't reach.

questions.stem: A car accelerates forward at 4.0 m/s². At what angle from vertical does a fuzzy die hang from the mirror (once it stops swinging)? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: The string lines up with $\vec g_{\text{eff}} = \vec g - \vec A$: $\tan\theta = A/g = 4.0/9.8$, so $\theta = 22.2^\circ$, tilted toward the rear. 24.1° uses $\sin\theta = A/g$; 67.8° inverts the ratio (that's the angle from horizontal); 0° forgets that the die must accelerate with the car.

questions.stem: An elevator accelerates downward at 2.0 m/s². What is the effective gravity inside it? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $\vec g_{\text{eff}} = \vec g - \vec A$. Both point down, so $g_{\text{eff}} = 9.8 - 2.0 = 7.8$ m/s²: objects inside feel lighter. 11.8 m/s² would be for upward acceleration; 9.8 m/s² ignores the elevator's acceleration; 2.0 m/s² is the acceleration itself.

questions.stem: A car brakes hard while moving forward. In the car's frame, the fictitious force on a passenger points
questions.explanation: Braking means the car's acceleration $\vec A$ points backward, and the fictitious force $-m\vec A$ points opposite to it: forward. That is the "push" that seems to throw passengers toward the windshield; from the ground, they simply keep moving while the car slows.

questions.stem: Which of these forces has no Newton's third-law partner?
choices: The centrifugal force on a rider, in the merry-go-round's frame
The normal force of a floor on a box
The tension a rope exerts on a bucket
The friction a road exerts on a tire
questions.explanation: Fictitious forces such as the centrifugal force come from the frame's acceleration, not from another object, so there is nothing for them to act back on. The other three are real interactions: the box pushes the floor, the bucket pulls the rope, and the tire pushes the road.

questions.stem: A ring-shaped space station of radius 50 m spins to give 1.0 $g$ of artificial gravity at its rim. What is its rotation period? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $\omega^2 r = g$ gives $\omega = \sqrt{9.8/50} = 0.443$ rad/s, so $T = 2\pi/\omega = 14.2$ s. 0.443 is $\omega$ itself (in rad/s, not a period); 2.26 s is $1/\omega$, missing the $2\pi$; 32.1 s uses $\omega = g/r$ without the square root.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, a long-range projectile is fired due north. Which way does the Coriolis force deflect it?
questions.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects moving objects to the right of their velocity. For motion due north, right is east.

questions.stem: In a space station rotating at $\omega = 0.25$ rad/s, an astronaut runs at 3.0 m/s along the floor (perpendicular to the rotation axis). What is the size of her Coriolis acceleration?
questions.explanation: For motion perpendicular to the axis, the Coriolis acceleration is $2\omega v' = 2(0.25)(3.0) = 1.5$ m/s². 0.75 m/s² leaves out the factor 2; 3.0 m/s² uses $4\omega v'$; 0.19 m/s² is $\omega^2 v'$, which isn't an acceleration at all.

questions.stem: Forces such as $-m\vec A$ that appear only when you work in an accelerating frame, with no object exerting them, are called ___ forces.
questions.explanation: They are fictitious forces, also called inertial forces or pseudo-forces. They have no agent and no third-law partner.

questions.stem: Earth rotates at $\omega = 7.29 \times 10^{-5}$ rad/s and its equatorial radius is $6.38 \times 10^6$ m. The centrifugal acceleration at the equator is ___ m/s² (2 significant figures).
questions.explanation: $\omega^2R = (7.29\times10^{-5})^2(6.38\times10^6) = 0.034$ m/s², about 0.35% of $g$. It is part of why the measured free-fall acceleration is smaller at the equator than at the poles.

questions.stem: Each object is described in the frame named. Match it to the fictitious forces you must include.
left: A rider sitting still on a merry-go-round (merry-go-round frame)
A ball rolling across a merry-go-round (merry-go-round frame)
A passenger in a car speeding up in a straight line (car frame)
A ball thrown on a playground (ground frame treated as inertial)
choices: A force opposite the car's acceleration
questions.explanation: In a rotating frame every object gets the centrifugal force, and objects that move in that frame also get the Coriolis force. A frame accelerating in a straight line needs one fictitious force, $-m\vec A$. In an inertial frame there are no fictitious forces at all. (The ground is treated as inertial for everyday motions; Earth's rotation matters only for large or long ones.)

questions.stem: Which statements about the Coriolis force are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It is perpendicular to the object's velocity in the rotating frame
It does no work on the object
It acts on objects at rest in the rotating frame
It is proportional to the object's mass
It always points away from the rotation axis
questions.explanation: $-2m\vec\omega\times\vec v'$ is proportional to $m$ and perpendicular to $\vec v'$, so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed, doing no work. It is zero when $\vec v' = 0$. The force that always points away from the axis is the centrifugal force.

questions.stem: A pendulum hangs at rest inside a van that accelerates to the right. Viewed in the van's frame, name each numbered arrow.

image.alt: A van with a pendulum hanging from its ceiling, swung back to the left. Arrows from the bob: one up along the string, one straight down, a short dashed one to the left, and a dashed one down and to the left along the line of the string. An arrow above the van points right. Five arrows are numbered.

questions.explanation: The string pulls the bob along the string (1); gravity pulls it down (2). In the van's frame there is also the fictitious force $-m\vec A$, opposite the van's acceleration (3, left, because the van accelerates right, 5). Weight plus fictitious force is $m\vec g_{\text{eff}}$ (4), which lines up with the string, so the tension balances it and the bob hangs at rest. Nothing rotates, so there is no centrifugal force, and nothing touches the bob but the string.

questions.stem: A block sits on a frictionless $30^\circ$ wedge. What horizontal acceleration of the wedge keeps the block from sliding along it? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: In the wedge frame, the down-slope part of the weight must balance the up-slope part of the fictitious force: $mg\sin\theta = mA\cos\theta$, so $A = g\tan 30^\circ = 5.66$ m/s². 4.90 m/s² is $g\sin\theta$; 8.49 m/s² is $g\cos\theta$; 17.0 m/s² is $g/\tan\theta$.

questions.stem: A crate is dragged to the right across a rough floor by a rope. Name the numbered arrows.

image.alt: A crate on a floor with five numbered arrows: 1 points up and to the right from the crate at an angle, 2 points left along the floor, 3 points straight up, 4 points straight down, and 5 is a long arrow to the right below the floor.

questions.explanation: The rope pulls along its own direction, up and to the right (1). Kinetic friction opposes the sliding, so it points left along the floor (2). The floor pushes up (normal force, 3) and gravity pulls down (weight, 4). Arrow 5 is the displacement, to the right. The rope does positive work, friction negative work, and the normal force and weight do no work because they are perpendicular to the displacement.

questions.stem: A force $F(x) = 6x$ N ($x$ in m) acts on an object along the $x$ axis. The work it does as the object moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 2$ m is ___ J. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The force varies with position, so integrate: $W = \int_0^2 6x\,dx = \left[3x^2\right]_0^2 = 12$ J. That is the triangle under the $F$–$x$ line, $\tfrac12(2)(12) = 12$ J. Using $W = Fd$ with the final force, $12(2) = 24$ J, would double it.

questions.stem: Which forces do zero work on the object named? Select all that apply.
choices: The normal force on a block sliding across a level floor
The string tension on a ball whirled at constant speed in a horizontal circle
Kinetic friction on a box sliding to a stop
Gravity on a ball thrown straight up, while it rises
Your hands' upward force on a heavy bag you hold still
questions.explanation: Work is $Fd\cos\theta$. The normal force and the tension are perpendicular to the motion ($\cos 90^\circ = 0$), and the bag you hold still has no displacement, so all three do zero work. Friction on the sliding box points opposite the motion (negative work), and gravity on the rising ball points opposite its upward motion (negative work, which is why it slows).

questions.stem: Match each force to the sign of the work it does.
left: A rope pulling a sled forward along the snow
Friction on a hockey puck sliding across ice
The normal force on a car driving along a level road
Gravity on an apple falling from a tree
Gravity on a ball rising after it is thrown up
questions.explanation: The sign follows the angle between force and displacement. The rope and gravity on the falling apple point along the motion (positive). Friction on the puck and gravity on the rising ball point against the motion (negative). The normal force on the car is perpendicular to its motion (zero).

questions.stem: A force $F(x) = 3x^2 - 2x$ N acts along the $x$ axis. How much work does it do as an object moves from $x = 0$ to $x = 1$ m?
questions.explanation: $W = \int_0^1 (3x^2 - 2x)\,dx = \left[x^3 - x^2\right]_0^1 = 0$ J. The force is negative for $x < \tfrac23$ m and positive after, and the two areas cancel exactly. $-\tfrac{4}{27}$ J is only the negative part (from 0 to $\tfrac23$); 2 J comes from a sign slip ($x^3 + x^2$); 1 J multiplies the force at $x = 1$ by the distance, as if the force were constant.

questions.stem: The graph shows a potential energy curve $U(x)$ and a particle's total energy $E$ (dashed line). Name the numbered features.

image.alt: A double-well potential energy curve with a dashed horizontal total energy line. Marker 1 is at the bottom of the left well, 2 at the top of the central hump, 3 where the curve meets the dashed line on the right, 4 on a vertical arrow from the curve up to the dashed line, and 5 in a shaded region beyond the right crossing point.

questions.explanation: A minimum of $U$ is a stable equilibrium (1) and a maximum is unstable (2). Where the curve meets $E$ the kinetic energy is zero, so the particle stops and reverses: a turning point (3). The vertical gap from the curve up to $E$ is $K = E - U$ (4). Beyond a turning point $U > E$, which would need negative kinetic energy, so the particle can't be there (5).

questions.stem: An elevator motor lifts a car at constant speed. Put the steps for finding the electrical energy the motor draws during the trip in order.
choices: Find the cable tension: at constant speed it equals the weight $mg$
Multiply the tension by the speed to get the output power $P = Tv$
Divide the output power by the efficiency to get the input power
Multiply the input power by the travel time to get the energy drawn
questions.explanation: Each step uses the result of the one before: the tension gives the output power ($P = Tv$), the efficiency turns output power into input power ($P_{\text{in}} = P/\eta$), and power times time is energy.

questions.stem: A space heater uses 2.5 kWh of energy. That is ___ MJ. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $1\text{ kWh} = (1000\text{ W})(3600\text{ s}) = 3.6\times10^6$ J $= 3.6$ MJ, so $2.5(3.6) = 9.0$ MJ. A kilowatt-hour is an energy unit, not a power.

questions.stem: Which of these forces are conservative, so that a potential energy can describe them? Select all that apply.
choices: The force of an ideal spring
The push of a car's engine through its wheels
questions.explanation: Gravity and an ideal spring do work that depends only on the endpoints, so they have potential energies $mgy$ and $\tfrac12kx^2$. Kinetic friction and drag always oppose the motion, so a longer path does more negative work. An engine's push is a nonconservative force: it adds energy from fuel, and its work goes in $W_{\text{nc}}$.

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its SI unit or the unit a utility bills it in.
questions.explanation: Power is in watts (J/s); utilities bill energy in kilowatt-hours ($3.6\times10^6$ J each); work, like all energy, is in joules; a spring constant is force per stretch, N/m. The newton-second is the unit of impulse.

questions.stem: A person walks from one end of a raft to the other on still water. Name the numbered parts of the before-and-after picture.

image.alt: Two scenes, before and after. Before: a stick figure stands at the left end of a raft. After: the figure stands at the right end and the raft has shifted left. A dashed vertical line crosses both scenes; an arrow points left and another points right between the scenes. Five numbered markers.

choices: Center of mass of person and raft
Person's displacement relative to the water
questions.explanation: The person (1) stands on the raft (2). With no horizontal external force and everything starting at rest, the center of mass of person plus raft (3) cannot move, so the dashed line is the same in both scenes. As she walks right, the raft moves left (4), and her own displacement relative to the water (5) is less than the raft's length.

questions.stem: A force on a ball rises steadily from 0 to 600 N and falls steadily back to 0, a triangular pulse lasting 0.020 s in all. The impulse is ___ N·s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Impulse is the area under the force–time graph. For a triangle, $\tfrac12(0.020\text{ s})(600\text{ N}) = 6.0$ N·s. Using the peak force for the whole time would give 12 N·s, twice too much.

questions.stem: A ball rebounds from a bat. Put the steps for finding the average force on it in order.
choices: Write the initial and final velocities with their signs
Compute the change in momentum $m(v_f - v_i)$
Divide by the contact time to get the average force
questions.explanation: The signs of the velocities only make sense once a positive direction is chosen; the change in momentum needs those signed velocities (a rebound makes $v_f - v_i$ large); and the impulse–momentum theorem $F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta p$ then gives the force.

questions.stem: In which cases is the momentum of the named system conserved, at least approximately or along the stated direction? Select all that apply.
choices: Two skaters push apart on frictionless ice (system: both skaters)
A ball falls freely (system: the ball)
A cannon on a cart on frictionless rails fires a shell horizontally; horizontal momentum (system: cannon, cart and shell)
A car brakes to a stop on a road (system: the car)
A firework shell bursts in midair, during the brief explosion (system: all the fragments)
questions.explanation: The skaters' pushes are internal, and the vertical forces cancel. For the cannon, gravity and the rails' normal force are vertical, so horizontal momentum is conserved. During a brief explosion the internal forces dwarf gravity, so momentum is conserved approximately. The falling ball has an unbalanced external force (gravity), and the braking car has road friction acting on it, so their momenta change.

questions.stem: A 50 kg person stands at one end of a 150 kg, 4.0 m boat at rest on still water (ignore water friction). She walks to the other end. How far does the boat move?
questions.explanation: The center of mass stays put. If the boat moves $d$ backward, she moves $4.0 - d$ forward relative to the water: $50(4.0 - d) = 150d$, so $200 = 200d$ and $d = 1.0$ m. 3.0 m is her own displacement; 1.33 m ($4.0 \times 50/150$) forgets that her displacement is $4.0 - d$, not 4.0 m; 4.0 m assumes the boat moves as far as she walks.

questions.stem: A car heading east and a truck heading north collide and stick together. Name the numbered parts of the momentum diagram.

image.alt: A right triangle of arrows: 1 points east along the bottom, 2 points north from its tip, 3 runs diagonally from the start of 1 to the tip of 2, and 4 marks the angle between arrows 1 and 3. A compass arrow shows north up.

choices: Direction of the wreckage north of east
questions.explanation: The car moves east, so its momentum is the horizontal arrow (1); the truck's points north (2). Momentum is conserved as a vector, so the wreckage carries their tip-to-tail sum (3), at angle $\tan^{-1}(p_{\text{truck}}/p_{\text{car}})$ north of east (4). No momentum is lost in the crash; only kinetic energy is.

questions.stem: Classify each collision.
left: Two lumps of clay collide and stick together
Two ideal steel balls bounce apart with no loss of kinetic energy
A car bumper crumples and the cars bounce apart
A bullet embeds itself in a wooden block
questions.explanation: Objects that stick together share one final velocity: perfectly inelastic (the clay, the bullet in the block). Kinetic energy conserved means elastic (the ideal steel balls). Objects that separate but lose some kinetic energy to deformation and heat are inelastic (the crumpled bumper).

questions.stem: A 0.40 kg ball moving at 3.0 m/s hits an identical ball at rest head-on, and the collision is elastic. Afterward the first ball moves at ___ m/s and the second at ___ m/s. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: For equal masses, $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m - m}{2m}(3.0) = 0$ and $v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m}{2m}(3.0) = 3.0$ m/s: the moving ball stops and the target takes all its velocity, as in Newton's cradle. Check: momentum $0.40(3.0) = 1.2$ kg·m/s before and after.

questions.stem: Two carts on a frictionless track collide and stick together. Which statements are always true? Select all that apply.
choices: The carts move with a common final velocity
Some kinetic energy becomes other forms of energy
The lighter cart ends up at rest
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved in every collision, and sticking together means one common velocity. A perfectly inelastic collision loses the most kinetic energy momentum allows (the relative part, $\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$), so kinetic energy is not conserved. Neither cart has to stop: the pair moves at $v_f = (m_1v_{1i} + m_2v_{2i})/(m_1 + m_2)$.

questions.stem: In a head-on elastic collision with the target initially at rest, for which mass ratios $m_1/m_2$ does the projectile bounce backward?
questions.explanation: $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i}$ is negative exactly when $m_1 < m_2$: a light ball bounces back off a heavier one. At $m_1 = m_2$ the projectile stops, and for $m_1 > m_2$ it keeps going forward, more slowly.

questions.stem: Is the force $\vec F = (3y,\; 3x)$ N ($x$, $y$ in m) conservative? If so, what is its potential energy?
choices: No; it does work around a closed loop
questions.explanation: Curl test: $\partial F_y/\partial x = 3 = \partial F_x/\partial y$, so the curl is zero and the force is conservative. $U = -\int 3y\,dx = -3xy + g(y)$; then $-\partial U/\partial y = 3x$ matches $F_y$, so $g$ is constant. $U = -3xy$. Leaving out the minus sign gives $3xy$, whose negative gradient is $-\vec F$; the curl is 0, not 6 (that would be $3 - (-3)$, a sign slip).

questions.stem: The force $\vec F = (-y,\; x)$ N acts on a bead pushed once counterclockwise around a circle of radius 1.5 m centered at the origin. How much work does the force do?
questions.explanation: On the circle the force is tangent to the path (counterclockwise) with magnitude $r = 1.5$ N, so $W = (1.5)(2\pi \times 1.5) = 2\pi(1.5)^2 = 14.1$ J. Green's theorem agrees: the curl is 2 everywhere, times the area $\pi(1.5)^2$. 0 J assumes every closed loop gives zero, which holds only for conservative forces; 7.07 J drops the factor 2; 9.42 J is the circumference alone, forgetting the force is 1.5 N.

questions.stem: A force $\vec F = (y,\; 0)$ N acts in the plane. How much work does it do on a particle moving from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$ m along the parabola $y = x^2$?
questions.explanation: Only $F_x\,dx = y\,dx$ contributes. On the parabola $y = x^2$, so $W = \int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \tfrac13$ J. Along the straight line $y = x$ the work would be $\tfrac12$ J; the paths disagree, so this force is not conservative. $\tfrac23$ J comes from integrating $x\,dy$ (the wrong component), and 1 J multiplies the final force by the $x$ displacement.

questions.stem: The force $\vec F = (2x + y,\; x + 4y)$ N is conservative. Which is its potential energy (up to a constant)?
questions.explanation: $U = -\int(2x + y)\,dx = -(x^2 + xy) + g(y)$. Then $-\partial U/\partial y = x - g'(y)$ must equal $x + 4y$, so $g'(y) = -4y$ and $g = -2y^2$. $U = -(x^2 + xy + 2y^2)$. Check: $-\partial U/\partial x = 2x + y$. ✓ Writing $2xy$ counts the cross term twice (once from each component); dropping $xy$ loses it; omitting the overall minus sign gives $+\nabla U$ instead of $-\nabla U$.

questions.stem: A particle has potential energy $U(x, y) = x^2 + 4y^2$ J ($x$, $y$ in m). What is the force on it at $(2.0, 1.0)$ m?
questions.explanation: $\vec F = -\nabla U = (-2x,\; -8y) = (-4.0, -8.0)$ N, magnitude 8.9 N, pointing downhill on the potential. $(4.0, 8.0)$ N is $+\nabla U$ (sign dropped); $(-2.0, -4.0)$ N forgets the factor 2 from each power rule; $(-4.0, -4.0)$ N differentiates $4y^2$ as $4y$.

questions.stem: A central force has $\vec F = -cr^3\,\hat r$ with $c > 0$. Taking $U = 0$ at $r = 0$, what is its potential energy?
questions.explanation: $U(r) = -\int f(r)\,dr = -\int(-cr^3)\,dr = \tfrac14cr^4$. It grows with $r$, as it must for a force that pulls inward. $-\tfrac14cr^4$ drops the minus sign in $U = -\int f\,dr$; $3cr^2$ differentiates instead of integrating; $cr^3$ just copies the force.

questions.stem: You compute the work a force field does between points $A$ and $B$ along two different paths and get the same answer. What can you conclude?
choices: Nothing yet: other paths might give different work
The curl of the force is nonzero
questions.explanation: Conservative means the work is the same along every path. Two agreeing paths are consistent with that but don't prove it (Example 1's $\vec F_2$ gives 0 J along some paths and 2 J along others). Use the curl test, or find a potential. One disagreement, on the other hand, proves a force is not conservative.

questions.stem: Why can't kinetic friction be described by a potential energy?
choices: Its direction follows the velocity, so it does negative work on every path, including closed ones
It acts perpendicular to the motion
questions.explanation: Kinetic friction always opposes the velocity, so it isn't even a function of position alone, and it does negative work around any closed path; no $U(x, y, z)$ can do that. A constant magnitude is no obstacle (uniform gravity has one); friction is not perpendicular to the motion (it does do work); and "zero curl" would point the other way.

questions.stem: A 0.25 kg puck on a frictionless table has $U(x, y) = 3x^2 + 3y^2$ J ($x$, $y$ in m). It is released from rest at $(1.0, 0)$ m and moves straight toward the origin. How fast is it moving at the origin?
questions.explanation: $U(1.0, 0) = 3.0$ J and $U(0, 0) = 0$, so $\tfrac12(0.25)v^2 = 3.0$ J and $v = \sqrt{24} = 4.90$ m/s. 3.46 m/s forgets the $\tfrac12$ in kinetic energy; 6.93 m/s uses $U = 6$ J (doubling the potential); 24 m/s is $v^2$ without the square root.

questions.stem: The force $\vec F = (6xy,\; 3x^2 + 2y)$ N is conservative. The work it does on a particle moving from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 2)$ m is ___ J. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $U = -\int 6xy\,dx = -3x^2y + g(y)$, and $-\partial U/\partial y = 3x^2 - g'(y) = 3x^2 + 2y$ gives $g = -y^2$. So $U = -(3x^2y + y^2)$ and $W = -\Delta U = 3(1)^2(2) + 2^2 = 10$ J, along any path.

questions.stem: Which of these force fields (in N, with $x$, $y$ in m) are conservative in the whole plane? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Compare $\partial F_y/\partial x$ with $\partial F_x/\partial y$: $(2x, 2y)$: 0 and 0 ✓; $(y, x)$: 1 and 1 ✓; $(-y, x)$: 1 and $-1$ ✗; $(y^2, 2xy)$: $2y$ and $2y$ ✓; $(x^2y, 0)$: 0 and $x^2$ ✗. Their potentials are $-(x^2 + y^2)$, $-xy$ and $-xy^2$.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the potential energy of a force field in three dimensions in order.
choices: Check that the curl is zero, so a potential exists
Integrate $-F_x$ with respect to $x$, adding an unknown $g(y, z)$
Match $-\partial U/\partial y$ to $F_y$ to find $g$ up to an unknown $h(z)$
Match $-\partial U/\partial z$ to $F_z$ to find $h$
questions.explanation: There is no point building $U$ until the curl test shows one exists. Each later step pins down the unknown function left by the one before: $g(y, z)$, then $h(z)$, leaving only a true constant (the choice of zero).

questions.stem: Sort each force field ($x$, $y$ in m).
questions.explanation: $(-x, -y)$ points straight at the origin with size $r$: central, so conservative ($U = \tfrac12r^2$). $(2xy, x^2)$ and uniform gravity pass the curl test but don't point toward a center. $(-y, x)$ and $(y, -x)$ circulate around the origin; their curls are $2$ and $-2$.

questions.stem: The picture is a contour map of $U = 2x^2 + 8y^2$ with a puck at $P$. Name the numbered features.

image.alt: Nested ellipses labeled U = 1, 2, 4 and 6 J around the origin. A point P sits on the U = 4 J ellipse. Marker 1 is at the origin, 2 on the outer ellipse, 3 on a solid arrow from P pointing inward across the ellipses, 4 on a dashed arrow from P pointing outward, and 5 on a dotted line from P to the origin.

questions.explanation: $U$ is smallest at the origin (1), a stable equilibrium. Each ellipse is a curve of constant $U$, an equipotential (2). The gradient points straight uphill, perpendicular to the ellipse (4), and the force is its negative (3). The force does not point along the line to the origin (5), because the $y$ springs are stiffer: it crosses the local contour at right angles instead.

questions.stem: A $5.0\times10^4$ kg rocket on the launch pad burns 250 kg/s of propellant with exhaust speed 2800 m/s. What is its acceleration at liftoff?
questions.explanation: Thrust $uR = 2800(250) = 7.0\times10^5$ N. $a = \dfrac{uR}{m} - g = \dfrac{7.0\times10^5}{5.0\times10^4} - 9.8 = 14 - 9.8 = 4.2$ m/s². 14 m/s² ignores the weight; 23.8 m/s² adds $g$ instead of subtracting it; 1.43 is the thrust-to-weight ratio, not an acceleration.

questions.stem: A rocket rising vertically has exhaust speed 2000 m/s and mass ratio $m_i/m_f = 3.0$, and its burn lasts 100 s. Ignoring drag, what is its speed at burnout?
questions.explanation: $v = u\ln\dfrac{m_i}{m_f} - gt_b = 2000\ln 3.0 - 9.8(100) = 2197 - 980 = 1220$ m/s. 2200 m/s leaves out the gravity loss; 3180 m/s adds it; 353 m/s uses $u(1 - m_f/m_i)$ in place of the logarithm.

questions.stem: A cart coasting at 3.0 m/s on a frictionless level track leaks sand straight down through a hole in its floor until it has lost half its mass. What is its speed then?
questions.explanation: The sand leaves with the cart's own horizontal velocity, so $u_{\text{rel}} = 0$ and $m\,dv/dt = 0$: the speed stays 3.0 m/s. 6.0 m/s comes from assuming $mv$ of the cart alone stays constant (the sand carries momentum away with it); 4.2 m/s assumes the cart's kinetic energy stays constant; 1.5 m/s halves the speed with the mass.

questions.stem: An open 20 kg cart rolls at 4.0 m/s on a frictionless level track through a downpour. Rain falling vertically adds 5.0 kg of water. What is the cart's speed then?
questions.explanation: The rain brings no horizontal momentum, so horizontal momentum is conserved: $20(4.0) = 25v$, $v = 3.2$ m/s. (The rain has to be brought up to speed: $u_{\text{rel}} = -v$ slows the cart.) 4.0 m/s ignores the added mass; 3.6 m/s wrongly conserves kinetic energy; 5.0 m/s inverts the mass ratio.

questions.stem: Sand falls onto a conveyor belt at 30 kg/s, and the belt moves at a constant 1.5 m/s. What extra power must the motor supply?
questions.explanation: Force $F = Rv = 30(1.5) = 45$ N; power $P = Fv = Rv^2 = 30(1.5)^2 = 67.5$ W. Half of it, 33.8 W, becomes the sand's kinetic energy and half becomes heat, so 33.8 W counts only the kinetic energy. 45 is the force in newtons; 135 W doubles the correct answer.

questions.stem: A water jet 1.0 cm in diameter hits a wall head-on at 30 m/s and splashes out sideways. What force does it exert on the wall? ($\rho = 1000$ kg/m³)
questions.explanation: $A = \pi(0.0050)^2 = 7.85\times10^{-5}$ m², mass rate $\rho Av = 2.36$ kg/s, force $\rho Av^2 = 2.36(30) = 70.7$ N. 2.36 is the mass rate, not a force; 141 N is for a jet turned straight back; 283 N uses the diameter as the radius (four times the area).

questions.stem: In an ideal Pelton wheel, buckets turn a jet of speed $v$ straight back. At what bucket speed does the wheel extract the most power?
questions.explanation: The force is $2\rho Av(v - V)$ and the power $2\rho Av(v - V)V$, a parabola in $V$ with its peak at $V = v/2$. Then the water leaves the bucket at $V - (v - V) = 0$ in the ground frame, so the jet keeps none of its kinetic energy. At $V = 0$ there is force but no motion; at $V = v$ the jet never catches the buckets.

questions.stem: An idealized 3.0 kg chain hangs with its lower end just touching a scale pan and is released. What does the scale read just before the last link lands?
questions.explanation: With length $y = L$ landed, the scale supports the whole weight $\lambda gL = 29.4$ N and also stops links arriving at $v^2 = 2gL$, a momentum flux $\lambda v^2 = 2\lambda gL = 58.8$ N. Total: $3(29.4) = 88.2$ N. 29.4 N is the weight alone; 58.8 N is the flux alone; 147 N doubles the flux ($29.4 + 2 \times 58.8$), as if each link bounced back up instead of stopping.

questions.stem: A cart leaks sand straight down as it coasts with no horizontal external force. What does the (incorrect) equation $F = d(mv)/dt = m\,dv/dt + v\,dm/dt$, applied to the cart alone with $F = 0$, predict?
choices: The cart speeds up as it loses mass, which is wrong
The cart slows down as it loses mass
The speed stays the same, which is right
The cart stops once half the sand is gone
questions.explanation: With $F = 0$: $m\,dv/dt = -v\,dm/dt$, and $dm/dt < 0$, so $dv/dt > 0$: it predicts speeding up. In fact the sand leaves with the cart's velocity ($u_{\text{rel}} = 0$), so the speed is constant. The shortcut fails because it ignores the momentum the leaving sand carries away.

questions.stem: Sand drops onto a conveyor belt at 40 kg/s, and the belt moves at a constant 2.5 m/s. Energy is turned into heat at ___ W. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The motor supplies $Rv^2 = 40(2.5)^2 = 250$ W. The sand gains kinetic energy at $\tfrac12Rv^2 = 125$ W, and the rest, 125 W, becomes heat as the sand slides on the belt.

questions.stem: For a rocket rising vertically with a constant burn rate (no drag, uniform $g$), which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It lifts off only if its thrust exceeds its initial weight
The gravity loss grows with the burn time
The thrust uses the exhaust speed relative to the ground
Burning the same propellant faster (same exhaust speed) reduces the gravity loss
In free space the gravity-loss term disappears
questions.explanation: $m\,dv/dt = uR - mg$ needs $uR > m_ig$ to start upward. The gravity loss is $gt_b$, so it grows with burn time, and a faster burn of the same propellant shortens $t_b$. With no gravity the $-gt$ term is gone, leaving $u\ln(m_i/m_f)$. The thrust uses the exhaust speed relative to the rocket, not the ground.

questions.stem: An idealized chain hangs with its lower end just touching a scale pan and is released. Put the scale readings in time order.
choices: Zero (the chain hangs, just touching the pan)
1.5 times the chain's weight (half has landed)
3 times the chain's weight (the last link is about to land)
1 times the chain's weight (the whole chain lies at rest)
questions.explanation: The reading is $3\lambda gy$ while the chain falls: 0 at the start, $3\lambda g(L/2) = 1.5$ weights at half, and $3\lambda gL = 3$ weights just before the end. Once everything has landed and stopped there is no momentum flux, so the reading drops to one weight.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the force involved.
left: Thrust of a rocket ejecting mass at rate $R$ with exhaust speed $u$
Force a belt at speed $v$ needs while loading sand at rate $R$
Force of a jet stopped by a wall
Force of a jet turned straight back
choices: Density times area times speed squared
Twice density times area times speed squared
questions.explanation: Rocket thrust is $uR$; the belt needs $Rv$; a jet's momentum flux is $\rho Av^2$, and reversing it doubles the momentum change to $2\rho Av^2$. $\rho Av$ is the mass flow rate, not a force.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the loading conveyor.

image.alt: A funnel at the top drops a column of dots onto a long belt looped around two rollers. Marker 1 is on the funnel, 2 on the falling dots, 3 on a small shaded zone of the belt where the dots land, 4 on an arrow pointing right below the belt, and 5 on a box connected to the right roller.

choices: Slipping zone where heat is produced
questions.explanation: Sand leaves the hopper (1) and falls straight down (2), so it arrives with no horizontal velocity. Where it lands (3) it slides on the belt until kinetic friction brings it up to the belt's speed; that sliding turns half the motor's extra work into heat. The belt moves at constant speed (4), kept up by the motor (5), which must supply the extra force $Rv$.

questions.stem: What is the reduced mass of a 3.0 kg object and a 6.0 kg object?
questions.explanation: $\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{18}{9.0} = 2.0$ kg, less than either mass. 4.5 kg is the average; 9.0 kg the total; 0.50 is the reciprocal, $(m_1 + m_2)/(m_1m_2)$.

questions.stem: A 4.0 kg cart moving at 5.0 m/s hits a 1.0 kg cart at rest. What is the most kinetic energy the collision can possibly convert to other forms?
questions.explanation: Only the relative kinetic energy can be lost: $\mu = \dfrac{4.0(1.0)}{5.0} = 0.80$ kg, so $\tfrac12(0.80)(5.0)^2 = 10$ J (lost if they stick). The total is 50 J, but the CM part, $\tfrac12(5.0)(4.0)^2 = 40$ J, must remain because $v_{\text{cm}}$ can't change. 25 J assumes half is always lost.

questions.stem: A 3.0 kg puck at 4.0 m/s hits an identical puck at rest head-on, with coefficient of restitution 0.60. How much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.explanation: $\mu = 1.5$ kg and the relative kinetic energy is $\tfrac12(1.5)(4.0)^2 = 12$ J. Lost: $(1 - 0.60^2)(12) = 0.64(12) = 7.68$ J. 4.32 J is the relative energy that remains ($e^2 \times 12$); 4.80 J uses $(1 - e)$ instead of $(1 - e^2)$; 15.4 J applies the factor to the total 24 J, including the CM part that can't be lost.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg cart moves at $+6.0$ m/s toward a 3.0 kg cart moving at $-4.0$ m/s. What is the velocity of their center of mass?
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{2.0(6.0) + 3.0(-4.0)}{5.0} = \dfrac{12 - 12}{5.0} = 0$. Here the lab frame already is the CM frame. $+1.0$ m/s averages the velocities without weighting by mass; $+4.8$ m/s adds the momentum magnitudes; $+2.0$ m/s is the sum $6.0 + (-4.0)$.

questions.stem: A 1.0 kg ball at 9.0 m/s hits a 2.0 kg ball at rest head-on, elastically. Working in the CM frame, what is the 1.0 kg ball's final velocity?
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{cm}} = 9.0/3.0 = 3.0$ m/s. In the CM frame the ball moves at $9.0 - 3.0 = 6.0$ m/s; the elastic collision reverses it to $-6.0$ m/s; adding $v_{\text{cm}}$ back gives $-3.0$ m/s. (Formula check: $\tfrac{1 - 2}{3}(9.0) = -3.0$.) $+3.0$ m/s forgets the reversal, $-9.0$ m/s reverses the lab velocity, and 0 is the equal-mass result.

questions.stem: An alpha particle (4 u) hits a carbon-12 nucleus (12 u) at rest head-on, elastically. What fraction of its kinetic energy does the carbon nucleus receive?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2} = \dfrac{4(4)(12)}{16^2} = \dfrac{192}{256} = 0.75$. 25% is what the alpha keeps; 33% is just the mass ratio $4/12$; 100% happens only for equal masses.

questions.stem: A 6.0 kg puck slides into a 2.0 kg puck at rest and they collide elastically, off-center. What is the largest angle through which the 6.0 kg puck can be deflected?
questions.explanation: Heavy on light: $\sin\theta_{\max} = m_2/m_1 = 2.0/6.0$, so $\theta_{\max} = 19.5°$. 18.4° uses the tangent and 70.5° the cosine; 90° would need equal masses or a lighter projectile.

questions.stem: A neutron (1 u) collides head-on and elastically with a carbon-12 nucleus at rest. What fraction of its kinetic energy does the neutron keep?
questions.explanation: It keeps $\left(\dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{11}{13}\right)^2 = 0.72$, so 72% (it gives away $48/169 = 28\%$). 28% is the fraction given away; 85% is the velocity ratio $11/13$ without squaring; 8.3% is $1/12$.

questions.stem: In the Geiger–Marsden experiments, some alpha particles bounced back from a thin metal foil. Why couldn't collisions with the atoms' electrons explain this?
choices: An electron is about 7300 times lighter than an alpha, so it can deflect an alpha by at most about 0.008°
Electrons attract alpha particles instead of repelling them
Electrons move too fast to collide with alpha particles
The foil contained too few electrons
questions.explanation: For a heavy projectile on a light target, $\sin\theta_{\max} = m_2/m_1 \approx 1/7300$, about 0.008°. No number of such collisions along a thin foil could plausibly turn an alpha around, so the large deflections needed a target heavier than the alpha: a massive nucleus. (The electrons do attract the positive alpha, but that is not why they fail; the limit comes from momentum and energy alone.)

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg cart at 5.0 m/s approaches a 3.0 kg cart at rest. Their reduced mass is ___ kg, and their relative kinetic energy is ___ J. Give only the numbers.
questions.explanation: $\mu = \dfrac{2.0(3.0)}{5.0} = 1.2$ kg and $\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2 = \tfrac12(1.2)(5.0)^2 = 15$ J. The other 10 J of the 25 J total belongs to the center of mass and survives any collision.

questions.stem: Which statements about the center-of-mass frame of a two-object collision are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The two momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction
In an elastic collision each object keeps its speed
After any collision both objects are at rest
questions.explanation: The CM frame is defined so that total momentum is zero, which makes the momenta $\pm\mu\vec v_{\text{rel}}$, and the kinetic energy there is the relative part $\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$. Elastic collisions keep that energy and so each speed. Both objects end at rest only in a perfectly inelastic collision.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving a collision through the CM frame in order.
choices: Apply the collision rule (reverse, scale by $e$, or turn) in the CM frame
Add $v_{\text{cm}}$ back to get the final lab velocities
questions.explanation: You need $v_{\text{cm}}$ before you can change frames, the collision rule applies to CM-frame velocities, and the answers must be brought back to the lab frame at the end.

questions.stem: Match what happens in the CM frame to the kind of event (head-on, one dimension).
left: Both velocities reverse with the same speeds
Both velocities reverse and shrink by a factor $e$ between 0 and 1
Both objects end moving apart faster than they approached
choices: Explosion or release of stored energy
questions.explanation: In the CM frame the relative kinetic energy is all there is. Elastic keeps it (same speeds), restitution $e$ multiplies it by $e^2$, perfectly inelastic removes it (both at rest), and an explosion or a released spring adds to it.

questions.stem: The velocity diagram is for an elastic collision of a heavy projectile with a light target at rest. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: An arrow across the top points right. Below, an arrow runs from point O to point C, the center of a large shaded circle. Another arrow runs from C to a point on the circle, and a third from O to that same point, tangent to the circle. Marker 1 is on the O-to-C arrow, 2 on the C-to-circle arrow, 3 on the O-to-circle arrow, 4 on the angle at O, and 5 on the circle.

choices: Velocity of the center of mass
Projectile's velocity in the CM frame after the collision
Projectile's final velocity in the lab frame
Possible tips of the final lab velocity
questions.explanation: The CM velocity runs from O to the circle's center C (1). In the CM frame the projectile keeps its speed, so after the collision its CM-frame velocity (2) reaches from C to some point of the circle, and the circle (5) is the set of all possible tips. The lab velocity is their sum, from O to that point (3). Because the circle doesn't enclose O, the lab velocity can only tilt until it is tangent to the circle, which gives the largest deflection angle (4), with $\sin\theta_{\max} = m_2/m_1$.

questions.stem: A disk turns counterclockwise and is slowing down. Name the numbered parts of the drawing.

image.alt: A disk with a dot at its center, a radius drawn to a point on the rim, a thick arc along the rim from a dashed reference line to that point, and three arrows at the point: a long one tangent to the rim pointing counterclockwise, a short one tangent to the rim pointing clockwise, and one along the radius toward the center. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The axis (1) is the fixed center. The thick arc (2) is the distance the point has traveled along the rim, $s = r\theta$. The velocity (3) is tangent to the rim in the direction of rotation, with size $v = r\omega$. The arrow along the radius toward the axis (4) is the centripetal acceleration $r\omega^2$. (The short unnumbered arrow pointing backward along the rim is the tangential acceleration $r\alpha$, backward because the disk is slowing.) Angular velocity is shared by the whole disk and points along the axis, not along any arrow drawn here.

questions.stem: A wheel slows uniformly from 10 rev/s to rest in 4.0 s. It makes ___ revolutions while stopping. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: With constant angular acceleration the average rate is $\tfrac12(10 + 0) = 5$ rev/s, so $\Delta\theta = \tfrac12(\omega_0 + \omega)t = 5(4.0) = 20$ rev. Working in revolutions is fine here because no formula mixes $\omega$ with a length. (In radians: $\omega_0 = 62.8$ rad/s, $\Delta\theta = 125.7$ rad $= 20$ rev.)

questions.stem: Match each rotational quantity to its SI unit.
questions.explanation: $\omega = d\theta/dt$ is in rad/s and $\alpha = d\omega/dt$ in rad/s². $I = \sum mr^2$ is a mass times a distance squared, kg·m². $\tfrac12I\omega^2$ has units kg·m²/s² = J (the radian is dimensionless). N·m/s is a unit of power (W), not one of these.

questions.stem: Which of these change an object's moment of inertia about an axis? Select all that apply.
choices: Moving the axis to a different place on the object
Moving some of its mass farther from the axis
Adding mass to the object some distance from the axis
questions.explanation: $I = \sum m_ir_i^2$ depends on how much mass there is and how far each piece is from the axis, so moving the axis, moving mass outward or adding mass off the axis all change it. The spin rate doesn't appear in $I$ at all: spinning faster raises $\omega$, $L$ and $K$, not $I$.

questions.stem: Each object has the same mass $M$ and radius $R$. Put them in order of moment of inertia about a central axis, smallest first.
choices: Solid disk (axis along its own axis)
Thin hoop (axis perpendicular to its plane)
questions.explanation: $I = cMR^2$ with $c = \tfrac25 = 0.40$ (solid sphere), $\tfrac12 = 0.50$ (solid disk), $\tfrac23 \approx 0.67$ (thin shell) and $1$ (hoop). The more of the mass that sits near the full radius $R$, the larger $I$; the hoop has all of it there.

questions.stem: A force turns a bar about an axis (top view). Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A bar with a pivot at its left end. An arrow above the bar runs from the pivot to the bar's right end. At the right end an arrow points up and to the right at an angle to the bar, and a dashed line extends that arrow's line backward below the bar. A line from the pivot meets the dashed line at a right angle. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The bar turns about the axis (1). The position vector $\vec r$ (2) runs from the axis to the point where the force (3) is applied. Extending the force along its own direction gives its line of action (4), and the perpendicular distance from the axis to that line is the lever arm (5), $\ell = r\sin\theta$, so $\tau = \ell F$. The torque vector itself points out of the page (right-hand rule), so it isn't drawn in this top view.

questions.stem: A 40 N force is applied at the end of a 0.50 m wrench, at $30^\circ$ to the handle. The torque about the bolt is ___ N·m. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\theta = 0.50(40)\sin 30^\circ = 0.50(40)(0.5) = 10$ N·m. Using $\cos 30^\circ$ would give 17.3 N·m, and a perpendicular push would give the maximum, 20 N·m.

questions.stem: Each force acts horizontally on a door 0.80 m wide, hinged along one vertical edge. Put them in order of torque about the hinge, smallest first.
choices: 60 N at the outer edge, pushing straight toward the hinge
30 N perpendicular to the door, 0.20 m from the hinge
20 N perpendicular to the door, at the outer edge
50 N at $30^\circ$ to the door, at the outer edge
30 N perpendicular to the door, at the outer edge
questions.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$: toward the hinge, $\theta = 0$, so $0$; $0.20(30) = 6$ N·m; $0.80(20) = 16$ N·m; $0.80(50)\sin 30^\circ = 20$ N·m; $0.80(30) = 24$ N·m. The biggest force (60 N) gives the smallest torque because it points at the axis.

questions.stem: Which forces exert zero torque about a given axis? Select all that apply.
choices: A force whose line of action passes through the axis
A force applied at the axis itself
A force parallel to the position vector from the axis to its point of application
A force perpendicular to the position vector, applied far from the axis
questions.explanation: $\tau = rF\sin\theta = \ell F$. A line of action through the axis has lever arm $\ell = 0$; a force at the axis has $r = 0$; a force parallel (or antiparallel) to $\vec r$ has $\sin\theta = 0$. A perpendicular force far from the axis gives the largest torque, $rF$.

questions.stem: Match each rotational quantity or formula to its linear (translational) counterpart.
questions.explanation: Torque plays the role of force ($\sum\tau = I\alpha$ mirrors $\sum F = ma$), moment of inertia the role of mass, angular momentum $I\omega$ the role of $mv$, and work by a torque through an angle mirrors work by a force through a distance. The counterpart of acceleration is $\alpha$, which isn't listed.

questions.stem: Rolling is built from two simpler motions. Name the numbered parts of the drawing.

image.alt: Three wheels in a row joined by a plus sign and an equals sign, with velocity arrows. The first wheel has equal arrows at its top, center and bottom. The second has an arrow forward at the top, none at the center and one backward at the bottom. The third has a long arrow at the top, a shorter one at the center and none at the bottom. Each wheel is numbered, and so are the top and bottom points of the third wheel.

questions.explanation: In translation (1) every point moves at $v$. In rotation about the center (2) the top moves forward at $R\omega = v$ and the bottom backward at $v$. Adding them point by point gives rolling (3): the top moves at $v + v = 2v$ (4) and the contact point at $v - v = 0$ (5), which is what "without slipping" means.

questions.stem: For a thin hoop rolling without slipping, ___ of its kinetic energy is rotational. Give a fraction or a decimal.
questions.explanation: For a hoop $I = MR^2$, so $K_{\text{rot}} = \tfrac12MR^2\omega^2 = \tfrac12Mv^2 = K_{\text{trans}}$. The two parts are equal, so rotation holds $\dfrac{c}{1 + c} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ of the total.

questions.stem: Rolling objects have $I_{\text{cm}} = cMR^2$. Match each object to its value of $c$ (central axis).
questions.explanation: Hoop $MR^2$, solid cylinder $\tfrac12MR^2$, solid sphere $\tfrac25MR^2$, thin spherical shell $\tfrac23MR^2$. The value $\tfrac13$ belongs to a thin rod about one end ($\tfrac13ML^2$), which isn't a rolling shape.

questions.stem: In which situations is angular momentum conserved about the stated axis? Select all that apply.
choices: A skater spinning on frictionless ice, about her vertical spin axis
Two disks on a frictionless axle that grab each other and spin together, about the axle
A planet orbiting the Sun, about the Sun
A spinning wheel being slowed by a brake pad, about its axle
A ball rolling down a ramp, about the ball's center
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved when the net external torque about that axis is zero. The ice exerts no torque about the skater's axis; the disks' friction on each other is internal; gravity on a planet points at the Sun, so it has no lever arm. The brake pad's friction exerts an external torque on the wheel. On the ramp, friction at the contact point exerts a torque $fR$ about the center, which is exactly what spins the ball up as it goes faster.

questions.stem: Each object starts from rest at the same height on the same ramp. Put them in order of speed at the bottom, fastest first. (The block slides without friction; the others roll without slipping.)
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1 + c)}$ with $c = 0$ (block, no rotation), $0.40$, $0.50$, $0.67$ and $1$. The smaller the share of energy tied up in rotation, the faster the object goes. Mass and radius cancel.

questions.stem: This is the free-body diagram of a beam hinged to a wall, held by a cable, with a sign hanging from its end. Name the numbered forces.

image.alt: A horizontal beam hinged to a wall at the left, with a cable from its right end up to the wall and a box labeled SIGN hanging below the right end. Five force arrows are numbered: one along the cable toward the wall, one pointing down from the middle of the beam, one pointing down beside the sign, one pointing horizontally away from the wall at the hinge, and one pointing up at the hinge.

questions.explanation: The cable can only pull along itself, so its tension (1) points along the cable toward the wall. The uniform beam's weight (2) acts at its middle and the sign's weight (3) at the end where it hangs. The hinge can push in any direction, so its force is drawn as a horizontal part (4), pushing the beam away from the wall to balance the cable's pull toward it, and a vertical part (5). Nothing touches a floor here.

questions.stem: A uniform seesaw is pivoted at its center. A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot. To balance, a 60 kg child must sit ___ m from the pivot on the other side. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Torques about the pivot balance: $40g(1.5) = 60g\,x$, so $x = 60/60 = 1.0$ m. The heavier child sits closer to the pivot.

questions.stem: A uniform horizontal beam is hinged at a wall and held by a cable from its far end. Put these cable angles (measured from the beam) in order of cable tension, largest first.
questions.explanation: Torques about the hinge: $T\sin\theta\cdot L = W\cdot\tfrac L2$, so $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$. Smaller angles have smaller $\sin\theta$ and need more tension: $1.93W$, $W$, $0.71W$ and $0.58W$.

questions.stem: Which statements are true for every rigid object in static equilibrium? Select all that apply.
choices: The net force on it is zero
The net torque on it is zero about every point
Every individual force on it is zero
The net torque is zero only about its center of mass
Its center of mass is at rest
questions.explanation: Static equilibrium means at rest and staying at rest: $\sum\vec F = 0$, and with zero net force the net torque is the same about every point, so it is zero about every point. The individual forces need not be zero (a shelf bracket carries large forces); they just cancel.

questions.stem: Match each elastic modulus to the deformation it describes.
choices: Stretching or compressing a rod along its length
Sliding one face sideways relative to the opposite face
Squeezing from all sides with added pressure
questions.explanation: $F/A = Y\,\Delta L/L$ (tension or compression along a length), $F/A = S\,\Delta x/L$ (shear, force parallel to a face) and $\Delta P = -B\,\Delta V/V$ (uniform squeezing). Thermal expansion is described by a coefficient of expansion, not an elastic modulus.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this elliptical orbit.

image.alt: An ellipse with a large yellow circle on the long axis right of center and a small open circle the same distance left of center. Two shaded wedges spread from the yellow circle, a short wide one to the near end of the ellipse and a long thin one to the far end. A bracket above runs from the center to the right end. Five points are numbered.

questions.explanation: Kepler's first law puts the Sun at one focus (1); the other focus (2) is empty, the same distance on the other side of the center (the center itself is halfway between them and isn't numbered). The nearest point to the Sun is perihelion (3) and the farthest is aphelion (4). The semimajor axis (5) is half the long axis; it sets the period through $T^2 \propto a^3$. The two shaded wedges have equal areas, swept in equal times.

questions.stem: A planet has the same mass as Earth but half its radius. Its surface gravity is ___ times Earth's. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $g = GM/R^2$. Same $M$ and $R \to R/2$ gives $g \to GM/(R/2)^2 = 4\,GM/R^2$: four times as large.

questions.stem: Put these Earth satellites in order of orbital period, shortest first.
choices: The International Space Station (about 400 km up)
questions.explanation: Kepler's third law: $T^2 \propto r^3$, so a larger orbit always has a longer period. The ISS takes about 92 min, a GPS satellite about 12 h, a geostationary satellite one sidereal day, about 23 h 56 min (by design, so it keeps pace with Earth's rotation) and the Moon about 27 days.

questions.stem: A satellite is in a circular orbit with total mechanical energy $E$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its orbital speed doesn't depend on its own mass
A lower circular orbit would have a longer period
questions.explanation: $K = \dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ and $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, so $K = -E$ and $U = 2E$. $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ has no $m$ in it. A lower orbit is faster and shorter, so its period is shorter, and $E$ is negative because the satellite is bound.

questions.stem: Match each of Kepler's laws to the physics that explains it.
left: Second law (equal areas in equal times)
choices: An inverse-square attractive force gives conic-section paths
Gravity exerts no torque about the Sun so angular momentum is conserved
Setting the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force
Conservation of the planet's linear momentum
questions.explanation: Newton showed that an inverse-square force produces conic-section orbits (first law). Gravity points toward the Sun, so the planet's angular momentum about the Sun is constant and the swept area per unit time, $L/2m$, is too (second law). For a circular orbit, $GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r$ with $v = 2\pi r/T$ gives $T^2 = (4\pi^2/GM)r^3$ (third law). A planet's linear momentum is not conserved: its direction changes all the time because gravity acts on it.

questions.stem: A bowling ball is released sliding along a level lane with no spin. While it slides, kinetic friction on it points
choices: forward, in the direction of motion
backward, opposite the sliding of the contact point
nowhere: there is no friction until it rolls
straight up, like the normal force
questions.explanation: The slip velocity $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$ starts at $v_0 > 0$: the contact point slides forward, so kinetic friction points backward. It slows the center and, acting below the center, spins the ball up. Friction acts as long as the contact point slides; it is parallel to the floor, not perpendicular.

questions.stem: A uniform solid ball is launched along a level floor at 7.0 m/s with no spin. What is its speed once it rolls without slipping?
questions.explanation: Angular momentum about a point on the floor is conserved: $Mv_0R = (1 + c)Mv_fR$, so $v_f = v_0/(1 + c) = 7.0/1.4 = 5.0$ m/s. 7.0 m/s ignores friction; 5.9 m/s ($7.0/\sqrt{1.4}$) wrongly assumes kinetic energy is conserved, but sliding friction turns some into heat; 2.0 m/s is the fraction lost, $\tfrac27$, times 7.0.

questions.stem: A uniform solid ball is launched along a level floor at 7.0 m/s with no spin. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.20. How long does it slide before it rolls without slipping? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $t^* = \dfrac{c\,v_0}{(1 + c)\mu_kg} = \dfrac{0.4(7.0)}{1.4(0.20)(9.8)} = 1.02$ s. 3.6 s is $v_0/(\mu_kg)$, the time to stop if friction only slowed the ball; 1.4 s leaves out the $(1 + c)$; 2.6 s leaves out the $c$.

questions.stem: A uniform solid cylinder is launched along a level floor with no spin. What fraction of its initial kinetic energy is lost to kinetic friction before it rolls?
questions.explanation: The lost fraction is $\dfrac{c}{1 + c} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.5} = \dfrac13$, whatever $\mu_k$ is. 1/2 is the hoop's ($c = 1$); 2/7 is the solid sphere's; 2/3 is the fraction kept.

questions.stem: Why is the angular momentum of a skidding ball conserved about a fixed point $P$ on the floor (on the line along which it touches the floor)?
choices: Because kinetic friction is too small to matter
Because the ball's center moves in a straight line
Because friction acts along the floor through $P$, and the torques of the weight and the normal force about $P$ cancel
Because angular momentum is always conserved about the center of mass
questions.explanation: Friction lies along the floor line through $P$, so its lever arm about $P$ is zero. The weight and the normal force are equal, opposite and act along the same vertical line, so their torques about $P$ cancel. Friction is not negligible (it changes $v$ and $\omega$), and about the center of mass it has a lever arm $R$, so angular momentum about the center is not conserved.

questions.stem: A thin hoop is launched along a level floor at 2.0 m/s with backspin such that $R|\omega_0| = 3.0$ m/s. What is its velocity once it rolls without slipping (forward positive)?
questions.explanation: $v_f = \dfrac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c} = \dfrac{2.0 + 1(-3.0)}{2} = -0.50$ m/s: it comes back. +0.50 m/s drops the sign; +2.5 m/s treats the backspin as topspin; −1.0 m/s forgets to divide by $1 + c$.

questions.stem: A uniform rod 1.2 m long is held at one end and struck at right angles. How far from the hand is its center of percussion?
questions.explanation: $b = \dfrac{I_P}{Md} = \dfrac{\tfrac13ML^2}{M(L/2)} = \tfrac23L = 0.80$ m. 0.60 m is the center of mass; a blow there pushes the whole rod sideways and jolts the hand. 0.40 m is $L/3$; 1.2 m is the far end.

questions.stem: A uniform solid billiard ball of radius $R$ is struck with a horizontal cue. At what height above the table must it be hit to roll at once, with no sliding?
questions.explanation: Rolling at once needs $v = R\omega$ with $v = J/M$ and $\omega = J(b - R)/(\tfrac25MR^2)$, giving $b = (1 + c)R = 1.4R$, that is $0.4R$ above the center. At $R$ (the center) the ball starts with no spin and slides; $0.4R$ is the height above the center, not above the table; $2R$ is the top of the ball, which gives too much topspin.

questions.stem: A thin hoop is launched along a level floor at 6.0 m/s with no spin. Once it rolls without slipping its speed is ___ m/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $v_f = v_0/(1 + c) = 6.0/2 = 3.0$ m/s, independent of the friction coefficient.

questions.stem: A uniform solid sphere launched with no spin loses ___ of its kinetic energy to friction before it starts rolling. Give a fraction.
questions.explanation: The fraction kept is $\dfrac{(1 + c)v_f^2}{v_0^2} = \dfrac{1}{1 + c} = \dfrac57$, so $\dfrac{c}{1 + c} = \dfrac{0.4}{1.4} = \dfrac27 \approx 0.286$ is lost.

questions.stem: Each object is launched along a level floor at the same speed with no spin. Put them in order of their final rolling speed, fastest first.
questions.explanation: $v_f = v_0/(1 + c)$: $\tfrac{1}{1.4} = 0.71v_0$ (sphere), $\tfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.67v_0$ (cylinder), $\tfrac{1}{1.67} = 0.60v_0$ (shell), $\tfrac12v_0$ (hoop). The more inertia an object has for spinning, the more forward speed it gives up to spin up.

questions.stem: A ball is launched along a level floor (forward positive, $I = cMR^2$). Match each starting condition to what happens.
choices: Slows and spins up then rolls forward more slowly
Rolls on at constant speed with no kinetic friction
Stops and then rolls back toward the start
Comes to rest with no spin and stays there
questions.explanation: All four follow from $v_f = \dfrac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c}$ with $\omega_0$ negative for backspin. No spin: $v_f = v_0/(1 + c)$. Already rolling: no slip, so no kinetic friction. Strong backspin makes $v_f$ negative. Backspin exactly $v_0/(cR)$ makes $v_f = 0$, and since $\omega_f = v_f/R$, the spin is zero too.

questions.stem: A ball slides to the right with too little spin. Name the numbered parts of the drawing.

image.alt: A ball on a level floor. An arrow points right from its center; a curved arrow near its top shows clockwise spin; an arrow points left along the floor from the contact point; an arrow points down from the center; and an arrow points up to the contact point from below. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The contact point slides forward, so kinetic friction (1) points backward along the floor. The center moves to the right (2), and the ball spins clockwise (3), the rolling sense for rightward motion, though not yet fast enough to roll. The floor pushes up at the contact point (4) and gravity pulls down at the center (5). Friction here is kinetic, not static, because the contact point is sliding.

questions.stem: A ball is launched with no spin along a level floor. Which of these do NOT depend on the coefficient of kinetic friction? Select all that apply.
choices: The fraction of its kinetic energy lost
questions.explanation: $v_f = v_0/(1 + c)$ and the lost fraction $c/(1 + c)$ contain no $\mu_k$; they follow from conservation of angular momentum about a floor point. The sliding time $t^* = cv_0/[(1 + c)\mu_kg]$ and the sliding distance both scale as $1/\mu_k$: a slicker floor means longer sliding, but the same final state.

questions.stem: A gyroscope's 0.20 kg rotor has $I = 4.0\times10^{-4}$ kg·m² and spins at 250 rad/s. Its center of mass is 5.0 cm from the pivot and its axle is horizontal. What is its precession rate? ($g = 9.8$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $L = I\omega = 4.0\times10^{-4}(250) = 0.10$ kg·m²/s and $\tau = Mgr = 0.20(9.8)(0.050) = 0.098$ N·m, so $\Omega = \tau/L = 0.98$ rad/s. 0.098 is the torque itself; 0.10 leaves out $g$ (uses $Mr$ for the torque); 1.02 is $L/\tau$, upside down.

questions.stem: A gyroscope precesses at rate $\Omega$. If its spin rate is doubled (same torque), its precession rate becomes
questions.explanation: $\Omega = \tau/(I\omega)$: doubling $\omega$ doubles $L$, and the same torque swings a twice-as-long $\vec L$ half as fast. That is why a top precesses faster as it slows down.

questions.stem: A spinning top precesses with its axis tilted at angle $\theta$ from the vertical. How does its precession rate depend on $\theta$ (in the gyroscopic approximation)?
choices: It doesn't: the rate is the same at any tilt
questions.explanation: The torque is $Mgr\sin\theta$, but only the horizontal part of $\vec L$, $L\sin\theta$, swings around. $\Omega = \dfrac{Mgr\sin\theta}{L\sin\theta} = \dfrac{Mgr}{I\omega}$: the $\sin\theta$ cancels.

questions.stem: A gyroscope's pivot is at the origin, its axle points along $+x$ and its spin angular momentum is along $+x$; $z$ is up. In which direction does the free end of the axle start to move?
questions.explanation: Gravity acts at $(r, 0, 0)$: $\vec\tau = r\hat\imath\times(-Mg\hat k) = Mgr\,\hat\jmath$. Since $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$, the tip of $\vec L$, and the axle with it, moves toward $+y$: counterclockwise seen from above. It doesn't fall (to first order), and $-y$ would be the direction for the opposite spin.

questions.stem: A fast gyroscope is released with its axle horizontal and held still. What happens in the first moments?
choices: It starts precessing at full rate instantly, with no other motion
It falls straight down until the spin stops
Its axle dips slightly and bobs up and down (nutation) while it settles into precession
It rises above the horizontal and stays there
questions.explanation: It can't be precessing at the moment of release, so it begins to fall; that motion swings $\vec L$ sideways, and the axle settles into precession while bobbing about the steady path. For a fast rotor the dip and the bobs are small, and pivot friction damps them. The small dip also supplies the kinetic energy of the precession.

questions.stem: What causes the precession of Earth's rotation axis (period about 26,000 years)?
choices: The Sun's and Moon's gravity acting on Earth's equatorial bulge
Friction between Earth's core and mantle
The pressure of sunlight on Earth's day side
Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun
questions.explanation: Earth's spin makes it bulge at the equator. The Sun and Moon pull harder on the nearer part of the tilted bulge, producing a torque that tends to line the equator up with the orbital plane. As for a top, that torque makes the spin axis precess instead of tipping it. Hipparchus discovered the effect in the 2nd century BCE.

questions.stem: Two 0.20 kg masses are 0.10 m from the center of a light rod mounted on a shaft at $\beta = 60^\circ$ to the shaft. The shaft turns at 30 rad/s. What torque must the bearings supply?
questions.explanation: $\tau = \omega L_\perp = 2ma^2\omega^2\sin\beta\cos\beta = 2(0.20)(0.10)^2(30)^2\sin 60^\circ\cos 60^\circ = 1.56$ N·m. 3.1 N·m leaves out $\cos\beta$; 1.8 N·m leaves out $\sin\beta$; 0.052 N·m uses $\omega$ instead of $\omega^2$ (that is $L_\perp$ itself, in kg·m²/s).

questions.stem: A student on a freely turning stool (student and stool $I = 2.5$ kg·m², initially at rest) holds a bicycle wheel ($I = 0.10$ kg·m²) spinning at 15 rad/s with its axle vertical. She flips the wheel upside down. How fast does she then turn?
questions.explanation: Vertical angular momentum is conserved: $0.10(15) = 1.5$ up before. After, the wheel has $1.5$ down, so she must have $3.0$ up: $\omega = 3.0/2.5 = 1.2$ rad/s. 0.60 rad/s forgets that the wheel's angular momentum reverses (a change of $2L$, not $L$); 2.4 rad/s doubles it again.

questions.stem: A gyroscope precesses at 0.50 rad/s. If its spin rate is tripled and the torque stays the same, it precesses at ___ rad/s. Give a fraction or a decimal.
questions.explanation: $\Omega = \tau/(I\omega)$ is inversely proportional to the spin rate: $0.50/3 = 1/6 \approx 0.167$ rad/s.

questions.stem: The small up-and-down bobbing of a gyroscope's axle on top of its steady precession is called ___.
questions.explanation: Nutation appears when the gyroscope is released from rest or disturbed; for a fast rotor it is small and quick, and friction damps it out.

questions.stem: Match each term to its description.
choices: Slow turning of a spin axis caused by a torque
Bobbing of the axis about its steady precession
An axis about which angular momentum is parallel to angular velocity
Lining up a principal axis with the axle
Putting the center of mass on the axle
questions.explanation: Precession is the steady swing of $\vec L$ under a perpendicular torque; nutation is the bobbing on top of it. About a principal axis, $\vec L \parallel \vec\omega$, so spinning needs no bearing torque. Dynamic balancing aligns a principal axis with the axle; putting the center of mass on the axle is static balancing, a different (and also necessary) step.

questions.stem: Which changes make a precessing top precess faster? Select all that apply.
choices: Moving its center of mass farther from the pivot
Making the rotor twice as heavy, same shape, size and spin
Tilting its axis further from vertical
Moving the rotor's mass toward its rim, same total mass and spin
questions.explanation: $\Omega = Mgr/(I\omega)$. A slower spin or a larger $r$ increases $\Omega$. Doubling the mass doubles both the torque and $I$, so $\Omega$ doesn't change. The tilt cancels out. Moving mass to the rim increases $I$, so $\Omega$ decreases.

questions.stem: A gyroscope precesses on a pivot. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A gyroscope drawn in perspective: a vertical post with its top as the pivot, a horizontal axle from the pivot to a spinning disk, an arrow continuing along the axle beyond the disk, an arrow pointing down from the disk's center, an arrow at the end of the axle arrow pointing sideways into the page, and a curved arrow circling above the post. Five parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: $\vec L$ (1) points along the spinning axle. The weight (2) acts at the rotor's center, and its torque about the pivot (4) is horizontal and perpendicular to the axle (3). Since $d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$, the end of $\vec L$ moves in the direction of the torque, so the axle precesses around the vertical (5). No centrifugal force is needed in this explanation.

questions.stem: Which statement about why a moving bicycle stays upright is best supported by experiments?
choices: Only the wheels' gyroscopic effect keeps it up
A bicycle can be self-stable even with the wheels' spin angular momentum canceled
Bicycles cannot balance at all without a rider
