Stability comes only from the wheels being thin
questions.explanation: In 2011 Kooijman and coworkers built a riderless bicycle whose wheels' spin angular momentum was canceled by counter-rotating wheels, and it still steered itself upright. Gyroscopic effects contribute in ordinary bicycles, but stability comes from several interacting design features (steering geometry, mass placement), and riderless bicycles can be self-stable at suitable speeds.

questions.stem: A small mass is placed somewhere inside a thin, uniform spherical shell, not at its center. The net gravitational force on it from the shell is
choices: toward the nearest part of the shell
toward the center of the shell
toward the farthest part of the shell
questions.explanation: Inside the shell the potential is the constant $-GM/R$, so its slope, and therefore the force, is zero everywhere inside. The nearby part of the shell pulls harder but contains less mass in the matching direction; the two effects cancel exactly for an inverse-square force.

questions.stem: Inside a uniform planet with surface gravity 9.8 m/s², what is $g$ halfway to the center ($r = R/2$)?
questions.explanation: Only the mass inside $r$ counts, $M(r) = M(r/R)^3$, so $g = g_s\,r/R = 9.8/2 = 4.9$ m/s². 39.2 m/s² applies the outside rule $1/r^2$ inside the planet; 2.45 m/s² uses $(r/R)^2$; 19.6 m/s² uses $1/r$.

questions.stem: A frictionless tunnel runs straight through the center of a uniform planet with $R = 3.39\times10^6$ m and surface gravity 3.7 m/s². How long does an object dropped in at one end take to reach the other end?
questions.explanation: The motion is simple harmonic with $\omega = \sqrt{g_s/R}$ and period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g_s} = 2\pi\sqrt{3.39\times10^6/3.7} = 6.01\times10^3$ s $= 100$ min. One end to the other is half a period, 50 min. 100 min is the round trip; 16 min is $\sqrt{R/g_s}$ without the $\pi$; 42 min is the answer for Earth.

questions.stem: In the real Earth, $g$ increases slightly as you go down through the mantle, instead of falling as in a uniform-planet model. Why?
choices: The rock above you pulls you downward
Earth's dense core holds a large share of its mass, so the mass inside your radius shrinks only slowly while $1/r^2$ grows
Earth's rotation is faster at depth
questions.explanation: $g(r) = GM(r)/r^2$. The rock you pass is relatively light, so $M(r)$ falls slowly while $r^2$ shrinks, and $g$ rises to about 10.7 m/s² near the core–mantle boundary before falling to zero at the center. The shell of rock above you exerts no net force at all (shell theorem), so it can't pull you down.

questions.stem: If the Moon were twice as far from Earth, its tidal acceleration on Earth would be
questions.explanation: Tidal acceleration is about $2GMd/D^3$, so doubling $D$ divides it by $2^3 = 8$. 1/4 is the change in the Moon's direct pull, which goes as $1/D^2$.

questions.stem: Why is there a tidal bulge on the side of Earth facing away from the Moon?
choices: The Moon's gravity pushes the far-side ocean away
Earth's rotation flings water outward only on that side
The Sun always pulls on the far side
The far side is pulled toward the Moon less than Earth's center is, so relative to the center it is left behind
questions.explanation: Gravity only attracts. Earth's center accelerates toward the Moon at $GM/D^2$; the far side, at $D + R$, is pulled less, so relative to the center it moves away from the Moon by about $2GMR/D^3$, the same size as the near-side bulge. The Sun's position changes during the month, so it can't explain a bulge that always faces away from the Moon.

questions.stem: The Sun's gravitational pull on Earth is about 180 times the Moon's, yet its tidal effect is only about half as large. Why?
choices: Tidal effects depend on the difference in pull across Earth, which falls off as $1/D^3$
Sunlight heats the ocean and cancels most of the Sun's tide
The Moon is denser than the Sun
The Sun's pull acts only on the day side
questions.explanation: The tidal acceleration $2GMd/D^3$ has one more power of distance than the direct pull $GM/D^2$. The Sun is about 390 times farther away than the Moon, so that extra factor of $1/D$ more than cancels its huge mass: the Sun's tide is about 0.46 of the Moon's.

questions.stem: Spring tides, with the largest tidal range, happen
choices: in the spring months of each year
at first and third quarter moon
at new moon and full moon
questions.explanation: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are lined up and the two tidal effects add. At the quarter moons they act at right angles and partly cancel (neap tides). "Spring" here has nothing to do with the season, and the alignment need not be exact enough for an eclipse.

questions.stem: Use the rigid-body estimate $D = R_p(2\rho_p/\rho_m)^{1/3}$ to find the Roche limit for an icy rubble-pile moon of density 1400 kg/m³ around a planet of radius 60,000 km and density 700 kg/m³.
questions.explanation: $(2\rho_p/\rho_m)^{1/3} = (2\times700/1400)^{1/3} = 1^{1/3} = 1$, so $D = 60{,}000$ km. 95,200 km swaps the two densities; 47,600 km leaves out the 2; 120,000 km is $2R_p$, multiplying by the 2 outside the cube root.

questions.stem: If the Earth–Moon distance were halved, the Moon's tidal acceleration on Earth would be multiplied by ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Tidal acceleration $\propto 1/D^3$, and $(1/2)^{-3} = 8$.

questions.stem: The Moon always keeps the same face toward Earth because tidal friction long ago matched its spin to its orbit. This state is called ___.
questions.explanation: Tidal locking (synchronous rotation): the Moon turns once on its axis per orbit, so the same hemisphere always faces Earth.

questions.stem: For a uniform planet of radius $R$, put these places in order of gravitational acceleration, smallest first.
questions.explanation: Inside, $g = g_s r/R$; outside, $g = g_s(R/r)^2$. Center: 0. $2R$: $0.25g_s$. $1.5R$: $0.44g_s$. $R/2$: $0.50g_s$. Surface: $g_s$, the largest anywhere.

questions.stem: Match each effect to its cause.
choices: Sun and Moon lined up with Earth
Sun and Moon at right angles as seen from Earth
Tidal friction braking its spin until it matched its orbit
Angular momentum passed from Earth's spin to the Moon's orbit
Earth's shadow falling on the Moon
questions.explanation: Aligned, the solar and lunar tides add (spring); at right angles they partly cancel (neap). Tidal friction slowed the Moon's spin to one turn per orbit (locking), and the tidal bulges on Earth, dragged ahead by its spin, transfer angular momentum to the Moon's orbit, which grows by about 3.8 cm a year. Earth's shadow causes lunar eclipses, not any of these.

questions.stem: The arrows show the tidal acceleration around Earth due to a distant body. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A circle with a dashed oval around it, stretched left and right. Small arrows around the circle point outward on the left and right sides and inward at the top and bottom. A small gray circle sits far to the right. Four places are numbered: the right end of the oval, the left end of the oval, the top of the circle, and the small gray circle.

choices: High tide facing away from the Moon
questions.explanation: The body producing the tide is the Moon (4). The ocean bulges toward it (1) and away from it (2), where the tidal acceleration points outward, and is drawn down where the arrows point inward, at right angles to the Earth–Moon line (3). The Sun also raises tides, but about half as large, and it isn't the body drawn here.

questions.stem: Which statements follow from the shell theorem? Select all that apply.
choices: A uniform spherical shell attracts an outside mass as if all its mass were at its center
Inside a uniform spherical shell the net gravitational force is zero
Inside a uniform spherical shell the gravitational potential is zero
An irregular asteroid attracts a nearby probe exactly like a point mass at its center
questions.explanation: Outside, the shell's potential is $-GM/r$, a point mass's; inside it is the constant $-GM/R$, so the force (its slope) is zero, but the potential itself is not zero. The theorem needs spherical symmetry; an irregular asteroid close up does not act like a point mass.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this pendulum diagram.

image.alt: A pendulum hanging from a pivot in the ceiling, pulled aside from the dashed vertical by an angle. A downward arrow comes from the bob, and two blue arrows split it into a part along the string and a part along the arc. Five points are numbered.

questions.explanation: The string (2) hangs from the pivot (1) and holds the bob (3). The only forces on the bob are its weight (4), straight down, and the string's tension (not drawn). The weight's component along the arc, $mg\sin\theta$ (5), points back toward the bottom and is the restoring force; the dashed arrow along the string is $mg\cos\theta$. There is no normal force or friction on a pendulum bob.

questions.stem: A 0.50 kg block on a spring with $k = 50$ N/m oscillates. Its angular frequency is ___ rad/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\omega = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{50/0.50} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ rad/s. (The frequency in hertz would be $10/2\pi = 1.59$ Hz.)

questions.stem: A block on a spring is released from rest at $x = +A$. Put these moments of its first full cycle in order.
choices: Passes $x = 0$ at top speed, moving in the $-x$ direction
Passes $x = 0$ at top speed, moving in the $+x$ direction
questions.explanation: With $x = A\cos\omega t$, the block reaches equilibrium (moving left) after $T/4$, the far end $x = -A$ after $T/2$, equilibrium again (moving right) after $3T/4$, and its starting point after one period $T$. The speed is largest at $x = 0$ and zero at the turning points.

questions.stem: Match each quantity for simple harmonic motion with amplitude $A$ and angular frequency $\omega$ to its formula.
left: Total mechanical energy of a mass on a spring
questions.explanation: $v_{\max} = A\omega$ at equilibrium; $a_{\max} = A\omega^2$ at the turning points; the energy is all spring energy $\tfrac12kA^2$ at the turning points; a pendulum has $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$. $2\pi\sqrt{k/m}$ has the ratio upside down (the spring period is $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$), and $A/\omega$ is not a quantity of SHM.

questions.stem: Treat a pendulum as an ideal simple pendulum swinging through small angles. Which changes would change its period? Select all that apply.
choices: Making the string four times as long
Using a bob with twice the mass
Pulling it aside to the left instead of to the right
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ depends only on the length and on $g$. Four times the length doubles the period; Mars has a smaller $g$, so the period is longer. The mass cancels out of the equation of motion, and the direction of the release makes no difference to the motion's timing.

questions.stem: This setup is a driven, damped oscillator. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A wheel at the left, turned by a motor, pushes a plate back and forth through a rod. The plate is joined by a zigzag coil to a block on a track, and the block is joined by a rod to a piston in a cylinder fixed to the right wall. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: The motor-driven wheel (1) is the driver: it moves the end of the spring back and forth, supplying the periodic force at the driving frequency. The spring (2) supplies $-kx$, the block (3) is the mass $m$, and the piston in oil (4) is the damper, which supplies the drag force $-bv$. There is no pulley or pendulum in the setup.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg mass hangs on a spring with $k = 50$ N/m. The damping constant that makes it critically damped is $b =$ ___ kg/s. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Critical damping means $\gamma = \omega_0$, i.e. $b = 2\sqrt{mk} = 2\sqrt{2.0 \times 50} = 2\sqrt{100} = 20$ kg/s.

questions.stem: Match each oscillator to how it moves.
left: Driven, after the transient dies away
choices: Oscillates forever at its natural frequency
questions.explanation: Light damping ($\gamma < \omega_0$) leaves an oscillation at $\omega'$ inside the envelope $e^{-\gamma t}$; $\gamma = \omega_0$ is the fastest return with no overshoot; $\gamma > \omega_0$ is a slow creep. A driven oscillator's steady state is at the driving frequency, not its own. Only an undamped, undriven oscillator would oscillate forever at $\omega_0$.

questions.stem: A lightly damped oscillator is driven exactly at its natural frequency $\omega_0$, in the steady state. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Its displacement lags the driving force by $90^\circ$
Halving the damping constant $b$ halves the amplitude
Its displacement is in phase with the driving force
questions.explanation: At $\omega = \omega_0$ the spring and inertia terms cancel, leaving $A = F_0/(b\omega_0)$ and $\tan\delta = \infty$, so $\delta = 90^\circ$ (the velocity, not the displacement, is in step with the force). Since $A \propto 1/b$, halving $b$ doubles the amplitude.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg mass on a spring ($k = 80$ N/m, so $\omega_0 = 20$ rad/s) with $b = 0.80$ kg/s is driven by a force of amplitude 2.0 N. Order these driving frequencies from the largest steady-state amplitude to the smallest.
questions.explanation: $A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (b\omega/m)^2}}$ with $F_0/m = 10$ and $b/m = 4.0$ s⁻¹ gives 0.125 m at 20 rad/s, 0.0955 m at 18, 0.0330 m at 10, 0.0194 m at 30 and 0.0031 m at 60 rad/s. Near resonance the response is largest; far above it inertia keeps the amplitude tiny.

questions.stem: The top picture is a transverse wave and the bottom one a longitudinal wave. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Top: a sine wave along a dashed horizontal line, with a double arrow between two neighboring high points and a short arrow from the dashed line up to a high point. Bottom: vertical lines in a tube, crowded together in some places and spread apart in others. Six points are numbered.

questions.explanation: A crest (1) is a high point and a trough (2) a low point. The distance between neighboring crests (3) is the wavelength, and the height of a crest above the equilibrium line (4) is the amplitude. In the longitudinal wave, the crowded region (5) is a compression and the spread-out region (6) a rarefaction. Nodes and antinodes belong to standing waves, not to a single traveling wave.

questions.stem: Waves travel along a rope at 120 m/s. A 40 Hz wave on it has a wavelength of ___ m. Give only the number.
Match each wave to its kind.
left: A pulse on a stretched guitar string
A surface wave on the ocean
questions.explanation: Air molecules move back and forth along the direction sound travels (longitudinal). A string moves sideways to the wave's direction (transverse). Water parcels in a surface wave move in small circles, a mix of both. Radio waves are electromagnetic and need no medium.

questions.stem: A wave on a light string passes into a heavier string (larger $\mu$) under the same tension. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$ falls when $\mu$ rises. The frequency is set by the source (every point of the joint shakes the next string at the same rate), so it stays the same, and $\lambda = v/f$ shrinks along with $v$.

questions.stem: You know a string's mass, length and tension. Put the steps for finding its third harmonic in order.
choices: Find the linear mass density $\mu = m/L$
questions.explanation: Each step needs the one before: the speed needs $\mu$, the fundamental needs the speed, and the harmonics are whole-number multiples of the fundamental. (Example 2 of the lesson follows exactly these steps.)

questions.stem: One machine produces 70 dB at a certain spot. Two identical machines running together produce ___ dB there. Give the answer to the nearest whole decibel; give only the number.
questions.explanation: Two machines double the intensity, which adds $10\log_{10}2 = 3.01$ dB: $70 + 3 = 73$ dB. Decibel levels don't add directly (140 dB would be wrong).

questions.stem: Match each standing wave to how its length $L$ compares with the wavelength.
left: Pipe open at both ends, fundamental
Pipe closed at one end, fundamental
Pipe closed at one end, third harmonic
String fixed at both ends, second harmonic
choices: L is a quarter of a wavelength
L is three quarters of a wavelength
questions.explanation: Open–open: antinode, node, antinode, so $L = \lambda/2$. Closed–open: node to antinode is $\lambda/4$, and the third harmonic fits three of those, $3\lambda/4$. A string's $n$th harmonic has $L = n\lambda/2$, so the second has $L = \lambda$.

questions.stem: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 110 Hz. Which of these frequencies can it also resonate at? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A closed–open pipe resonates only at odd multiples of its fundamental: 110, 330, 550, 770 Hz… 220 Hz and 440 Hz are even multiples, which a closed pipe lacks.

questions.stem: Put these sounds in order from the lowest sound intensity level to the highest.
questions.explanation: The threshold of hearing is 0 dB ($10^{-12}$ W/m²), conversation about 60 dB, a rock concert about 110 dB and the threshold of pain about 120 dB (1 W/m²).

questions.stem: Air is still. In which situations does a listener hear a higher frequency than the source emits? Select all that apply.
choices: The source moves toward a stationary listener
The listener moves toward a stationary source
Source and listener move in the same direction at the same speed
The source moves away from a stationary listener
questions.explanation: Any approach raises the frequency: the upper signs in $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$. If both move the same way at the same speed $u$, the listener recedes and the source approaches by equal amounts: $f' = f\dfrac{v - u}{v - u} = f$, no shift. A receding source lowers the frequency.

questions.stem: A square wave (equal $+A$ and $-A$ halves) repeats 100 times per second. Which frequencies does its spectrum contain?
questions.explanation: The fundamental is $1/T = 100$ Hz, and the square wave's half-wave symmetry removes every even harmonic, leaving 100, 300, 500 Hz… The first choice includes the missing even harmonics; 200, 400, 600 Hz… leaves out the fundamental and keeps only even harmonics; 50, 150, 250 Hz… are not multiples of 100 Hz at all.

questions.stem: A square wave switches between $+3.0$ V and $-3.0$ V. What is the amplitude of its third harmonic?
questions.explanation: $b_n = \dfrac{4A}{n\pi}$, so $b_3 = \dfrac{4(3.0)}{3\pi} = 1.27 \approx 1.3$ V. 1.0 V is $A/3$ (forgetting the $4/\pi$); 3.8 V is the fundamental, $4A/\pi$; 0.42 V is $4/(3\pi)$ without the factor $A$.

questions.stem: The constant term $a_0$ of a Fourier series equals the ___ value of the signal over one period.
questions.explanation: $a_0 = \dfrac1T\displaystyle\int_0^T y\,dt$, the average (mean) of the signal over a period. Every harmonic averages to zero, so only $a_0$ survives the averaging.

questions.stem: What fraction of a square wave's average power is carried by its fundamental alone?
questions.explanation: By Parseval's theorem the fundamental contributes $\tfrac12c_1^2 = \tfrac12(4A/\pi)^2 = (8/\pi^2)A^2 = 0.81A^2$ out of $\overline{y^2} = A^2$. 93% is the first three odd harmonics together; 64% is $\tfrac12(4/\pi)$, the amplitude ratio without squaring; 41% has an extra factor $\tfrac12$.

questions.stem: Which of these contain only odd harmonics? Select all that apply.
choices: A square wave with equal $+A$ and $-A$ halves
A string plucked at its exact middle
A string plucked one quarter of the way along
questions.explanation: The square wave has half-wave symmetry, so its even harmonics vanish. A string plucked at the middle has $\sin(n\pi/2) = 0$ for every even $n$ (the middle is a node of every even harmonic). A sawtooth has every harmonic, and a string plucked at $L/4$ has a strong 2nd harmonic (it lacks only the 4th, 8th, …).

questions.stem: As more and more terms of a square wave's Fourier series are added, what happens to the overshoot beside each jump?
choices: It stays about 9% of the jump but gets wider
It stays about 9% of the jump but gets narrower
questions.explanation: This is the Gibbs phenomenon: the peak of the partial sum next to a jump stays about 9% of the jump above the flat top (about $1.18A$ for a jump from $-A$ to $+A$), while the region it occupies narrows as more terms are added.

questions.stem: A string is plucked one quarter of the way along. Order these harmonics from the largest starting amplitude to the smallest.
questions.explanation: $B_n/B_1 = \dfrac{\sin(n\pi/4)}{n^2\sin(\pi/4)}$ gives 1, 0.354, 0.111, then 0.040 for $n = 5$. The 4th harmonic has $\sin\pi = 0$: the pluck point $L/4$ is one of its nodes, so it is missing entirely.

questions.stem: Match each signal to its spectrum.
questions.explanation: Square wave: $4A/(n\pi)$ for odd $n$. Sawtooth: $2A/(n\pi)$ for every $n$. Plucked string: $B_n \propto \sin(n\pi d/L)/n^2$, and at $d = L/2$ the even ones vanish. A pure sine is already a single harmonic.

questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends is plucked one fifth of the way along its length. The lowest harmonic missing from its sound is harmonic number $n =$ ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $B_n \propto \sin(n\pi/5)$, which is first zero at $n = 5$: the point $L/5$ is a node of the 5th harmonic (and of the 10th, 15th, …).

questions.stem: A string is plucked one third of the way along. What is the starting amplitude of its 2nd harmonic relative to the fundamental?
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{\sin(2\pi/3)}{2^2\sin(\pi/3)} = \dfrac14 = 0.25$, since $\sin(2\pi/3) = \sin(\pi/3)$. 0.50 forgets to square $n$; 0.125 uses $n^3$; 0 would need the pluck point to be a node of the 2nd harmonic, but its only interior node is at $L/2$.

questions.stem: A periodic signal is $y(t) = 2 + 3\cos\omega_1t + 4\sin\omega_1t$. What is the amplitude of its fundamental?
questions.explanation: The cosine and sine of the same frequency combine into one sinusoid of amplitude $c_1 = \sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$. 7 adds the coefficients, 9 also adds the constant (which is $a_0$, not part of any harmonic), and 1 subtracts them.

questions.stem: A click lasts about 1 ms. Roughly what range of frequencies does it contain?
questions.explanation: $\Delta f \sim 1/\Delta t = 1/(10^{-3}\text{ s}) = 10^3$ Hz, a spread of about 1 kHz (order of magnitude only). A short pulse is never a single frequency; only a signal lasting many cycles can be nearly pure.

questions.stem: A periodic signal is an even function of time, $y(-t) = y(t)$. What does its Fourier series contain?
choices: Only cosine terms, plus possibly a constant
questions.explanation: $\sin(n\omega_1t)$ is odd, so multiplying an even $y$ by it and integrating over a symmetric period gives zero: every $b_n = 0$. Cosines and the constant are even and can remain. Evenness says nothing about which harmonic numbers appear; that takes half-wave symmetry.

questions.stem: With $\omega_1 = 2\pi/T$ and every integral taken over one full period $T$, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Different harmonics are orthogonal, and a sine is orthogonal to every cosine, even of the same frequency ($\sin\cos = \tfrac12\sin(6\omega_1t)$ integrates to zero). A harmonic times itself averages to $\tfrac12$, so its integral is $T/2$, not zero.

questions.stem: Two 1.0 kg blocks are connected wall–spring–block–spring–block–spring–wall, with outer springs $k = 100$ N/m and coupling spring $k' = 25$ N/m. What are the two normal-mode angular frequencies?
questions.explanation: In phase: $\omega_1 = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{100} = 10.0$ rad/s. Out of phase: $\omega_2 = \sqrt{(k + 2k')/m} = \sqrt{150} = 12.2$ rad/s. 11.2 uses $k + k'$ (forgetting the coupling spring stretches twice as far); 14.1 uses $k + 4k'$; giving the in-phase mode 11.2 wrongly lets the idle middle spring act.

questions.stem: Two equal masses are joined wall–spring–mass–spring–mass–spring–wall. In the in-phase normal mode, the stretch of the middle (coupling) spring is always ___.
questions.explanation: In phase, $x_1 = x_2$ at every instant, so the middle spring's stretch $x_2 - x_1$ is always zero. That is why this mode's frequency, $\sqrt{k/m}$, doesn't depend on $k'$.

questions.stem: For two equal masses joined by springs $k$, $k'$, $k$ between two walls, which mode has the higher frequency, and why?
choices: The in-phase mode, because both masses move together
The out-of-phase mode, because the coupling spring adds stiffness
It depends on the amplitude of the motion
questions.explanation: In the out-of-phase mode the coupling spring is stretched and compressed, adding $2k'$ to each mass's effective stiffness: $\omega_2 = \sqrt{(k + 2k')/m} > \sqrt{k/m}$. Normal-mode frequencies of a linear system don't depend on amplitude.

questions.stem: Which statements describe a normal mode of a system of coupled oscillators? Select all that apply.
choices: Every part oscillates at the same frequency
The ratios of the parts' amplitudes stay fixed
Energy flows back and forth between the masses
Each mass oscillates at its own different frequency
questions.explanation: In a normal mode the whole system moves at one frequency with a fixed shape, so nothing flows from one part to another. Energy sloshing between masses (beats) happens when two modes with different frequencies are mixed.

questions.stem: Two identical pendulums, 1.00 m long with 0.50 kg bobs, are joined at the bobs by a weak spring with $k' = 0.10$ N/m. One is released while the other hangs still. About how long until all the motion has passed to the second pendulum? ($g = 9.80$ m/s²)
questions.explanation: $\omega_1 = \sqrt{g/L} = 3.1305$ rad/s and $\omega_2 = \sqrt{g/L + 2k'/m} = \sqrt{10.20} = 3.1937$ rad/s, so $\Delta\omega = 0.0632$ rad/s and $t = \pi/\Delta\omega = 49.7 \approx 50$ s. 99 s is $2\pi/\Delta\omega$, the time for the motion to come all the way back; 16 s is $1/\Delta\omega$; 2.0 s is one swing of a single pendulum.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding the normal modes of a set of coupled masses in order.
choices: Write Newton's second law for each mass
Assume every coordinate oscillates as $a_j\cos\omega t$
Set the determinant of the amplitude equations to zero
For each frequency, find the amplitude ratios
questions.explanation: The equations of motion come first; the trial solution turns them into linear equations for the amplitudes; a nonzero solution needs a zero determinant, which gives the frequencies; putting each frequency back gives that mode's shape.

questions.stem: Two equal masses are joined wall–spring–mass–spring–mass–spring–wall and released from rest. Match each starting position to the motion that follows.
choices: Beats: the motion passes back and forth between the masses
questions.explanation: Starting in a mode's exact shape gives that mode alone. $x_1 = A$, $x_2 = 0$ is half in-phase plus half out-of-phase ($q_1 = q_2 = A$), and the two frequencies beat. Any displacement from equilibrium makes the masses move.

questions.stem: Two equal beads sit on a light string under tension, dividing it into three equal segments. What is the ratio of the higher mode frequency to the lower?
questions.explanation: The beads act like the two-mass system with $k = k' = F/a$, so $\omega_2/\omega_1 = \sqrt{(k + 2k')/k} = \sqrt3 \approx 1.73$. The ratio 2 belongs to a continuous string's harmonics; with only two beads the second mode falls below that.

questions.stem: Three masses on a track are joined to each other and to two walls by springs, each moving only along the track. The system has ___ normal modes. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Each mass has one coordinate, so there are 3 coordinates and therefore 3 normal modes.

questions.stem: As a beaded string gets more and more beads (same length, tension and total mass per length), what do the frequencies of its lowest modes approach?
choices: Zero, because each bead's mass shrinks
The harmonics $f_n = nv/(2L)$ of a continuous string
questions.explanation: For small angles $\sin\dfrac{n\pi}{2(N+1)} \approx \dfrac{n\pi a}{2L}$, so $\omega_n \to \dfrac{n\pi}{L}\sqrt{F/\mu}$ and $f_n = nv/(2L)$ with $v = \sqrt{F/\mu}$. Odd harmonics only, $nv/(4L)$, belong to a pipe closed at one end.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a medium to show dispersion?
choices: Its wave speed depends on frequency (or wavelength)
Its waves lose energy as they travel
Its waves spread out over a larger area with distance
It reflects waves at its boundaries
questions.explanation: Dispersion means the wave speed depends on frequency, as for the high modes of a beaded string, where short waves travel more slowly. Energy loss is damping (absorption), and spreading over a larger area is what gives the inverse-square law.

questions.stem: Which vibrational modes of a CO₂ molecule absorb infrared light? Select all that apply.
choices: Motion of the whole molecule in a straight line
questions.explanation: The asymmetric stretch and the two bending modes absorb infrared, which makes CO₂ a greenhouse gas; the symmetric stretch does not. Moving the whole molecule along a line is not a vibration at all, so it is not one of the four vibrational modes.

questions.stem: Two 0.50 kg blocks with $k = 200$ N/m and $k' = 50$ N/m have modes at 20.0 and 24.5 rad/s. Block 1 is pulled aside and released while block 2 is held at equilibrium and released at the same instant. About when is block 1 first momentarily without motion while block 2 swings fully?
questions.explanation: $\Delta\omega = 24.49 - 20.00 = 4.49$ rad/s, so the transfer time is $\pi/\Delta\omega = 0.70$ s. 1.40 s is $2\pi/\Delta\omega$, when the motion is back in block 1; 0.22 s is $1/\Delta\omega$; 0.14 s is $\pi$ divided by the average frequency.

questions.stem: For the two-mass system, $(k + k' - m\omega^2)a_1 - k'a_2 = 0$. Put in $\omega^2 = (k + 2k')/m$. What is the amplitude ratio $a_2/a_1$?
questions.explanation: $k + k' - (k + 2k') = -k'$, so $-k'a_1 - k'a_2 = 0$ and $a_2 = -a_1$: the masses move in opposite directions, the out-of-phase mode. $+1$ is the in-phase mode's ratio, from $\omega^2 = k/m$.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this hydraulic lift.

image.alt: A U-shaped container of fluid. A narrow tube on the left has a small piston pushed down by an arrow from above; a wide tube on the right has a large piston carrying a load, with an arrow pointing up under it.

questions.explanation: You push down on the small piston (1) with the input force (3). That creates a pressure $F_1/A_1$, which the hydraulic fluid (5) passes on undiminished (Pascal's principle) to the large piston (2), so the output force (4) is $F_2 = F_1A_2/A_1$, much larger than $F_1$.

questions.stem: Using the rule that every 10 m of water adds about 1 atm, the gauge pressure on a diver 25 m below the surface of a lake is about ___ atm. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Gauge pressure counts only the water: 25 m is 2.5 times 10 m, so about 2.5 atm. The absolute pressure adds the atmosphere on top: about 3.5 atm. (The exact gauge value is $\rho gh = 1000(9.8)(25) = 2.45\times10^5$ Pa $= 2.42$ atm, so 2.4 is also accepted.)

questions.stem: Which changes would increase the buoyant force on an object held completely under water? Select all that apply.
choices: Moving it from fresh water into seawater
Replacing it with an object of the same volume but greater density
Making its volume larger while keeping it submerged
Lowering it to a greater depth in the same water
questions.explanation: $F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ depends only on the fluid's density and the displaced volume. Seawater is denser than fresh water, and a larger object displaces more water, so both increase $F_B$. The object's own density changes its weight, not the buoyant force, and depth doesn't matter: the pressure difference between bottom and top is the same at any depth.

questions.stem: Each object is held completely under fresh water (1000 kg/m³) and released. Match it to what happens.
left: Sealed jar weighted to an average of 1000 kg/m³
choices: Floats with about 92% of its volume submerged
Floats with half its volume submerged
Floats with about 8% of its volume submerged
questions.explanation: An object denser than the fluid sinks; a less dense one rises and floats with the fraction $\rho_{\text{obj}}/\rho_{\text{fluid}}$ submerged: $917/1000 \approx 92\%$ for ice and $500/1000 = 50\%$ for pine. Equal densities give neutral buoyancy. About 8% is the fraction of the ice above the water.

questions.stem: The picture shows the pressure forces on a block held under water. Why is the net force from the water upward?

image.alt: A block under water with short arrows pushing down on its top face, longer arrows pushing up on its bottom face, and equal arrows pushing on its two sides.

choices: The bottom face is deeper, so the water pressure on it is greater than on the top face
The water pushes harder on the sides than on the top, squeezing the block upward
Air pressing on the surface pushes up on the block from below
The block's weight pushes the water down, and the water pushes back up equally
questions.explanation: Pressure grows with depth, $P = P_0 + \rho gh$, so the upward push on the deeper bottom face beats the downward push on the top face; the side forces cancel. The difference is $\rho_{\text{fluid}}Vg$, the weight of the displaced water. Atmospheric pressure acts on both faces and cancels. The last choice is a third-law pairing, and the buoyant force doesn't depend on the block's weight.

questions.stem: Water flows from left to right through this Venturi tube. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A horizontal pipe that narrows in the middle and widens again, with dashed lines running along it that crowd together in the narrow part. Two thin vertical tubes rise from the top of the pipe, one over the wide part and one over the narrow part, holding liquid columns of different heights.

questions.explanation: By continuity the water speeds up in the narrow throat (2) and is slower in the wide section (1); by Bernoulli's equation, at the same height faster flow means lower pressure. The vertical tubes show it: the liquid column over the wide part (4) stands higher than the one over the throat. The dashed lines are streamlines (3), which crowd together where the flow is fast.

questions.stem: Water flows at 2.0 m/s in a hose of diameter 2.0 cm. A nozzle narrows the opening to a diameter of 0.50 cm. The water leaves the nozzle at ___ m/s. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Continuity: $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$, and area goes as diameter squared. The diameter shrinks by a factor of 4, so the area shrinks by 16 and the speed rises by 16: $v_2 = 16(2.0) = 32$ m/s. (Scaling by the diameter alone would give 8 m/s.)

questions.stem: Which assumptions belong to the ideal-fluid model used with Bernoulli's equation? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: An ideal fluid is incompressible, nonviscous, steady and irrotational. Turbulent flow, full of eddies, is the opposite of the smooth, steady flow the model describes, and Bernoulli's equation applies to it only roughly.

questions.stem: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe whose diameter changes along its length. Order these sections from the highest pressure to the lowest.
questions.explanation: By continuity, the narrower the section, the faster the water ($v \propto 1/D^2$). For a horizontal pipe Bernoulli's equation gives $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 = \text{constant}$, so the faster the flow, the lower the pressure. The widest section has the highest pressure and the narrowest the lowest.

questions.stem: An open tank of cross-section $A$, filled with water to a depth of 2.0 m, drains through a small hole of area $a = A/100$ in its bottom. Using $t = \dfrac Aa\sqrt{\dfrac{2h_0}{g}}$ with $g = 9.8$ m/s², how long does it take to empty?
questions.explanation: $t = 100\sqrt{2(2.0)/9.8} = 100(0.639) = 63.9$ s. Assuming the water keeps leaving at its initial Torricelli speed $\sqrt{2gh_0} = 6.26$ m/s gives $Ah_0/(av_0) = 31.9$ s, half the true time, because the outflow slows as the level drops. 45.2 s drops the 2 inside the square root, and 626 s is $100\sqrt{2gh_0}$, a speed times 100, not a time.

questions.stem: Heat moves in three different ways in this kitchen scene. Name the way marked at each number.

image.alt: A pot of water on a glowing stove burner. Arrows run along the metal handle, loops of arrows circulate inside the water, and wavy arrows go from the burner to a hand held beside it.

questions.explanation: Heat travels along the solid metal handle by conduction (1), molecule to molecule. In the water, hot water rises and cooler water sinks, carrying heat by convection (2), bulk motion of the fluid. The glowing burner warms the hand across the air gap by radiation (3), electromagnetic waves that need no medium.

questions.stem: Melting 2.0 kg of ice that is already at 0°C takes ___ kJ of heat. ($L_f = 3.34\times10^5$ J/kg; give only the number.)
questions.explanation: During a phase change the temperature stays put, so only the latent heat counts: $Q = mL_f = 2.0(3.34\times10^5) = 6.68\times10^5$ J $= 668$ kJ.

questions.stem: 1 kg of ice at −20°C is heated steadily until it is steam at 110°C. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The temperature stays at 0°C while the ice melts
Boiling the water takes more heat than melting the ice
Heat added while the ice melts raises the average kinetic energy of its molecules
Warming the liquid water from 0°C to 100°C takes more heat than melting the ice
questions.explanation: At a phase change the heat breaks bonds instead of raising the temperature, so the temperature (and the average kinetic energy) stays fixed while ice melts. Boiling takes $L_v = 2260$ kJ against $L_f = 334$ kJ for melting, and warming the water by 100 K takes $4186(100) = 419$ kJ, also more than 334 kJ.

questions.stem: Put the steps for solving a calorimetry problem in order.
choices: List each object's mass, specific heat and starting temperature
Write $Q = mc(T_f - T_i)$ for each object, adding $\pm mL$ for any phase change
Set the sum of all the $Q$ values equal to zero
Check that $T_f$ lies between the starting temperatures
questions.explanation: Calorimetry is energy bookkeeping: gather the data, write each object's heat with the same sign convention ($T_f - T_i$), use conservation ($\sum Q = 0$ in an insulated container), solve, and then check the answer makes sense. A final temperature outside the starting range means a sign error or a wrong assumption about phases.

questions.stem: Coffee at 90°C cools in a 20°C room following Newton's law of cooling with $\kappa = 0.05$ per minute. What is its temperature after 20 minutes?
questions.explanation: $T = T_s + (T_0 - T_s)e^{-\kappa t} = 20 + 70e^{-1} = 20 + 25.8 = 45.8$°C. Applying the decay to the whole temperature, $90e^{-1}$, gives 33.1°C; it's the difference from the room that decays. 62.5°C is the value after 10 minutes. 20.0°C comes from assuming the initial cooling rate, $0.05(70) = 3.5$°C/min, lasts all 20 minutes; in fact the rate slows as the coffee approaches room temperature.

questions.stem: A 200 m steel bridge ($\alpha = 12\times10^{-6}$ K⁻¹) warms by 30 K. It gets longer by ___ cm. (Give only the number.)
The picture shows the kinetic-theory model of gas pressure. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Molecules in a rectangular box. One molecule travels toward the right-hand wall, which is shaded, bounces off it and travels back to the left. A double-headed arrow runs along the bottom of the box.

questions.explanation: A molecule moving toward the wall (2) with $x$-component $+v_x$ bounces off the wall (1) and leaves (3) with $-v_x$, giving the wall momentum $2mv_x$. It crosses the box and back, a distance $2L$ where $L$ is the box's length (4), before hitting the same wall again, so it hits every $2L/v_x$ seconds. Averaging over all molecules gives $PV = \tfrac13Nm\overline{v^2}$.

questions.stem: Match each situation with the gas law to use.
left: A fixed amount of gas at constant temperature
A fixed amount of gas at constant pressure
A fixed amount of gas at constant volume
Finding how many moles a tank holds
questions.explanation: Boyle: $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$ at constant $T$. Charles: $V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2$ at constant $P$. Gay-Lussac: $P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2$ at constant $V$. When the amount of gas is asked for or changes, use $PV = nRT$. Bernoulli's equation is for flowing fluids.

questions.stem: At the same temperature, hydrogen molecules ($M = 2$ g/mol) have an rms speed ___ times that of oxygen molecules ($M = 32$ g/mol).
questions.explanation: $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$, so at equal $T$ the ratio is $\sqrt{M_{\text{O}_2}/M_{\text{H}_2}} = \sqrt{32/2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$. (Not 16: the speed goes as the square root.)

questions.stem: The absolute temperature of a fixed amount of ideal gas is doubled. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The average translational kinetic energy per molecule doubles
The rms speed of the molecules doubles
The pressure doubles if the volume is held fixed
The mass of each molecule doubles
questions.explanation: $\tfrac12m\overline{v^2} = \tfrac32k_BT$, so the average kinetic energy is proportional to $T$ and doubles. The rms speed goes as $\sqrt T$, so it rises by $\sqrt2 \approx 1.41$, not 2. At fixed volume $P \propto T$ (Gay-Lussac), so the pressure doubles. Molecular mass doesn't depend on temperature.

questions.stem: 1.00 mol of an ideal gas at 127°C occupies 20.0 L. What is its pressure?
questions.explanation: Convert first: $T = 127 + 273 = 400$ K and $V = 20.0\times10^{-3}$ m³. Then $P = \dfrac{nRT}{V} = \dfrac{1.00(8.314)(400)}{0.0200} = 1.66\times10^5$ Pa $= 166$ kPa. Using 127 (Celsius) gives 52.8 kPa; leaving $V$ as 20.0 gives 166 Pa; and converting 20.0 L to 0.200 m³ (1 L taken as $10^{-2}$ m³) gives 16.6 kPa.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this piston-and-cylinder setup.

image.alt: A gas in a vertical cylinder under a movable piston that holds up a load. The cylinder sits on a hot plate; two arrows point up from the plate into the gas, and a third arrow beside the cylinder points up.

questions.explanation: The gas (2) is the system. Heat $Q$ flows into it (4) from the hot plate, a hot reservoir (5). The gas pushes the piston (1) and its load upward, doing work $W$ on the surroundings (3). The first law, $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$, says what's left changes the gas's internal energy.

questions.stem: Match each ideal-gas process to the statement that defines or follows directly from it.
choices: No heat flows in or out
Pressure and volume both stay constant
questions.explanation: Isobaric means constant pressure. Isochoric means constant volume, so $W = \int P\,dV = 0$. Isothermal means constant temperature, and an ideal gas's internal energy depends only on $T$, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$. Adiabatic means $Q = 0$. If both $P$ and $V$ stayed constant, nothing would happen to an ideal gas at all.

questions.stem: A gas goes around the rectangular cycle A (1.0 L, 300 kPa) → B (4.0 L, 300 kPa) → C (4.0 L, 100 kPa) → D (1.0 L, 100 kPa) → A. The net work done by the gas per cycle is ___ J. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: The net work is the enclosed area: $(300 - 100)\text{ kPa}\times(4.0 - 1.0)\text{ L} = 200\times10^3\text{ Pa}\times3.0\times10^{-3}\text{ m}^3 = 600$ J. Along A → B the gas does 900 J; along C → D, 300 J is done on it; the vertical legs do no work. (1 kPa·L = 1 J.)

questions.stem: An ideal gas goes once around a clockwise cycle that encloses a nonzero area on a PV diagram. Which quantities are zero for the complete cycle? Select all that apply.
choices: The net work done by the gas
The net heat absorbed by the gas
questions.explanation: The gas returns to its starting state, so every state variable, including $T$ and $E_{\text{int}}$, is back where it started. Work and heat are not state variables: the net work is the enclosed area (positive for a clockwise loop), and the first law with $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$ makes the net heat equal to it, $Q_{\text{net}} = W_{\text{net}} > 0$.

questions.stem: A gas is compressed adiabatically, with 250 J of work done on it. What are $Q$ and $\Delta E_{\text{int}}$? (Use $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$, with $W$ the work done by the gas.)
questions.explanation: Adiabatic means $Q = 0$. Work done on the gas is 250 J, so the work done by it is $W = -250$ J, and $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0 - (-250) = +250$ J: compression heats the gas. $-250$ J is the sign error of using $W = +250$ J. The choices with $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$ describe an isothermal compression, which has to give off heat.

questions.stem: The picture shows energy-flow diagrams for a heat engine (left) and a refrigerator (right). Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Two diagrams, each with a box at the top, a box at the bottom and a circle between them. Left, labeled Heat engine: arrows point down from the top box into the circle and from the circle to the bottom box, and an arrow points out of the circle to the right. Right, labeled Refrigerator: arrows point up from the bottom box into the circle and from the circle to the top box, and an arrow points into the circle from the left.

choices: Heat removed from the cold space
Heat flowing spontaneously from cold to hot
Heat rejected to the cold reservoir
questions.explanation: An engine takes heat $Q_H$ from the hot reservoir (1), turns part of it into work output (3) and rejects $Q_C$ to the cold reservoir (2). A refrigerator runs the other way: work input (4) drives heat out of the cold space (5) and delivers $Q_H = Q_C + W$ to the hot side. That heat moves "uphill" only because work is supplied; it never flows from cold to hot on its own.

questions.stem: Put the four steps of the Carnot cycle in order, starting with the step in which the gas takes in heat from the hot reservoir.
questions.explanation: The gas absorbs $Q_H$ while expanding at $T_H$, keeps expanding with no heat flow so it cools to $T_C$, is compressed at $T_C$ while rejecting $Q_C$, and finally is compressed adiabatically back up to $T_H$, ready to start again.

questions.stem: A Carnot engine runs between reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is ___ %. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - T_C/T_H = 1 - 300/600 = 0.50$, or 50%. No engine running between these two reservoirs can do better.

questions.stem: Which of these processes increase the total entropy of the universe? Select all that apply.
choices: Heat flowing from a hot pan into cooler air
A gas expanding freely into a vacuum
An ideal Carnot engine completing one cycle
A sliding block brought to rest by friction
questions.explanation: Heat flow across a finite temperature difference, free expansion and friction are all irreversible, so they increase the total entropy. An ideal Carnot engine is reversible: over a cycle the gas returns to its start and the reservoirs' changes cancel, $Q_H/T_H = Q_C/T_C$, so the total entropy change is zero.

questions.stem: A heat pump keeps a house at 20°C when it is 0°C outside. What is the largest possible coefficient of performance for heating, $Q_H/W$?
questions.explanation: The Carnot limit for heating is $\dfrac{T_H}{T_H - T_C} = \dfrac{293}{293 - 273} = 14.7$, in kelvins. 13.7 is the refrigerator COP $T_C/(T_H - T_C)$, 1.0 comes from using Celsius ($20/20$), and 0.068 is the Carnot efficiency $1 - T_C/T_H$ of an engine between these temperatures. Real heat pumps typically reach 2 to 4 in such conditions, well below the limit.

questions.stem: What is the air-standard efficiency of an Otto cycle with compression ratio 8 ($\gamma = 1.4$)?
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - r^{1-\gamma} = 1 - 8^{-0.4} = 1 - 0.435 = 0.565$. Using $r^{-\gamma}$ instead gives 94.6%, and $1 - 1/r$ gives 87.5%. 44.8% uses the Brayton exponent $(\gamma - 1)/\gamma$, which belongs with a pressure ratio, not a volume ratio.

questions.stem: Air at 290 K is compressed adiabatically in an engine with compression ratio 9 ($\gamma = 1.4$). What is its temperature at the end of the compression stroke?
questions.explanation: Along an adiabat $TV^{\gamma-1}$ is constant, so $T_2 = T_1r^{\gamma-1} = 290(9)^{0.4} = 290(2.41) = 698$ K. 543 K uses the exponent $(\gamma - 1)/\gamma$ (for pressure ratios), 2610 K multiplies by $r$ itself, and 6290 K uses $r^\gamma$, which is the pressure ratio $P_2/P_1$.

questions.stem: In the air-standard Otto cycle, the burning of the fuel is modeled as heat added at constant ___.
questions.explanation: Gasoline burns so quickly after the spark that the piston barely moves, so the Otto cycle adds heat at constant volume (the vertical line 2 → 3 on the PV diagram). The Diesel and Brayton cycles add heat at constant pressure.

questions.stem: Name the numbered steps of this Otto cycle.

image.alt: A PV diagram with a closed loop: a vertical line at small volume, two curves falling from left to right, and a short vertical line at large volume. Arrows run up the left vertical line, down along the upper curve, down the right vertical line and back up along the lower curve.

questions.explanation: The loop runs clockwise. The lower curve (3) is the adiabatic compression from large to small volume; the vertical line at small volume (1) is the spark, heat added at constant volume; the upper curve (2) is the adiabatic power stroke; and the short vertical line at large volume (4) is heat rejected at constant volume when the exhaust valve opens. There is no isothermal step, and the Otto cycle adds heat at constant volume, not constant pressure.

questions.stem: Starting with the piston at the bottom and the cylinder full of fresh air (state 1), put the four steps of the Otto cycle in order.
choices: Heat rejected at constant volume (exhaust valve opens)
questions.explanation: 1 → 2: the piston compresses the air with no heat flow. 2 → 3: the spark fires and the fuel burns at almost constant volume. 3 → 4: the hot gas pushes the piston down. 4 → 1: the exhaust valve opens and the pressure falls at the bottom of the stroke, returning to state 1.

questions.stem: Match each ideal cycle to the machine it models.
choices: Engine that ignites its fuel by compressing air
A theoretical limit too slow to build
questions.explanation: Otto: spark ignition, heat added at constant volume. Diesel: compression ignition, heat added at constant pressure. Brayton: continuous flow through compressor, combustor and turbine, heat added and rejected at constant pressure. Carnot: two isotherms and two adiabats, the efficiency limit, but its isothermal steps would be impractically slow.

questions.stem: Which changes raise the air-standard efficiency of an Otto cycle? Select all that apply.
choices: A working gas with a larger $\gamma$
Burning more fuel in each cycle
A larger cylinder with the same compression ratio
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - 1/r^{\gamma-1}$ depends only on $r$ and $\gamma$, and it grows when either grows. More fuel or a bigger cylinder gives more work per cycle, but not a larger fraction of the heat turned into work.

questions.stem: What mainly limits the compression ratio of a gasoline engine to about 8–12?
choices: The cylinder walls cannot withstand higher pressures
The fuel–air mixture would ignite on its own before the spark (knock)
The Otto efficiency formula stops increasing above $r = 12$
Higher ratios would make the intake stroke do net work
questions.explanation: Gasoline engines compress fuel and air together, and compression heats the mixture. Too much compression makes it autoignite in uncontrolled pockets: engine knock. Diesel engines, which compress only air, routinely run at 14–22, so the walls can take it. The ideal efficiency keeps rising with $r$, just more slowly.

questions.stem: Find the air-standard efficiency of a Diesel cycle with compression ratio 20 and cutoff ratio 2.5 ($\gamma = 1.4$).
questions.explanation: $r^{\gamma - 1} = 20^{0.4} = 3.31$, and the cutoff factor is $\dfrac{2.5^{1.4} - 1}{1.4(2.5 - 1)} = \dfrac{3.607 - 1}{2.1} = 1.241$. So $e = 1 - 1.241/3.31 = 0.625$. 69.8% leaves out the cutoff factor (it's the Otto efficiency at $r = 20$), 75.7% divides by the factor instead of multiplying, and 98.1% uses $r^{\gamma}$ in place of $r^{\gamma-1}$.

questions.stem: At the same compression ratio, an ideal Diesel cycle is less efficient than an Otto cycle. Why are real diesel engines usually more efficient than gasoline engines?
choices: Diesel fuel releases more energy per kilogram than gasoline
Diesel engines reject no heat to the surroundings
They compress only air, so they can use much higher compression ratios without knock
Adding heat at constant pressure always beats adding it at constant volume
questions.explanation: The efficiency of both cycles rises with the compression ratio. Because a diesel injects fuel only at the top of the stroke, it can compress air to ratios of about 14–22 without knock, which more than makes up for the less favorable constant-pressure heat addition. Every engine must reject heat (second law), and the cycle efficiency doesn't depend on the fuel's energy content.

questions.stem: What is the ideal efficiency of a Brayton cycle with pressure ratio 15 ($\gamma = 1.4$)?
questions.explanation: $e = 1 - r_p^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma} = 1 - 15^{-0.2857} = 1 - 0.461 = 0.539$. 66.1% uses the Otto exponent $\gamma - 1$, which belongs with a volume ratio; 93.3% is $1 - 1/r_p$; and 97.7% uses $r_p^{-\gamma}$.

questions.stem: Air at 300 K passes through an ideal (adiabatic, reversible) compressor with pressure ratio 10 ($\gamma = 1.4$). It leaves at ___ K, to the nearest kelvin.
An ideal Otto engine and a Carnot engine both work between a lowest temperature of 300 K and a highest of 2000 K. Why is the Otto efficiency lower?
choices: The Otto cycle takes in and gives out heat over a range of temperatures, not only at the extremes
The Otto cycle has friction and the Carnot cycle does not
The Otto cycle uses air, and the Carnot cycle needs a monatomic gas
The Otto cycle does no work during its constant-volume steps, which wastes heat
questions.explanation: Both are ideal and reversible in the air-standard model. The Carnot engine takes in all its heat at the top temperature and rejects all of it at the bottom; the Otto cycle takes in heat while the gas warms from $T_2$ to $T_3$ and rejects it while the gas cools from $T_4$ to $T_1$, so on average its heat enters cooler and leaves hotter. The Carnot limit holds for any working gas, and no work during a constant-volume step is not by itself a loss.

questions.stem: An ideal Otto engine with compression ratio 10 takes in air at 300 K, and combustion heats it to 1800 K ($\gamma = 1.4$, $C_V = \tfrac52R$). How much net work does it do per mole of air per cycle?
questions.explanation: $T_2 = 300(10)^{0.4} = 754$ K, so $Q_H = nC_V(T_3 - T_2) = 20.8(1800 - 754) = 21.8$ kJ per mole. With $e = 1 - 10^{-0.4} = 0.602$, $W = 0.602(21.8) = 13.1$ kJ. 21.8 kJ is the heat input, not the work; 18.1 kJ uses the Carnot efficiency $1 - 300/1800$; and 22.5 kJ takes $Q_H = C_VT_3$, forgetting that the gas was already at 754 K.

questions.stem: When 6 coins are tossed, the macrostate "exactly 3 heads" has a multiplicity of ___.
questions.explanation: $\Omega = \binom63 = \dfrac{6!}{3!\,3!} = \dfrac{720}{36} = 20$ of the $2^6 = 64$ microstates.

questions.stem: Four fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of exactly 2 heads?
questions.explanation: All 16 microstates are equally likely, and 6 of them have 2 heads: $6/16 = 0.375$. 0.200 treats the 5 macrostates (0 to 4 heads) as equally likely, which they are not; 0.500 is $2/4$; 0.0625 is the probability of one particular microstate, such as HHTT.

questions.stem: A system has $\Omega = 10^{20}$ accessible microstates. What is its entropy?
questions.explanation: $S = k_B\ln\Omega = (1.38\times10^{-23})\ln(10^{20}) = (1.38\times10^{-23})(46.05) = 6.36\times10^{-22}$ J/K. $2.76\times10^{-22}$ uses $\log_{10}$ (20) instead of the natural log; $1.38\times10^{-3}$ multiplies $k_B$ by $\Omega$ itself; 46.1 J/K forgets $k_B$.

questions.stem: 2.0 mol of an ideal gas expands freely into a vacuum, tripling its volume. By counting microstates, what is its entropy change?
questions.explanation: Each molecule has 3 times as many positions available, so $\Omega$ grows by $3^N$ and $\Delta S = Nk_B\ln3 = nR\ln3 = 2.0(8.314)(1.099) = 18.3$ J/K, positive as an irreversible process requires. 49.9 J/K uses 3 instead of $\ln3$, −18.3 J/K has the ratio upside down, and 9.13 J/K is for one mole.

questions.stem: Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Two independent systems together have $\Omega = \Omega_A\Omega_B$ microstates
The entropies of two independent systems add
In an isolated system in equilibrium, some microstates are more likely than others
For very large numbers of particles, the most probable macrostate is overwhelmingly likely
questions.explanation: Each microstate of A can pair with each of B, so multiplicities multiply, and because $\ln(\Omega_A\Omega_B) = \ln\Omega_A + \ln\Omega_B$, entropies add. The fundamental assumption is that every accessible microstate is equally likely; macrostates differ only in how many microstates they contain, and for large $N$ the largest one dominates.

questions.stem: Order these macrostates of 6 tossed coins from lowest entropy to highest.
questions.explanation: $S = k_B\ln\Omega$ grows with the multiplicity: $\binom66 = 1$, $\binom65 = 6$, $\binom64 = 15$ and $\binom63 = 20$. The evenly mixed macrostate has the most microstates and the highest entropy.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning.
choices: A complete description of every particle
A description by measurable quantities such as P, V and T
The number of microstates in a macrostate
The relative weight of a state of energy E at temperature T
The heat needed to melt 1 kg of a solid
questions.explanation: A microstate lists every particle's state; a macrostate gives only what we can measure. The multiplicity $\Omega$ counts the microstates in a macrostate, and $S = k_B\ln\Omega$. The Boltzmann factor $e^{-E/(k_BT)}$ weights a state of energy $E$ in a system at temperature $T$. The heat to melt 1 kg is the latent heat of fusion.

questions.stem: Two large objects are in thermal contact: A at 300 K and B at 400 K. When 1.0 J of energy flows from B to A, by how much does the total entropy change?
questions.explanation: A gains $1.0/300$ J/K and B loses $1.0/400$ J/K, so $\Delta S = \dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{400} = +8.3\times10^{-4}$ J/K. It is positive, which is why energy flows from hot to cold. The negative value has the direction reversed, $1/100$ divides by the temperature difference, and $5.8\times10^{-3}$ adds the two terms.

questions.stem: An Einstein solid has 4 oscillators sharing 3 quanta of energy. How many microstates does it have?
questions.explanation: $\Omega(N, q) = \binom{q + N - 1}{q} = \binom{6}{3} = 20$. The quanta are identical, so only how many sit in each oscillator matters. 64 is $4^3$, which treats the quanta as distinguishable; 35 is $\binom{7}{3}$, using $q + N$ instead of $q + N - 1$; and 12 is $4\times3$.

questions.stem: At 300 K, $k_BT = 0.0259$ eV. How does the probability of a particular state 0.10 eV above another compare with the probability of that lower state?
questions.explanation: The ratio of Boltzmann factors is $e^{-\Delta E/(k_BT)} = e^{-0.10/0.0259} = e^{-3.87} = 0.021$, about 1 in 48. 0.90 is $e^{-0.10}$, forgetting to divide by $k_BT$; 0.26 is $0.0259/0.10$; and 0.77 is $e^{-0.0259/0.10}$, with the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: Treating each gas separately in a still atmosphere at a uniform 300 K, what is the scale height $H = RT/(Mg)$ of argon ($M = 0.040$ kg/mol, $g = 9.8$ m/s²)?
questions.explanation: $H = \dfrac{8.314(300)}{0.040(9.8)} = 6.36\times10^3$ m $= 6.36$ km. 6.36 m uses $M = 40$ (grams per mole, not kg/mol); 0.573 km uses $T = 27$ (Celsius); 63.6 km is helium's scale height. (In the real lower atmosphere winds keep the gases mixed, so each gas does not follow its own scale height.)

questions.stem: According to the third law of thermodynamics, the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches ___ as its temperature approaches absolute zero.
questions.explanation: At absolute zero a perfect crystal is in its single lowest-energy microstate, so $\Omega = 1$ and $S = k_B\ln1 = 0$.

questions.stem: A box holds 10 gas molecules moving at random. At a given instant, what is the probability that all 10 are in the left half?
questions.explanation: Each molecule is in the left half with probability 1/2, independently, so all 10 are there with probability $(1/2)^{10} = 1/1024$, about 1/1000. For a mole of molecules the same reasoning gives $2^{-6\times10^{23}}$: never observed. With only 10 molecules, such "entropy-lowering" fluctuations happen now and then.

questions.stem: The picture shows smooth (laminar) flow in a pipe, seen in a lengthwise cut. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A pipe seen in a lengthwise cut, with horizontal arrows starting on a vertical dashed line. The arrows are longest in the middle and shorter near the walls, and a dashed curve joins their tips.

choices: Pipe wall, where the fluid is at rest
questions.explanation: Viscous fluid sticks to the wall (1) (no slip) and moves fastest on the axis (2). Each layer is slowed by the slower layer outside it, so the speed falls toward the wall (3) along the parabola $v = \dfrac{\Delta P}{4\eta L}(R^2 - r^2)$ (4). In laminar flow there are no eddies, and the speed is not the same across the pipe.

questions.stem: Laminar flow passes through a pipe. If the pipe's radius is halved and the pressure difference, length and fluid stay the same, the flow rate becomes
questions.explanation: Poiseuille's law, $Q = \pi R^4\Delta P/(8\eta L)$, has $R^4$: $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$. Two factors of $R$ come from the cross-sectional area and two more from the speed: in a narrower pipe all the fluid is closer to the motionless wall, so the velocity profile $v = \dfrac{\Delta P}{4\eta L}(R^2 - r^2)$ is scaled down by $R^2$. 1/4 counts only the area.

questions.stem: In laminar Poiseuille flow, the average speed across the pipe is ___ times the speed on the axis.
questions.explanation: $Q = \pi R^4\Delta P/(8\eta L)$, so the average speed is $Q/(\pi R^2) = R^2\Delta P/(8\eta L)$, while the axis speed is $v(0) = R^2\Delta P/(4\eta L)$. The ratio is 1/2.

questions.stem: Olive oil ($\rho = 910$ kg/m³, $\eta = 0.080$ Pa·s) flows at an average 0.50 m/s through a pipe of diameter 2.0 cm. What is the Reynolds number, and is the flow laminar?
questions.explanation: $\text{Re} = \dfrac{\rho vD}{\eta} = \dfrac{910(0.50)(0.020)}{0.080} = 114$, far below about 2000, so the flow is laminar. 9100 uses water's viscosity ($1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s), 57 uses the radius in place of the diameter, and 0.0088 is the ratio upside down.

questions.stem: A glass bead of radius 0.025 mm and density 2500 kg/m³ sinks through water ($\eta = 1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s) at 20°C. Using Stokes' law, what is its terminal speed?
questions.explanation: $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{9\eta} = \dfrac{2(2.5\times10^{-5})^2(1500)(9.8)}{9(1.0\times10^{-3})} = 2.04\times10^{-3}$ m/s. Check: $\text{Re} = 1000(0.00204)(5.0\times10^{-5})/(1.0\times10^{-3}) = 0.10$, well below 1, so Stokes' law applies. 3.40 mm/s leaves out buoyancy (uses 2500 instead of 1500), 8.17 mm/s uses the diameter for $r$, and 9.19 mm/s drops the factor 2/9.

questions.stem: Which changes would increase the flow rate of laminar flow through a pipe? Select all that apply.
choices: A larger pressure difference between the ends
questions.explanation: $Q = \dfrac{\pi R^4\Delta P}{8\eta L}$: the flow rate grows with $\Delta P$ and (strongly) with $R$, and shrinks with the length $L$ and the viscosity $\eta$.

questions.stem: The same fluid flows through each pipe under the same pressure difference, all in laminar flow. Order the pipes from the smallest flow rate to the largest.
questions.explanation: $Q \propto R^4/L$. In units of the first pipe: $1^4/1 = 1$, $1^4/0.5 = 2$, $2^4/4 = 4$ and $2^4/1 = 16$. Doubling the radius wins even against a pipe four times as long.

questions.stem: Match each fluid to its approximate viscosity.
questions.explanation: Gases are far less viscous than liquids: air is about 1/55 as viscous as water. Olive oil is roughly 80 times as viscous as water, and glycerin over a thousand times. (500 Pa·s is more like a very stiff paste.)

questions.stem: In a falling-ball viscometer, a steel ball (radius 1.0 mm, density 7800 kg/m³) falls through glycerin (density 1260 kg/m³) at a steady 1.0 cm/s. What viscosity does Stokes' law give?
questions.explanation: Solve $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{9\eta}$ for $\eta$: $\eta = \dfrac{2(1.0\times10^{-3})^2(6540)(9.8)}{9(0.010)} = 1.42$ Pa·s. Check: $\text{Re} = 1260(0.010)(0.0020)/1.42 = 0.018 \ll 1$, so Stokes' law applies. 1.70 Pa·s leaves out buoyancy, 5.70 Pa·s uses the diameter for $r$, and 1.97 Pa·s adds the densities instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: For a small sphere sinking in the Stokes regime, doubling its radius (same material) multiplies its terminal speed by ___.
questions.explanation: $v_t = 2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g/(9\eta)$ grows as $r^2$: the weight minus buoyancy grows as $r^3$ but the drag $6\pi\eta rv$ only as $r$. So doubling $r$ gives 4 times the speed (as long as Re stays well below 1).

questions.stem: You compute a terminal speed with Stokes' law and then find $\text{Re} = 50$ for that speed. What should you conclude?
choices: The answer is fine, since Stokes' law holds for any laminar flow
Stokes' law does not apply; the real speed is higher than computed
The flow must be turbulent, so the drag is zero
Stokes' law does not apply; the real speed is lower than computed
questions.explanation: Stokes' law needs $\text{Re} \ll 1$. At larger Re the drag grows faster than linearly with speed, so the sphere reaches force balance at a lower speed than the linear law predicts. Turbulence makes drag larger, not zero.

questions.stem: Water ($\eta = 1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s) flows at $2.0\times10^{-7}$ m³/s through a needle of inner radius 0.15 mm and length 3.0 cm. Assuming laminar Poiseuille flow, what pressure difference drives it?
questions.explanation: $\Delta P = \dfrac{8\eta LQ}{\pi R^4} = \dfrac{8(1.0\times10^{-3})(0.030)(2.0\times10^{-7})}{\pi(1.5\times10^{-4})^4} = 3.02\times10^4$ Pa. 15.1 kPa uses 4 in place of 8, 1.89 kPa uses the diameter in place of the radius, and 3.02 MPa leaves the length in centimeters. (Re is about 850, so the flow is laminar.)

questions.stem: In laminar flow through a pipe of radius $R$, how fast does the fluid move at $r = R/2$, halfway from the axis to the wall?
questions.explanation: $v(r) \propto R^2 - r^2$, so $v(R/2)/v(0) = (R^2 - R^2/4)/R^2 = 3/4$. The profile is a parabola, not a straight line, so halfway out the speed has dropped by only a quarter.

cards.back: $L = T - U$ (kinetic minus potential), in generalized coordinates and their rates. Not the total energy.
$S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2}L\,dt$ (units J·s), one number for a whole path.
The true path between fixed endpoints makes the action stationary (not always a minimum).
$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\right) - \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$, one per generalized coordinate.
One per degree of freedom, chosen so the constraints hold automatically (pendulum: one angle).
$m\ddot x = -dU/dx$: Newton's second law.
$L = \tfrac12m\ell^2\dot\theta^2 + mg\ell\cos\theta$ gives $\ddot\theta = -(g/\ell)\sin\theta$.

cards.front: Atwood machine with a disk pulley
cards.back: $a = \dfrac{(m_1 - m_2)g}{m_1 + m_2 + \tfrac12M}$; the tensions never appear.

cards.front: Swinging uniform rod (pivot at one end)
cards.back: $\omega = \sqrt{3g/(2\ell)}$ for small swings.

cards.front: What $L = T - U$ does not handle directly
cards.back: Constraint forces (they don't appear; use Newton or Lagrange multipliers) and nonconservative forces like friction and drag (need generalized forces).
$p = \partial L/\partial\dot q$; Euler–Lagrange becomes $\dot p = \partial L/\partial q$.
$q$ absent from $L$ ⇒ $p$ conserved.
$L = \tfrac12m(\dot r^2 + r^2\dot\varphi^2) - U(r)$; $\varphi$ cyclic, so $mr^2\dot\varphi$ (angular momentum) is conserved.
Continuous symmetry ↔ conserved quantity: time shift → energy; position shift → momentum; rotation → angular momentum.

cards.front: Puck pulled inward on a string through a hole
cards.back: $\omega \propto 1/r^2$ (angular momentum conserved); kinetic energy rises because the puller does work.
$H = \sum p\dot q - L$; conserved if $L$ has no explicit $t$; equals $T + U$ for fixed constraints.
$\dot q = \partial H/\partial p$, $\dot p = -\partial H/\partial q$
An ellipse with semi-axes $x_{\max} = \sqrt{2E/k}$ and $p_{\max} = \sqrt{2mE}$; area $2\pi E/\omega$.
Energy to just reach the top: bottom speed $\sqrt{4g\ell}$. Divides swings (closed loops) from rotations.
Hamiltonian flow keeps phase-space area (volume) constant.
$\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$: two bodies reduce to one of mass $\mu$ moving about the center of mass.
$U_{\text{eff}} = \dfrac{\ell^2}{2mr^2} - \dfrac{GMm}{r}$; turning points where $E = U_{\text{eff}}$; minimum = circular orbit.
$r = \dfrac{p}{1 + e\cos\varphi}$ with $p = \ell^2/(GMm^2)$: a conic with the central body at a focus.
$e = 0$ circle; $0 < e < 1$ ellipse ($E < 0$); $e = 1$ parabola ($E = 0$); $e > 1$ hyperbola ($E > 0$).
$r_p = a(1 - e)$, $r_a = a(1 + e)$; $a = \tfrac12(r_p + r_a)$, $e = \dfrac{r_a - r_p}{r_a + r_p}$.
$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2a}$: depends only on the semimajor axis.
$v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{2}{r} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right)$
$T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$, independent of $e$ (use $G(m_1 + m_2)$ for exact two-body work).
$r_pv_p = r_av_a$ (angular momentum).
Compute $\varepsilon = v^2/2 - GM/r$: negative means an ellipse with $a = -GM/(2\varepsilon)$.
Only $F \propto 1/r^2$ and $F \propto r$ make all bound orbits close.

cards.front: Mass ratio for a given delta-v
cards.back: $m_i/m_f = e^{\Delta v/u}$ (rocket equation).

cards.front: Effect of a forward burn at periapsis
cards.back: Raises the apoapsis (the opposite side); the burn point stays put.
Half an ellipse with $a_t = \tfrac12(r_1 + r_2)$; trip time $\pi\sqrt{a_t^3/GM}$.
$\Delta v_1 = v_{\text{peri}} - \sqrt{GM/r_1}$, $\Delta v_2 = \sqrt{GM/r_2} - v_{\text{apo}}$; both forward, speeds from vis-viva.
About 2.4 + 1.5 = 3.9 km/s, about 5.3 h (ignoring any plane change).

cards.front: Earth to Mars by Hohmann (circular model)
cards.back: About 258 days; launch with Mars about 44° ahead; windows every 26 months.

cards.front: Departure burn for a hyperbolic excess speed
cards.back: $v = \sqrt{v_\infty^2 + v_{\text{esc}}^2}$ at the burn point; burn $= v - v_{\text{circ}}$.
A burn adds about $mv\,\Delta v$ of kinetic energy, so burn where $v$ is largest (low periapsis).
Same speed in the planet's frame, turned direction; in the Sun's frame the speed can change (up to $2U$ in the idealized head-on limit).

cards.front: How to report a result with its uncertainty
cards.back: Round $\delta x$ to 1 significant figure (2 if it starts with 1), then round the value to the same decimal place: $9.81 \pm 0.06$.
$\delta x/|x|$, usually as a percentage; unitless, so it compares the quality of different measurements.
Random error scatters readings both ways and averages down; systematic error shifts every reading the same way and does not.
$s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2}{n - 1}}$: the spread of single readings.
$\delta\bar x = s/\sqrt n$. Four times the readings halves it.
Roughly, when the discrepancy is within about 2 uncertainties (a rule of thumb). Much more points to a mistake or systematic error.

cards.front: Uncertainty of a sum or difference
cards.back: Add absolute uncertainties in quadrature: $\delta q = \sqrt{(\delta x)^2 + (\delta y)^2}$, even for a difference.

cards.front: Uncertainty of a product or quotient
cards.back: Add relative uncertainties in quadrature: $\dfrac{\delta q}{|q|} = \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\delta x}{x}\right)^2 + \left(\dfrac{\delta y}{y}\right)^2}$.
$\dfrac{\delta q}{|q|} = |n|\dfrac{\delta x}{|x|}$: squaring doubles the relative uncertainty.
$\delta q = |dq/dx|\,\delta x$; for several independent inputs, add the partial-derivative terms in quadrature. Angles in radians.

cards.front: Why subtracting nearly equal numbers is risky
cards.back: The absolute uncertainties add while the result gets small, so the relative uncertainty can become large.

cards.front: Scalar projection of A onto B
cards.back: $\vec A\cdot\hat B = A\cos\phi = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{|\vec B|}$

cards.front: Vector projection of A onto B
cards.back: $\vec A_\parallel = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{B^2}\vec B$; the rest, $\vec A_\perp = \vec A - \vec A_\parallel$, is perpendicular to $\vec B$.
$\cos\alpha = A_x/A$, $\cos\beta = A_y/A$, $\cos\gamma = A_z/A$; $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$.

cards.front: Components in axes rotated by φ (counterclockwise)
cards.back: $A_{x'} = A_x\cos\varphi + A_y\sin\varphi$, $A_{y'} = -A_x\sin\varphi + A_y\cos\varphi$

cards.front: What stays the same when the axes rotate?
cards.back: Magnitudes, angles between vectors and dot products. Components change.
$\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C)$ = the determinant of the components; $|\ldots|$ is the volume of the parallelepiped.
Their scalar triple product is zero.

cards.front: Cyclic property of the scalar triple product
cards.back: $\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C) = \vec B\cdot(\vec C\times\vec A) = \vec C\cdot(\vec A\times\vec B)$; swapping two vectors flips the sign.
$\vec A\times(\vec B\times\vec C) = \vec B(\vec A\cdot\vec C) - \vec C(\vec A\cdot\vec B)$
No: $(\hat\imath\times\hat\imath)\times\hat\jmath = \vec 0$ but $\hat\imath\times(\hat\imath\times\hat\jmath) = -\hat\jmath$.

cards.front: Centripetal acceleration as a triple product
cards.back: $\vec a = \vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r)$, which points at the axis with magnitude $\omega^2\rho$ ($\rho$ = distance from the axis).

cards.front: Launch angle to hit $(x, y)$: the equation
cards.back: With $u = \tan\theta$ and $k = gx^2/(2v_0^2)$: $ku^2 - xu + (y + k) = 0$. Two roots: low shot and lob; one root: edge of reach; none: out of reach.
$y = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2g} - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$: every trajectory touches it once; targets above it are out of reach.

cards.front: Highest and farthest points of the safety parabola
cards.back: Height $v_0^2/(2g)$ straight above the launch point; reaches the ground at $x = v_0^2/g$ (the $45^\circ$ range).

cards.front: Single launch angle for a point on the safety parabola
cards.back: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v_0^2}{gx}$

cards.front: Minimum launch speed to reach a point at height $y$, straight-line distance $d$
Best launch angle toward a target whose line of sight rises at $\alpha$
cards.back: $45^\circ + \alpha/2$: it bisects the angle between the vertical and the line of sight.

cards.front: Of two angles that hit a target, which arrives first?
cards.back: The lower one: time $= x/(v_0\cos\theta)$ and the lower angle has larger $\cos\theta$.

cards.front: Distance along a slope rising at $\alpha$ (launch angle $\theta$ from horizontal)
cards.back: $L = \dfrac{2v_0^2\cos\theta\sin(\theta - \alpha)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$

cards.front: Greatest distance along a slope of angle $\alpha$
cards.back: $L_{\max} = \dfrac{v_0^2}{g(1 + \sin\alpha)}$ at $\theta = 45^\circ + \alpha/2$ ($\alpha < 0$ downhill).

cards.front: Who proved projectile paths are parabolas?
cards.back: Galileo, in Two New Sciences (1638), along with equal ranges for elevations equally above and below $45^\circ$ (no air resistance).

cards.front: Acceleration in tangential and normal components
cards.back: $\vec a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}\hat T + \dfrac{v^2}{\rho}\hat N$

cards.front: Tangential acceleration from $\vec v$ and $\vec a$
cards.back: $a_t = \dfrac{\vec a\cdot\vec v}{v}$ (negative: slowing down).

cards.front: Normal acceleration from $\vec v$ and $\vec a$ (2D)
cards.back: $a_n = \dfrac{|v_xa_y - v_ya_x|}{v}$; check $a_t^2 + a_n^2 = a^2$.

cards.front: Radius of curvature from $\vec v$ and $\vec a$
cards.back: $\rho = \dfrac{v^2}{a_n} = \dfrac{v^3}{|v_xa_y - v_ya_x|}$
The circle matching a path's tangent and curvature at a point; radius $\rho$, center on the inside of the bend.
$\kappa = 1/\rho$; zero for a straight line.

cards.front: Why is $d\hat T/dt$ perpendicular to $\hat T$?
cards.back: $\hat T\cdot\hat T = 1$, so $2\hat T\cdot d\hat T/dt = 0$.

cards.front: Rate of change of speed vs size of acceleration
cards.back: $d|\vec v|/dt = a_t$, while $|d\vec v/dt| = \sqrt{a_t^2 + a_n^2}$; equal only on a straight path.
$\rho = v^3/(gv_x)$; smallest at the top, $\rho = v_x^2/g$; at launch $\rho = v_0^2/(g\cos\theta)$.
$s = \int_{t_1}^{t_2}|\vec v|\,dt$, never less than the displacement's magnitude.

cards.front: Largest acceleration of a load on a truck bed without slipping
cards.back: $a_{\max} = \mu_s g$, independent of the load's mass

cards.front: Direction of static friction on a box in a truck that speeds up
cards.back: Forward, the way the box accelerates; friction opposes relative sliding, not motion
Assume they move together, find $a$, find the friction the top block needs; if it exceeds $\mu_s n$, redo with $\mu_k n$ and separate accelerations

cards.front: Largest pull on the bottom of two stacked blocks before slipping (frictionless floor)
cards.back: $F_{\max} = (m_{\text{top}} + m_{\text{bottom}})\mu_s g$

cards.front: Force to drag a crate at angle θ (constant speed)
cards.back: $F = \dfrac{\mu mg}{\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta}$

cards.front: Best angle to drag a crate
cards.back: $\tan\theta = \mu$ (the angle of friction), giving $F_{\min} = \mu mg/\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}$
$T_{\text{load}} = T_{\text{hold}}e^{\mu\theta}$, with $\theta$ in radians; independent of the post's radius
$dT = \mu T\,d\theta$ (normal force on a rope element $dn = T\,d\theta$)

cards.front: Wrap angle of n full turns
cards.back: $\theta = 2\pi n$ radians
$F_D = \tfrac12C\rho Av^2 = cv^2$, opposite the velocity
$v_T = \sqrt{mg/c} = \sqrt{2mg/(C\rho A)}$, proportional to $\sqrt m$ for a fixed shape and size

cards.front: Falling from rest with quadratic drag
cards.back: $v = v_T\tanh(gt/v_T)$; $y = (v_T^2/g)\ln\cosh(gt/v_T)$

cards.front: Speed at t = v_T/g with quadratic drag
cards.back: $\tanh 1 \approx 76\%$ of $v_T$ (63% for linear drag)

cards.front: Time to the top of a vertical throw with quadratic drag
cards.back: $t_{\text{up}} = \dfrac{v_T}{g}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{v_0}{v_T}$

cards.front: Maximum height of a vertical throw with quadratic drag
cards.back: $h = \dfrac{v_T^2}{2g}\ln\!\left(1 + \dfrac{v_0^2}{v_T^2}\right)$

cards.front: Return speed of a vertical throw with quadratic drag
cards.back: $v = \dfrac{v_0v_T}{\sqrt{v_0^2 + v_T^2}}$, less than $v_0$; the trip down takes longer than the trip up
$v = \dfrac{v_0}{1 + cv_0t/m}$ in time; $v = v_0e^{-cx/m}$ in distance (halves every $(m/c)\ln 2$)
$\dfrac{dv}{dt} = v\dfrac{dv}{dx}$ turns $m\,dv/dt = F(v)$ into an equation for $v(x)$

cards.front: Fictitious force in a frame accelerating at A
cards.back: $-m\vec A$, opposite the frame's acceleration; no agent, no third-law partner

cards.front: Effective gravity in an accelerating frame
cards.back: $\vec g_{\text{eff}} = \vec g - \vec A$

cards.front: Pendulum hanging in a vehicle accelerating at A
