cards.back: $\tan\theta = A/g$, tilted toward the rear
$m\omega^2r_\perp$ away from the axis, on every object in a rotating frame
$-2m\vec\omega\times\vec v'$, only on objects moving in the rotating frame; perpendicular to $\vec v'$, does no work

cards.front: Newton's second law in a rotating frame
cards.back: $m\vec a' = \sum\vec F - m\vec\omega\times(\vec\omega\times\vec r) - 2m\vec\omega\times\vec v'$

cards.front: Artificial gravity on a ring of radius r
cards.back: $\omega = \sqrt{g/r}$; 100 m needs about 3 rpm
To the right of the motion in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern
$\omega^2R \approx 0.034$ m/s², about 0.35% of $g$
$23.93\text{ h}/\sin\lambda$ at latitude $\lambda$ (about 32 h in Paris)
$W = \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell = \int_{t_1}^{t_2}\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot\vec r\,'(t)\,dt$ after parametrizing the path.
Work is path independent; work around every closed path is zero; $\vec F = -\nabla U$ for some $U$.
$\dfrac{\partial F_y}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}$; necessary for a conservative force, and sufficient on a region without holes.
$\nabla\times\vec F = \left(\partial_yF_z - \partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x - \partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y - \partial_yF_x\right)$; zero for a conservative force.

cards.front: Why does a conservative force have zero curl?
cards.back: If $F_x = -\partial U/\partial x$ and $F_y = -\partial U/\partial y$, equal mixed partials of $U$ make $\partial F_y/\partial x = \partial F_x/\partial y$.
Integrate $-F_x$ in $x$ (constant becomes $g(y, z)$), match $-\partial U/\partial y$ to $F_y$, then $z$; check $-\nabla U = \vec F$.
No: $\partial F_y/\partial x = 1$ but $\partial F_x/\partial y = -1$. It circulates and does net work around loops.
$\vec F = f(r)\hat r$; always conservative, with $U(r) = -\int f(r)\,dr$.
$\vec F = -\nabla U$ is perpendicular to the equipotential through each point, points toward lower $U$, and is strongest where equipotentials crowd together.

cards.front: Green's theorem check for loop work
cards.back: Work around a counterclockwise loop in the plane $= \iint(\partial F_y/\partial x - \partial F_x/\partial y)\,dA$.

cards.front: Equation of motion with mass flowing in or out
cards.back: $m\,d\vec v/dt = \vec F_{\text{ext}} + \vec u_{\text{rel}}\,dm/dt$, with $\vec u_{\text{rel}}$ the crossing mass's velocity relative to the body.

cards.front: Why not $F = d(mv)/dt$ for a body losing mass?
cards.back: It ignores the momentum carried by the mass that leaves and gives different answers in different inertial frames; use the relative-velocity form or a closed system.

cards.front: Sand leaking straight down through a moving cart's floor
cards.back: The sand leaves with the cart's velocity ($u_{\text{rel}} = 0$), so the cart's speed does not change.
$v(t) = u\ln\dfrac{m_i}{m(t)} - gt$; liftoff needs thrust $uR > m_ig$.
$gt_b$: the speed a vertical burn of duration $t_b$ loses to the rocket's weight.

cards.front: Conveyor belt loading at rate $R$, speed $v$
cards.back: Force $Rv$, power $Rv^2$; half becomes the load's kinetic energy, half becomes heat.

cards.front: Force of a jet stopped by a wall
cards.back: Momentum flux $\rho Av^2$; if the jet is turned straight back, $2\rho Av^2$.
Buckets moving at half the jet speed turn the water back and leave it at rest: all of the jet's kinetic energy is extracted (real wheels about 90%).
Reading $= 3\lambda gy$: the landed weight $\lambda gy$ plus the momentum flux $\lambda v^2 = 2\lambda gy$.
$\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$; CM-frame momenta are $\pm\mu\vec v_{\text{rel}}$.
$K = \tfrac12Mv_{\text{cm}}^2 + \tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$; only the second part can be lost in a collision.
$K_{\text{lost}} = (1 - e^2)\,\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$.

cards.front: Elastic collision in the CM frame
cards.back: Each object keeps its speed; the collision only turns the pair of opposite momenta (reverses them, head-on).

cards.front: Head-on elastic collision: fraction of KE to a target at rest
cards.back: $\dfrac{4m_1m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)^2}$; equal to 1 only for equal masses.

cards.front: Why are reactor moderators made of light nuclei?
cards.back: A neutron loses the most energy per collision to a nucleus of similar mass: up to all of it to hydrogen, at most 28% to carbon, under 2% to uranium-238.

cards.front: Largest deflection of a heavy projectile by a light target at rest (elastic)
cards.back: $\sin\theta_{\max} = m_2/m_1$; for example 14.5° for an alpha particle on a proton.
After an elastic collision the projectile's lab velocity ends on a circle of radius $v_1'$ (its CM-frame speed) centered at the tip of $\vec v_{\text{cm}}$.

cards.front: Why couldn't electrons turn alpha particles back in the Geiger–Marsden experiment?
cards.back: An electron is about 1/7300 of an alpha's mass, so it can deflect an alpha by at most about 0.008°. Large-angle scattering needed a massive nucleus.

cards.front: Slip velocity of a rolling object
cards.back: $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$ (forward spin positive); zero when rolling without slipping. Kinetic friction points opposite to it.

cards.front: Ball launched with no spin: what does friction do?
cards.back: Points backward: slows the center ($a = -\mu_kg$) and spins it up ($\alpha = \mu_kg/(cR)$) until $v = R\omega$.

cards.front: Time to start rolling (launched with no spin)

cards.back: $v_f = \dfrac{v_0 + cR\omega_0}{1 + c}$; with no initial spin, $v_0/(1 + c)$ ($\tfrac57v_0$ for a solid sphere). Independent of $\mu_k$.

cards.front: Which angular momentum is conserved while a ball skids?
cards.back: About a fixed point on the floor line: friction passes through it and the torques of weight and normal force cancel. Not about the center.

cards.front: Kinetic energy lost while skidding to rolling (no initial spin)
cards.back: Fraction $\dfrac{c}{1 + c}$: $\tfrac27$ for a solid sphere, $\tfrac12$ for a hoop.
$b = \dfrac{I_P}{Md}$ from the pivot ($d$ = pivot to CM); $\tfrac23L$ for a uniform rod held at one end. A blow there gives no jolt at the pivot.

cards.front: Height to strike a solid ball so it rolls at once
cards.back: $(1 + c)R = 1.4R$ above the table ($0.4R$ above the center).
$\Omega = \dfrac{\tau}{L} = \dfrac{Mgr}{I\omega}$; faster spin, slower precession; independent of the tilt.
$d\vec L = \vec\tau\,dt$: the axle moves in the direction of the torque vector, at right angles to the force. Reversing the spin reverses it.
In the gyroscopic approximation, spin much faster than precession ($\omega \gg \Omega$).
Bobbing of a gyroscope's axis around its steady precession, e.g. after release from rest; small and quick for a fast rotor.
About 26,000 years per cycle; Sun and Moon torques on the equatorial bulge. Discovered by Hipparchus (2nd century BCE).

cards.front: Crooked rotor (dumbbell at angle $\beta$ to the shaft)
cards.back: $L_\perp = 2ma^2\omega\sin\beta\cos\beta$ turns with the shaft; bearings must supply $\tau = \omega L_\perp$.

cards.front: Static vs dynamic balance of a wheel
cards.back: Static: center of mass on the axle. Dynamic: a principal axis along the axle, so $\vec L \parallel \vec\omega$ and no rotating bearing torque.

cards.front: Flipping a spinning wheel while sitting on a free stool
cards.back: Vertical $L$ is conserved: reversing the wheel's $L_w$ gives you and the stool $2L_w$ in the wheel's original sense.

cards.front: Is a bicycle stable because its wheels are gyroscopes?
cards.back: Contested and mostly no: a bicycle with the wheels' spin angular momentum canceled can still be self-stable (Kooijman et al., 2011).
Uniform shell: outside, $V = -GM/r$ (like a point mass); inside, $V = -GM/R$ constant, so $g = 0$.
$g(r) = g_s\,r/R$, zero at the center. (The real Earth's $g$ rises to about 10.7 m/s² at the core–mantle boundary.)
Simple harmonic motion, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{R/g_s}$: 84 min for Earth, 42 min one way, the same as a surface-skimming orbit.
About $\dfrac{2GMd}{D^3}$ outward along the line to the body (both sides), $\dfrac{GMd}{D^3}$ inward across it.
Moon $1.1\times10^{-6}$ m/s², Sun $5.1\times10^{-7}$ m/s² (0.46 as much), although the Sun's direct pull is about 180 times the Moon's.
Spring: new and full moon, Sun and Moon aligned, effects add. Neap: quarter moons, at right angles, partly cancel.
Slows Earth's spin and passes angular momentum to the Moon's orbit; the Moon recedes about 3.8 cm/yr. It also tidally locked the Moon.
Rigid estimate $R_p(2\rho_p/\rho_m)^{1/3}$; fluid moon (Roche, 1849) $2.44R_p(\rho_p/\rho_m)^{1/3}$.

cards.front: Fourier series of a periodic signal
cards.back: $y = a_0 + \sum_n [a_n\cos(n\omega_1t) + b_n\sin(n\omega_1t)]$, with $\omega_1 = 2\pi/T$.
$a_0 = \tfrac1T\int y\,dt$ (the average); $a_n = \tfrac2T\int y\cos(n\omega_1t)\,dt$; $b_n = \tfrac2T\int y\sin(n\omega_1t)\,dt$, over one period.
$c_n = \sqrt{a_n^2 + b_n^2}$
$\dfrac{4A}{\pi}\left(\sin\omega_1t + \tfrac13\sin3\omega_1t + \tfrac15\sin5\omega_1t + \cdots\right)$: odd harmonics only.
Every harmonic, amplitude $2A/(n\pi)$.
Odd signal: sines only. Even signal: cosines (and a constant) only. $y(t + T/2) = -y(t)$: odd harmonics only.
Next to a jump, a partial Fourier sum overshoots by about 9% of the jump however many terms are used; the overshoot only narrows.
$\overline{y^2} = a_0^2 + \tfrac12\sum c_n^2$: power in the harmonics adds. A square wave has 81% of its power in the fundamental.
$B_n \propto \sin(n\pi d/L)/n^2$ for a pluck at distance $d$: a harmonic with a node at the pluck point is missing.

cards.front: Duration and bandwidth of a signal
cards.back: A signal lasting $\Delta t$ spans about $\Delta f \sim 1/\Delta t$ (order of magnitude).
Every part oscillates at one frequency with fixed amplitude ratios. $N$ coordinates give $N$ modes; any motion is a superposition of them.
In phase: $\omega_1 = \sqrt{k/m}$ (coupling spring idle). Out of phase: $\omega_2 = \sqrt{(k + 2k')/m}$.

cards.front: Normal coordinates for two equal masses
cards.back: $q_1 = x_1 + x_2$ and $q_2 = x_1 - x_2$, each obeying its own SHM equation.

cards.front: Energy transfer time between two coupled oscillators
cards.back: $t = \pi/(\omega_2 - \omega_1)$ after releasing one alone; back again after $2\pi/(\omega_2 - \omega_1)$.
$\omega_1 = \sqrt{g/L}$, $\omega_2 = \sqrt{g/L + 2k'/m}$.
Put $x_j = a_j\cos\omega t$ into the equations of motion and set the determinant to zero: eigenvalues give $\omega^2$, eigenvectors give mode shapes.
$\omega_n = 2\sqrt{F/(ma)}\,\sin\dfrac{n\pi}{2(N+1)}$; for many beads the low modes become $f_n = nv/(2L)$.
Wave speed that depends on frequency, e.g. short waves on a beaded string are slower.
$r = V_{\max}/V_{\min}$, the largest cylinder volume over the smallest.
Adiabatic compression; heat added at constant volume (spark); adiabatic expansion (power stroke); heat rejected at constant volume.
$e = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{\gamma-1}}$; depends only on the compression ratio and $\gamma$.

cards.front: Temperature after adiabatic compression by a volume ratio $r$
cards.back: $T_2 = T_1r^{\gamma-1}$ (and $P_2 = P_1r^{\gamma}$).
$e = 1 - \dfrac{1}{r^{\gamma-1}}\cdot\dfrac{r_c^{\gamma} - 1}{\gamma(r_c - 1)}$, with cutoff ratio $r_c = V_3/V_2$.

cards.front: Why diesels beat gasoline engines in practice
cards.back: They compress only air, so no knock: compression ratios of about 14–22 instead of 8–12.
$e = 1 - r_p^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$, with pressure ratio $r_p$.
Self-ignition of the compressed fuel–air mixture before the spark; it limits a gasoline engine's compression ratio.

cards.front: Why real cycles fall short of Carnot
cards.back: Heat enters and leaves over a range of temperatures, not only at the extremes (plus friction and heat losses in real engines).
Microstate: every particle specified. Macrostate: only measurable quantities (P, V, T, number of heads).

cards.front: Multiplicity of n heads in N coins
cards.back: $\Omega = \dbinom Nn = \dfrac{N!}{n!(N - n)!}$
$S = k_B\ln\Omega$; multiplicities multiply, entropies add.
An isolated system in equilibrium is equally likely to be in any accessible microstate.
$\Omega$ grows by $(V_2/V_1)^N$, so $\Delta S = Nk_B\ln(V_2/V_1) = nR\ln(V_2/V_1)$.
$\dfrac1T = \dfrac{\partial S}{\partial E}$ (volume and particle number fixed).
$\Omega(N, q) = \dbinom{q + N - 1}{q}$ for $N$ oscillators sharing $q$ quanta.
A state of energy $E$ has relative probability $e^{-E/(k_BT)}$; $k_BT \approx 0.026$ eV at 300 K.
$n(y) = n_0e^{-y/H}$, scale height $H = k_BT/(mg) = RT/(Mg)$, about 8.6 km for air.
A perfect crystal's entropy approaches zero as $T \to 0$ ($\Omega = 1$).
Shear stress $\tau = \eta\,dv/dy$; $\eta$ in Pa·s. Water at 20°C: $1.0\times10^{-3}$ Pa·s; air: $1.8\times10^{-5}$ Pa·s.

cards.front: Velocity profile of laminar pipe flow
cards.back: $v(r) = \dfrac{\Delta P}{4\eta L}(R^2 - r^2)$: a parabola, zero at the wall; average speed is half the maximum.
$Q = \dfrac{\pi R^4\Delta P}{8\eta L}$; halving $R$ cuts the flow to 1/16.
$\text{Re} = \rho vD/\eta$; pipes: laminar below about 2000, usually turbulent above about 3000.
$F = 6\pi\eta rv$ for a sphere when $\text{Re} \ll 1$.
$v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\rho_s - \rho_f)g}{9\eta}$; grows as $r^2$.
About $\tfrac12C\rho Av^2$, with $C \approx 0.5$ for a sphere.
Liquids become much less viscous when heated; gases become slightly more viscous.
A viscous fluid touching a surface moves with it; fluid at a pipe wall is at rest.

cards.front: SI base units for length, mass, time, current
cards.back: meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A)
$1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg·m/s}^2$
$1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N·m} = 1\text{ kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2$
Divide by 3.6 (since $1\text{ km/h} = \tfrac{1000}{3600}\text{ m/s}$).

cards.front: cm² to m² and cm³ to m³
cards.back: $1\text{ cm}^2 = 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$; $1\text{ cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\text{ m}^3$. Square or cube the factor.

cards.front: Prefixes: G, M, k, c, m, μ, n
Sig figs rule for multiplying and dividing
cards.back: Keep as many significant figures as the input with the fewest.

cards.front: Sig figs rule for adding and subtracting
cards.back: Keep as many decimal places as the input with the fewest decimal places.
Zeros between nonzero digits and trailing zeros after a decimal point. Leading zeros never are.

cards.front: What can dimensional analysis catch, and what can't it?
cards.back: It catches wrong powers and missing quantities, but not wrong pure-number factors like 2 or π.

cards.front: Arguments of sin, exp, ln must be…
cards.back: Dimensionless.

cards.front: Components of a vector at angle θ from +x
cards.back: $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$
$A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$ (add 180° if $A_x < 0$).
Add their components separately: $R_x = A_x + B_x$, $R_y = A_y + B_y$.
$\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$ (a scalar; zero when perpendicular).
$|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\phi$, perpendicular to both by the right-hand rule; $\vec B\times\vec A = -\vec A\times\vec B$.
Displacement $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ is signed (a vector); distance is total path length, always positive.
Velocity: displacement/time. Speed: distance/time.

cards.front: When does an object speed up?
cards.back: When $v$ and $a$ have the same sign. Opposite signs: it slows down.
Velocity.

cards.front: Slope of a v–t graph; area under a v–t graph
cards.back: Slope = acceleration; signed area = displacement.
$v = dx/dt$, $a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2$.
$v = v_0 + at$

cards.front: Constant-acceleration equation with no final v
cards.back: $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$
$v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$

cards.front: Stopping distance from speed $v_0$ at deceleration $a$
cards.back: $d = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}$ (proportional to $v_0^2$).
$g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ downward, the same for all masses (no air resistance).

cards.front: Dropped from height h: time and impact speed
cards.back: $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$, $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
The horizontal velocity $v_0\cos\theta$ (and the acceleration, $g$ down).

cards.front: Level-ground range, height, time of flight
cards.back: $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, $H = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, $T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$

cards.front: Launch angle for maximum range (level ground)
cards.back: 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges.
$\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$, and $\vec v_{BA} = -\vec v_{AB}$.

cards.front: Fastest way across a river vs landing directly opposite
cards.back: Fastest: head straight across (time = width/speed). Opposite: head upstream at $\sin\alpha = v_{\text{current}}/v_{\text{boat}}$.
No net force means no change in velocity (constant speed in a straight line, or rest).
$\sum F_x = ma_x$, $\sum F_y = ma_y$
$\vec F_{\text{A on B}} = -\vec F_{\text{B on A}}$: equal, opposite, on different objects, same type of force.
Mass (kg) measures inertia and never changes; weight $mg$ (N) is the gravitational force and depends on $g$.
Isolate the object; draw weight; add a force for each contact (normal, friction, tension, push); choose axes along $\vec a$; write $\sum F = ma$ per axis.

cards.front: Scale reading in an elevator accelerating at a (up positive)
cards.back: $n = m(g + a)$
$f_k = \mu_k n$, opposite the sliding velocity.
$f_s \le \mu_s n$; equals $\mu_s n$ only on the verge of slipping.

cards.front: Weight components on an incline at θ
cards.back: $mg\sin\theta$ down the slope, $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope; $n = mg\cos\theta$.
$a = g\sin\theta$

cards.front: Acceleration sliding down an incline with friction
cards.back: $a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$

cards.front: Angle at which an object just starts to slide
cards.back: $\tan\theta = \mu_s$

cards.front: Block on table (μk) pulled by hanging mass $m_2$
cards.back: $a = \dfrac{m_2 - \mu_k m_1}{m_1 + m_2}g$
$a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{4\pi^2 r}{T^2} = \omega^2 r$, toward the center.
$v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T} = 2\pi r f$

cards.front: Max speed on a flat curve
cards.back: $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^2}{rg}$

cards.front: Minimum speed at the top of a vertical loop
cards.back: $v_{\min} = \sqrt{gr}$ (normal force zero there).
$W = Fd\cos\theta$ (θ between $\vec F$ and $\vec d$); zero if perpendicular, negative if opposing.
$W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K = \tfrac12mv_f^2 - \tfrac12mv_i^2$
$F = -kx$; $U = \tfrac12kx^2$ (= work to stretch by $x$).
$W = \int_{x_1}^{x_2}F(x)\,dx$ = area under the $F$–$x$ graph.
$U_g = mgy$ (zero level is your choice).
$K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$ when only conservative forces do work.
$K_i + U_i + W_{\text{nc}} = K_f + U_f$, with $W_{\text{friction}} = -f_kd$.

cards.front: Speed after falling height h (any frictionless path)
cards.back: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
$F = -\dfrac{dU}{dx}$; equilibrium where $dU/dx = 0$, stable if $U$ is a minimum.
$P = W/\Delta t = Fv$; 1 W = 1 J/s; 1 hp = 746 W.
$\vec p = m\vec v$; $K = p^2/(2m)$.
$\vec J = \vec F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \Delta\vec p$ (generally $\int\vec F\,dt$).

cards.front: Why do air bags and crumple zones help?
cards.back: They lengthen the stopping time, so the same $\Delta p$ needs a smaller average force.
When the net external force on the system is zero (component by component).
$\Delta v = u\ln(m_i/m_f)$, $u$ = exhaust speed relative to the rocket (no external force).
$u\,|dm/dt|$: exhaust speed times mass ejected per second.
$x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{M}$, or $\dfrac1M\int x\,dm$; $\vec F_{\text{ext}} = M\vec a_{\text{cm}}$.

cards.front: Elastic vs inelastic vs perfectly inelastic
cards.back: All conserve momentum. Elastic also conserves KE; perfectly inelastic objects stick and lose the most KE.
It reverses: $v_{1i} - v_{2i} = -(v_{1f} - v_{2f})$.
Momentum conservation for the collision, then energy conservation for the swing: $v = \dfrac{m + M}{m}\sqrt{2gh}$.
Multiply by $2\pi/60 \approx 0.1047$.
$s = r\theta$, $v = r\omega$, $a_t = r\alpha$, $a_c = r\omega^2$ (θ in radians).
$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t$; $\Delta\theta = \omega_0t + \tfrac12\alpha t^2$; $\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\Delta\theta$
$I = \sum m_ir_i^2 = \int r^2\,dm$

cards.front: I for hoop, solid disk, solid sphere, hollow sphere (central axis)
cards.back: $MR^2$, $\tfrac12MR^2$, $\tfrac25MR^2$, $\tfrac23MR^2$
$I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$
$K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$
$\tau = rF\sin\theta = rF_\perp$; $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$; counterclockwise positive.
$\sum\tau = I\alpha$

cards.front: Mass m hanging from a solid cylinder pulley of mass M
cards.back: $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + \tfrac12M}$, $T = \tfrac12Ma$
$v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega$; $K = \tfrac12Mv^2 + \tfrac12I\omega^2$

cards.front: Speed at the bottom of a ramp for a rolling object with $I = cMR^2$
cards.back: $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2gh}{1 + c}}$
Solid sphere, solid cylinder, hollow sphere, hoop (smallest $c$ first).
$L = I\omega$; particle: $L = mvr_\perp$; vector: $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$.
$\vec\tau_{\text{net}} = d\vec L/dt$
No external torque: $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$ (KE need not be conserved).
$\sum\vec F = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$ about any point.

cards.front: Best pivot for an equilibrium torque equation
cards.back: A point where an unknown force acts, so it drops out.

cards.front: When does an object tip over?
cards.back: When its center of gravity moves beyond the edge of its base.
Stress $F/A$ = $Y$ × strain $\Delta L/L$, so $\Delta L = FL/(AY)$.
Shear: $F/A = S\,\Delta x/L$. Bulk: $\Delta P = -B\,\Delta V/V$.
$F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$, $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg²
$g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$
$v = \sqrt{GM/r}$; $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$
Elliptical orbits (Sun at a focus); equal areas in equal times; $T^2 \propto a^3$.
$v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ = $\sqrt2$ × low-orbit speed; 11.2 km/s for Earth.
$E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ ($K = -E$, $U = 2E$)

cards.front: Period of a mass on a spring
cards.back: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$; $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$

cards.front: Period of a simple pendulum (small angles)
cards.back: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, independent of mass and amplitude.

cards.front: SHM position, max speed, max acceleration
cards.back: $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$; $v_{\max} = A\omega$; $a_{\max} = A\omega^2$
$E = \tfrac12kA^2 = \tfrac12mv^2 + \tfrac12kx^2$; $v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$

cards.front: Does SHM period depend on amplitude?
cards.back: No (for ideal springs and small-angle pendulums).
$\ddot x = -\omega^2x$; whatever multiplies $-x$ is $\omega^2$.
Driving an oscillator at its natural frequency produces a large amplitude.
$m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx = 0$; write $\gamma = b/2m$, $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$.
$x = A_0e^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega' t + \phi)$ with $\omega' = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}$ (when $\gamma < \omega_0$).
$b = 2\sqrt{mk}$ ($\gamma = \omega_0$): fastest return to equilibrium with no overshoot. Overdamped is slower.
$Q = \omega_0/(2\gamma) = \sqrt{mk}/b$; amplitude falls by $e$ in about $Q/\pi$ cycles.

cards.front: Amplitude vs energy decay in a damped oscillator
cards.back: Amplitude $\propto e^{-bt/2m}$; energy $\propto e^{-bt/m}$ (twice as fast).

cards.front: Steady-state amplitude of a driven oscillator
cards.back: $A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (2\gamma\omega)^2}}$, oscillating at the driving frequency.
$A = F_0/(b\omega_0) = Q \times$ the static stretch $F_0/k$; displacement lags the force by $90^\circ$.
Half-power bandwidth $\Delta\omega = b/m$, so $Q = \omega_0/\Delta\omega$: high $Q$ means a tall, narrow peak.
$v = f\lambda = \lambda/T$

cards.front: What changes when a wave enters a new medium?
cards.back: Speed and wavelength change; frequency stays the same.
$v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$, $\mu$ = mass per length

cards.front: Average power of a wave on a string
cards.back: $P_{\text{avg}} = \tfrac12\mu A^2\omega^2v$, proportional to $A^2$ and $\omega^2$.
Transverse: medium moves ⊥ to travel (string). Longitudinal: medium moves ∥ (sound).
Constructive: $\Delta r = m\lambda$. Destructive: $\Delta r = (m + \tfrac12)\lambda$.

cards.front: Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends
cards.back: $\lambda_n = 2L/n$, $f_n = nv/(2L)$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
$y = A\sin(kx - \omega t)$, $k = 2\pi/\lambda$, $\omega = 2\pi f$, $v = \omega/k$

cards.front: Speed of sound in air at 20°C
cards.back: About 343 m/s; $v \approx 331 + 0.6\,T_C$ m/s.
×10 intensity: +10 dB. ×2 intensity: +3 dB. ×10 distance (point source): −20 dB.
$f_n = nv/(2L)$, all harmonics
$f_n = nv/(4L)$, odd harmonics only
$f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|$
$f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$; upper signs for motion toward.
$P = P_0 + \rho gh$ (depends only on depth)
Gauge = absolute − atmospheric; 1 atm = $1.013\times10^5$ Pa.
$F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$; volumes moved are equal, so $A_1d_1 = A_2d_2$.
$F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ (weight of displaced fluid).
$V_{\text{sub}}/V = \rho_{\text{obj}}/\rho_{\text{fluid}}$
$P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho gy$ = constant along a streamline
$v = \sqrt{2gh}$ for a hole at depth $h$
$\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T$; volume: $\Delta V = \beta V\Delta T$, $\beta \approx 3\alpha$
$Q = mc\Delta T$
$Q = mL$; water: $L_f = 3.34\times10^5$ J/kg, $L_v = 2.26\times10^6$ J/kg
$\sum m c(T_f - T_i) = 0$ (add $\pm mL$ for phase changes)
$Q/t = kA\Delta T/L$
$PV = nRT = Nk_BT$; $R = 8.314$ J/(mol·K)
$\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$ (absolute $P$, $T$ in K)

cards.front: Average translational KE of a gas molecule
cards.back: $\tfrac12m\overline{v^2} = \tfrac32k_BT$
$v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$ ($M$ in kg/mol)

cards.front: Internal energy of a monatomic ideal gas
cards.back: $E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32nRT$
$\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$ ($Q$ in, $W$ by the gas)
$W = \int P\,dV$ = area under the PV curve; $P\Delta V$ at constant pressure.
$W = nRT\ln(V_f/V_i)$, and $Q = W$
$Q = 0$; $PV^\gamma$ = const; $TV^{\gamma-1}$ = const; $\gamma = 5/3$ monatomic

cards.front: Monatomic ideal gas molar specific heats
cards.back: $C_V = \tfrac32R$, $C_P = \tfrac52R$, $C_P - C_V = R$
$e = W/Q_H = 1 - Q_C/Q_H$
$e_C = 1 - T_C/T_H$ (kelvins); no engine between the same two reservoirs can do better.
$K = Q_C/W$; Carnot limit $T_C/(T_H - T_C)$
$\Delta S = Q/T$
$\Delta S = mc\ln(T_2/T_1)$
The total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

glossary.definition: A condition that limits the possible positions of a system, such as a pendulum rod's fixed length ($x^2 + y^2 = \ell^2$) or an inextensible string.
The number of independent quantities needed to specify a system's configuration once its constraints are taken into account: one for a pendulum, two for a puck on a table, three for a free particle.
Any set of independent quantities $q_1, q_2, \ldots$ (lengths, angles, …) that fixes a system's configuration, one per degree of freedom, chosen so the constraints hold automatically.
Kinetic minus potential energy, $L = T - U$, written in generalized coordinates and their rates $\dot q$. Not the total energy.
The time integral of the Lagrangian along a path, $S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2}L\,dt$, with units of J·s.

The path a system actually follows between fixed endpoints makes the action stationary: small changes to the path don't change $S$ to first order. Often called "least" action, though the true path can be a saddle point.

The equation of motion for each generalized coordinate, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\right) - \dfrac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$, which follows from making the action stationary.
The momentum belonging to a generalized coordinate, $p = \partial L/\partial\dot q$: ordinary momentum for a length, angular momentum for an angle.

The quantity $\partial L/\partial q$ on the right of $dp/dt = \partial L/\partial q$; a force for a length coordinate and a torque for an angle. Also used for nonconservative forces added to the Euler–Lagrange equation.
A generalized coordinate that does not appear in the Lagrangian (its rate may). Its generalized momentum is conserved.
Every continuous symmetry of the action gives a conserved quantity (Emmy Noether, 1918): time shifts give energy, position shifts give linear momentum, rotations give angular momentum.

$H = \sum p\dot q - L$, written in terms of coordinates and momenta. Conserved when $L$ has no explicit time dependence; equal to $T + U$ when the constraints are fixed and $U$ doesn't depend on velocities.
The equations of motion in Hamiltonian form: $\dot q = \partial H/\partial p$ and $\dot p = -\partial H/\partial q$, two first-order equations per coordinate.
The space of all positions and momenta of a system, for one coordinate the $(q, p)$ plane. Each point is a complete state.
A drawing of the paths in phase space for many starting states, showing at a glance the kinds of motion a system can have.
A phase-space path that divides two kinds of motion; for a pendulum, the path at exactly the energy to reach the top, separating swinging from full rotation.
Under Hamilton's equations, a region of starting states in phase space moves and changes shape but keeps its area (volume). Stated without proof in this course.
Finding the motion of two bodies that attract each other with an inverse-square force, such as a planet and a star; its bound solutions are ellipses.
For a central force, $U_{\text{eff}}(r) = \dfrac{\ell^2}{2mr^2} + U(r)$: the radial motion behaves like one-dimensional motion in this potential. The first term is the centrifugal barrier.
The equation for an orbit's shape using $u = 1/r$ as a function of angle: $\dfrac{d^2u}{d\varphi^2} + u = \dfrac{GMm^2}{\ell^2}$ for gravity, with solution $r = \dfrac{p}{1 + e\cos\varphi}$.
Of all central force laws, only the inverse-square force and the linear (spring) force make every bound orbit close on itself.
A curve made by slicing a cone with a plane: circle, ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. Orbits under inverse-square forces are conic sections with the attracting body at a focus.
The number $e$ that sets an orbit's shape: $e = 0$ circle, $0 < e < 1$ ellipse, $e = 1$ parabola, $e > 1$ hyperbola. For an ellipse, $e = (r_a - r_p)/(r_a + r_p)$.
Half the longest diameter of an ellipse, $a = (r_p + r_a)/2$ for an orbit. It alone sets the orbit's energy, $E = -GMm/(2a)$, and period, $T^2 = 4\pi^2a^3/GM$.
The point of an orbit closest to the body being orbited, at $r_p = a(1 - e)$; perigee for Earth orbits, perihelion for orbits of the Sun. The speed is greatest there.
The point of an orbit farthest from the body being orbited, at $r_a = a(1 + e)$; apogee for Earth orbits, aphelion for orbits of the Sun. The speed is least there.
The speed at any point of a Kepler orbit: $v^2 = GM\left(\dfrac{2}{r} - \dfrac{1}{a}\right)$, from energy conservation with $E = -GMm/(2a)$.
Orbital energy per unit mass of the orbiting body, $\varepsilon = \dfrac{v^2}{2} - \dfrac{GM}{r} = -\dfrac{GM}{2a}$; negative for bound orbits, zero for a parabola, positive for a hyperbola.
The change in velocity a maneuver needs, or the total a spacecraft's propellant can provide ($u\ln(m_i/m_f)$ by the rocket equation). The basic budget unit of spaceflight.
A model of a rocket burn so short compared with the orbital period that the velocity changes instantly while the position stays the same.
A move between two coplanar circular orbits along half an ellipse that touches both, with one forward burn at each end; the cheapest two-burn transfer between them.
An orbit used to travel from one orbit to another, entered and left by burns; in a Hohmann transfer, an ellipse with periapsis on the inner orbit and apoapsis on the outer.
The speed $v_\infty$ an escaping spacecraft keeps far from a planet: $v_\infty^2 = v^2 - v_{\text{esc}}^2$ for speed $v$ at distance $r$.
A given $\Delta v$ changes kinetic energy by about $mv\,\Delta v$, so a burn is most effective where the spacecraft moves fastest, such as periapsis deep in a gravity well.
The time for one planet to gain a full lap on another as seen from the Sun, $1/S = |1/T_1 - 1/T_2|$; about 2.14 years (26 months) for Earth and Mars.
The period when the planets are positioned so that a planned transfer reaches its target; for Hohmann transfers to Mars, about once every 26 months.
A flyby in which a planet turns a spacecraft's velocity; its speed is unchanged in the planet's frame but can increase or decrease in the Sun's frame.
The amount $\delta x$ by which a measured or calculated value may differ from the true value, written $x \pm \delta x$ in the same units as $x$.
The uncertainty divided by the size of the value, $\delta x/|x|$, often given as a percentage; it has no units, so it compares quality across quantities.
Error that scatters repeated readings above and below the true value; averaging many readings reduces its effect.
Error that shifts every reading the same way, such as a zero offset or a miscalibrated instrument; averaging does not reduce it.
The typical spread of single readings about their mean: $s = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2/(n-1)}$.
The uncertainty of a mean of $n$ readings, $s/\sqrt n$; it shrinks as more readings are taken.
Working out the uncertainty of a calculated result from the uncertainties of the measurements it uses.
Combining independent uncertainties as the square root of the sum of their squares, $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$, rather than as a plain sum.
The difference between a result and an accepted value, or between two results; judged against the uncertainty to decide whether they agree.
The signed length of the part of $\vec A$ along $\vec B$: $\vec A\cdot\hat B = A\cos\phi$.
The part of $\vec A$ parallel to $\vec B$: $(\vec A\cdot\hat B)\,\hat B = \dfrac{\vec A\cdot\vec B}{B^2}\vec B$.
The cosines of the angles a vector makes with the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes, $A_x/A$, $A_y/A$, $A_z/A$; they are the components of $\hat A$ and their squares add to 1.
$\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C)$, the determinant of the three vectors' components; its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped they span.
Lying in one plane. Three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product is zero.
$\vec A\times(\vec B\times\vec C) = \vec B(\vec A\cdot\vec C) - \vec C(\vec A\cdot\vec B)$, a vector in the plane of $\vec B$ and $\vec C$.
The path of a projectile written as $y$ in terms of $x$: $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2\cos^2\theta}$, found by eliminating $t$ from the component equations.

The curve $y = \dfrac{v_0^2}{2g} - \dfrac{gx^2}{2v_0^2}$ that every trajectory launched at speed $v_0$ touches once and never crosses (their envelope). Points under it can be hit at two angles, points on it at one, points above it not at all (no air resistance).
The unit vector $\hat T = \vec v/|\vec v|$ pointing along a path in the direction of motion.
The unit vector $\hat N$ perpendicular to the path, pointing toward the inside of the bend (toward the center of curvature); $d\hat T/dt = (v/\rho)\hat N$.
The circle that best fits a curved path at a point: it has the same tangent and the same curvature there. Its radius is the radius of curvature and its center is the center of curvature.
The radius $\rho$ of the osculating circle at a point of a path; small $\rho$ means a sharp bend. For motion, $\rho = v^2/a_n = v^3/|v_xa_y - v_ya_x|$.
How sharply a path bends at a point: $\kappa = 1/\rho$, the reciprocal of the radius of curvature. A straight line has zero curvature.

The part of the acceleration perpendicular to the velocity, $a_n = v^2/\rho$, pointing toward the center of curvature; it changes the direction of motion, not the speed. Also called radial or centripetal acceleration.
Distance measured along a curved path: $s = \int |\vec v|\,dt$. It is never less than the magnitude of the displacement.
The acceleration of one object as measured from another, $\vec a_A - \vec a_B$; for slipping stacked blocks it sets how fast one slides along the other.
The angle whose tangent equals the coefficient of friction, $\tan\theta = \mu$: the steepest incline an object can rest on (with $\mu_s$) and the best angle for dragging a crate (with $\mu_k$).

$T_{\text{load}} = T_{\text{hold}}e^{\mu\theta}$: the largest load a rope wrapped through angle $\theta$ (radians) around a fixed post can hold against a smaller holding force, in the ideal flexible-rope model.
The total angle, in radians, through which a rope or belt touches a post or pulley; $2\pi$ for each full turn.
Drag proportional to speed, $F_D = bv$; it describes small, slow objects in a viscous fluid (Reynolds number much less than 1).
Drag proportional to the square of the speed, $F_D = \tfrac12C\rho Av^2$; it describes most everyday objects moving through air or water.
The dimensionless, measured number $C$ in the quadratic drag law $\tfrac12C\rho Av^2$; it depends on shape (roughly 0.5 for a sphere, about 1 for a person falling flat).
A term added to Newton's second law in an accelerating frame, such as $-m\vec A$; it has no agent and no third-law partner.
A reference frame that accelerates or rotates relative to inertial frames; Newton's laws hold in it only if fictitious forces are added.
In a frame accelerating at $\vec A$, the combination $\vec g_{\text{eff}} = \vec g - \vec A$ that objects behave as if it were gravity; a plumb line hangs along it.
The fictitious force $m\omega^2r$ pointing away from the axis that appears in a rotating frame; it is not a real force in an inertial frame.

The fictitious force $-2m\vec\omega\times\vec v'$ on an object moving in a rotating frame; it is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work. It deflects motion to the right in Earth's Northern Hemisphere.
A long pendulum whose plane of swing slowly turns relative to the ground because Earth rotates, once every $23.93\text{ h}/\sin\lambda$ at latitude $\lambda$; first shown in Paris in 1851.
A force that depends on position, $\vec F(x, y, z)$: it assigns a force vector to every point of a region.

The sum of $\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell$ along a path, $\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell$; for a force it is the work done along that path. Evaluate it by parametrizing the path: $\int\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot\vec r\,'(t)\,dt$.
The property that the work done by a force between two points is the same along every path joining them; it defines a conservative force.

The vector $\nabla\times\vec F$ built from the derivatives of a field's components; in the plane its one component is $\partial F_y/\partial x - \partial F_x/\partial y$. A conservative force has zero curl, and on a region without holes zero curl guarantees a potential energy.
A force that points along the line to a fixed center and whose size depends only on the distance $r$ from it, $\vec F = f(r)\hat r$. Every central force is conservative, with $U = -\int f(r)\,dr$.
A curve or surface on which the potential energy is constant. A conservative force is perpendicular to the equipotentials and points toward lower potential energy.
The speed a rocket fails to gain because its weight acts during the burn: $gt_b$ for a vertical burn of duration $t_b$ in uniform gravity, subtracted from $u\ln(m_i/m_f)$.
The rate at which a stream carries momentum across a surface; for a fluid jet of density $\rho$, area $A$ and speed $v$ it is $\rho Av^2$ (mass rate $\rho Av$ times speed $v$).
The reference frame in which a collision is observed or set up, usually with the target at rest.
The inertial frame moving with the center of mass of the colliding objects. In it the total momentum is zero, so the two objects have equal and opposite momenta.

For two objects, $\mu = \dfrac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$, smaller than either mass. The CM-frame momenta are $\pm\mu\vec v_{\text{rel}}$, and the kinetic energy in the CM frame is $\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$.
The kinetic energy of two objects in their center-of-mass frame, $\tfrac12\mu v_{\text{rel}}^2$; the only part of the kinetic energy a collision can convert to other forms.

The angle through which a collision turns a particle's velocity. In the CM frame an elastic collision only turns the momenta, by the CM scattering angle; the lab-frame angle is found by adding the CM velocity back.

A material of light nuclei, such as water, heavy water or graphite, that slows fast fission neutrons through elastic collisions, so that in a thermal reactor they are much more likely to cause further fission.
The velocity of a rolling object's contact point relative to the surface, $v_{\text{cm}} - R\omega$. It is zero for rolling without slipping; otherwise kinetic friction acts opposite to it.

The point of a pivoted rigid body where a blow produces no impulse at the pivot, a distance $b = I_P/(Md)$ from it; $\tfrac23L$ for a uniform rod held at one end. A simple model of a bat's sweet spot.
Treating a precessing gyroscope's angular momentum as pure spin, $L = I\omega$ along the axle; valid when the spin is much faster than the precession, giving $\Omega = \tau/(I\omega)$.
A small bobbing of a spinning body's axis on top of its steady precession, seen for example when a gyroscope is released with its axle held still.
The slow conical motion of Earth's spin axis, one cycle in about 26,000 years, caused by the Sun's and Moon's torques on Earth's equatorial bulge.

One of three perpendicular axes through a rigid body's center of mass about which its angular momentum is parallel to its angular velocity; symmetry axes are principal axes. Spinning about one needs no bearing torque.
Gravitational potential energy per unit mass, $V = U/m$ (J/kg); $-GM/r$ for a point mass. The field is its negative slope, $g_r = -dV/dr$.
A uniform spherical shell attracts outside masses as if all its mass were at its center, and exerts no net gravitational force anywhere inside it.
The difference between a body's gravitational pull at a point and at the center of the object it acts on; about $2GMd/D^3$ along the line to the body, and half that, inward, across it.
A tide of extra-large range at new and full moon, when the Sun's and Moon's tidal effects line up and add.
A tide of small range at first and third quarter moon, when the Sun's and Moon's tidal effects act at right angles and partly cancel.
The state of a body whose spin period equals its orbital period, so it always shows the same face to its partner; produced by tidal friction, as for the Moon.
The distance from a planet inside which its tides pull apart a moon held together only by gravity: roughly $R_p(2\rho_p/\rho_m)^{1/3}$ (rigid estimate) to $2.44R_p(\rho_p/\rho_m)^{1/3}$ (fluid moon).
Breaking a signal into sinusoids of different frequencies, to find which frequencies it contains and how strongly.
Any periodic signal with period $T$ (piecewise smooth, as in physics) is a sum of a constant and sinusoids at the frequencies $n/T$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$
The sum $a_0 + \sum_n [a_n\cos(n\omega_1t) + b_n\sin(n\omega_1t)]$, with $\omega_1 = 2\pi/T$, that represents a periodic signal.
The numbers $a_0$, $a_n$, $b_n$ in a Fourier series: $a_0$ is the average, and $a_n, b_n = \tfrac2T\int_0^T y\cos$ or $\sin(n\omega_1t)\,dt$.
Of two functions over an interval: the integral of their product over it is zero. Different harmonics are orthogonal over one period.
The overshoot of about 9% of the jump that a partial Fourier sum always shows next to a jump; more terms make it narrower, not smaller.
A graph or list of the amplitudes (or powers) of the frequency components in a signal.
The mean square of a periodic signal is the sum of its parts: $\overline{y^2} = a_0^2 + \tfrac12\sum_n c_n^2$, so the power in each harmonic adds separately.
Two or more oscillators connected so that each one exerts forces on the others, such as two pendulums joined by a spring.
The spring that connects two oscillators to each other, as opposed to the springs that hold each one to a fixed support.
A motion of a system in which every part oscillates at the same frequency with fixed amplitude ratios; any motion is a superposition of normal modes.
Combinations of the coordinates (such as $x_1 + x_2$ and $x_1 - x_2$ for two equal masses) that each obey a separate SHM equation.
Dependence of a wave's speed on its frequency or wavelength, as for the short waves on a beaded string.

The ideal cycle of a spark-ignition (gasoline) engine: adiabatic compression, heat added at constant volume, adiabatic expansion, heat rejected at constant volume. Its air-standard efficiency is $1 - 1/r^{\gamma-1}$.
The ideal cycle of a compression-ignition engine: adiabatic compression, heat added at constant pressure, adiabatic expansion, heat rejected at constant volume.

The ideal cycle of a gas turbine or jet engine: adiabatic compression, heat added at constant pressure, adiabatic expansion, heat rejected at constant pressure. Efficiency $1 - r_p^{-(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$.

A simplified model of an engine in which a fixed amount of air, treated as an ideal gas with constant specific heats, has heat added in place of combustion and removed in place of exhaust, with every step reversible.
In a piston engine, the largest cylinder volume divided by the smallest, $r = V_{\max}/V_{\min}$.
The stroke of a piston engine in which the hot, high-pressure gas pushes the piston and does work; in the Otto cycle, the adiabatic expansion.
Uncontrolled self-ignition of the compressed fuel–air mixture before or apart from the spark; it limits the compression ratio of gasoline engines.
In the Diesel cycle, the volume at the end of the constant-pressure heat addition divided by the volume at its start, $r_c = V_3/V_2$.
In the Brayton cycle, the highest pressure divided by the lowest, $r_p = P_{\max}/P_{\min}$, set by the compressor.
A power plant that uses a gas turbine's hot exhaust to make steam for a second, steam turbine; the best convert a little over 60% of the fuel's energy to electricity.
A complete description of a system at the level of its particles, such as which side each coin shows or the position and velocity of every molecule.
A description of a system by measurable quantities only, such as the number of heads or the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas. Many microstates usually share one macrostate.
The number of microstates $\Omega$ that belong to a given macrostate.
The assumption that an isolated system in equilibrium is equally likely to be in any of its accessible microstates.
$S = k_B\ln\Omega$: entropy is Boltzmann's constant times the natural log of the number of microstates.
$1/T = \partial S/\partial E$ at fixed volume and particle number: temperature measures how fast entropy grows as energy is added.
A simple model of a crystal as $N$ identical oscillators (three per atom) holding whole quanta of energy; $q$ quanta can be shared in $\binom{q + N - 1}{q}$ ways.
$e^{-E/(k_BT)}$, the relative probability of a particular state of energy $E$ for a system in contact with surroundings at temperature $T$.
The height over which the density of an isothermal atmosphere falls by a factor of $e$: $H = k_BT/(mg) = RT/(Mg)$, about 8.6 km for air near room temperature.
The entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as its temperature approaches absolute zero.
The observation that a viscous fluid touching a solid surface moves with that surface; in a pipe, the fluid at the wall is at rest.
Force per area parallel to a surface; in a fluid with viscosity $\eta$, $\tau = \eta\,dv/dy$.
A fluid whose shear stress is proportional to its velocity gradient, with a viscosity that does not depend on how fast it flows (water, air, most oils).
The flow rate of laminar flow through a pipe: $Q = \dfrac{\pi R^4\Delta P}{8\eta L}$.
The pressure difference needed per unit flow rate, $\Delta P/Q$; for laminar flow in a pipe, $8\eta L/(\pi R^4)$.
Smooth flow in which layers of fluid slide past one another without mixing; in a pipe, usually when the Reynolds number is below about 2000.
Chaotic flow full of eddies, which takes a larger pressure difference to drive; in a pipe, usually when the Reynolds number is above about 3000.
The dimensionless number $\text{Re} = \rho vD/\eta$, comparing inertial and viscous effects; it decides whether a flow is laminar or turbulent.
The drag on a sphere of radius $r$ moving slowly (Re much less than 1) through a fluid: $F = 6\pi\eta rv$.
A device that measures a liquid's viscosity from the terminal speed of a ball falling through it, using Stokes' law.
The International System of Units, built on seven base units including the meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K) and mole (mol).
A unit built from base units by multiplying and dividing, such as the newton ($\text{kg·m/s}^2$) or joule ($\text{kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2$).
Writing a number as $a \times 10^n$ with $1 \le |a| < 10$; every digit of $a$ is significant.
A ratio equal to 1, such as $\tfrac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}}$, used to change units without changing the quantity.
The digits of a measured value that carry real information: all nonzero digits, zeros between them, and trailing zeros after a decimal point.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How closely repeated measurements agree with each other, and how finely a value is stated.
The kind of physical quantity something is, written in brackets: length [L], mass [M], time [T]. Speed has dimension [L]/[T].
Checking or deriving relationships by requiring every term of an equation to have the same dimensions.
The power of ten closest to a value; used for quick estimates.
A quantity fully described by a number and a unit, with no direction (mass, time, energy, temperature).
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, force or momentum.
The vector sum of two or more vectors.
The projections of a vector onto the coordinate axes: $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ for an angle measured from $+x$.
Vectors of length 1 that mark directions; $\hat\imath$, $\hat\jmath$, $\hat k$ point along $+x$, $+y$, $+z$.
$\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$, a scalar measuring how much two vectors point the same way.
$\vec A\times\vec B$, a vector of magnitude $AB\sin\phi$ perpendicular to both, with direction given by the right-hand rule.
Point the fingers of your right hand along the first vector, curl them toward the second; the thumb gives the direction of the cross product.
The description of motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without regard to its causes.
An object's coordinate relative to a chosen origin and positive direction.
Change in position, $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ (a vector; can be negative or zero).
Total length of path traveled; always positive.
Displacement divided by elapsed time, $v_{\text{avg}} = \Delta x/\Delta t$.
Total distance divided by elapsed time.
The velocity at one instant, $v = dx/dt$: the slope of the position–time graph.
Rate of change of velocity, $a = dv/dt$, in m/s². It is a vector; its sign shows the direction of the change in velocity.
The free-fall acceleration near Earth's surface, $g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ directed downward.
Motion under the influence of gravity alone, with acceleration $g$ downward regardless of mass.
The constant speed a falling object reaches when air drag balances its weight.
Two-dimensional motion under gravity alone: constant horizontal velocity plus free fall vertically, giving a parabolic path.
Horizontal distance a projectile travels; on level ground $R = v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g$.
The component of acceleration along the velocity; it changes the speed.
The component of acceleration perpendicular to the velocity, toward the center of curvature; it changes the direction of motion.
A set of coordinate axes attached to some object, from which positions and velocities are measured.
Velocity measured in a particular frame; $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$.
A reference frame that is not accelerating; Newton's laws hold in it.
A push or pull by one object on another; a vector measured in newtons (N).
SI unit of force: $1\text{ N} = 1\text{ kg·m/s}^2$.
An object keeps a constant velocity (including rest) unless a net force acts on it.
The tendency of an object to keep its velocity; measured by its mass.
The vector sum of all forces acting on an object, $\sum\vec F$.
$\sum\vec F = m\vec a$, or generally $\vec F_{\text{net}} = d\vec p/dt$.
The measure of an object's inertia (resistance to acceleration), in kilograms; the same everywhere.
The state of zero net force (and, for extended objects, zero net torque): at rest or moving at constant velocity.
The gravitational force on an object, $W = mg$, directed downward.
The contact force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself; found from Newton's second law, not assumed equal to $mg$.
If A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The pair acts on different objects.
A sketch of one object showing every force acting on it as an arrow; the starting point of a dynamics problem.
The normal force (scale reading) supporting an object; differs from $mg$ when the object accelerates vertically.
A contact force parallel to surfaces that opposes sliding or the tendency to slide.
Friction between sliding surfaces, $f_k = \mu_k n$, opposite to the sliding velocity.
The dimensionless ratio $\mu_k = f_k/n$ for a pair of sliding surfaces.
Friction between surfaces not sliding; adjusts to prevent motion up to $f_s = \mu_s n$.
The ratio $\mu_s = f_{s,\max}/n$; equals $\tan\theta$ at the angle where an object just starts to slide down an incline.
The pulling force a taut rope, string or cable exerts along its length.
An idealized rope with no mass, which therefore has the same tension throughout.
A massless, frictionless pulley that changes a rope's direction without changing its tension.
Two masses hung over a pulley; $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$.
Motion in a circle at constant speed; the acceleration $v^2/r$ points to the center.
The time for one complete cycle (revolution or oscillation), $T = 1/f$.
Number of cycles per second, $f = 1/T$, in hertz (Hz).
The center-directed acceleration of circular motion, $a_c = v^2/r = \omega^2 r$.
The net inward force required for circular motion, $mv^2/r$, supplied by real forces such as tension, friction, gravity or the normal force.
Energy transferred by a force acting through a displacement: $W = Fd\cos\theta$, or $\int\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell$. A scalar, in joules.
SI unit of work and energy: $1\text{ J} = 1\text{ N·m} = 1\text{ kg·m}^2/\text{s}^2$.
The total work done by all forces on an object; equals its change in kinetic energy.
Energy of motion, $K = \tfrac12mv^2 = p^2/(2m)$.
The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy: $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$.
An ideal spring exerts $F = -kx$, proportional to its stretch or compression and directed back toward equilibrium.
The stiffness $k$ of a spring in N/m: the force per unit stretch.
Stored energy of position or configuration associated with a conservative force; $W_{\text{cons}} = -\Delta U$.
A force whose work between two points is independent of the path (gravity, springs, electrostatic force).
Near Earth's surface, $U_g = mgy$ relative to a chosen zero level; in general $U = -GMm/r$.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring, $U_s = \tfrac12kx^2$.
The sum of kinetic and potential energy, $E = K + U$.
If only conservative forces do work, $K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f$.
A force such as friction or drag whose work depends on the path; its work $W_{\text{nc}}$ changes the mechanical energy.
Rate of doing work or transferring energy: $P = W/\Delta t = \vec F\cdot\vec v$, in watts.
SI unit of power: $1\text{ W} = 1\text{ J/s}$. One horsepower is 746 W.
Ratio of useful output energy (or power) to input, $\eta = P_{\text{out}}/P_{\text{in}}$.
A position where $U(x) = E$, so the kinetic energy is zero and the particle reverses direction.
The product of mass and velocity, $\vec p = m\vec v$ (kg·m/s), a vector.
Force times the time it acts, $\vec J = \vec F_{\text{avg}}\Delta t = \int\vec F\,dt$, in N·s.
The impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: $\vec J = \Delta\vec p$.
The speed gained by a rocket with no external force, $\Delta v = u\ln(m_i/m_f)$, where $u$ is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket and $m_i/m_f$ the ratio of initial to final mass.
The forward force on a rocket from its exhaust, $u\,|dm/dt|$: exhaust speed relative to the rocket times the rate mass is ejected.
With zero net external force, a system's total momentum stays constant.
The mass-weighted average position, $x_{\text{cm}} = \sum m_ix_i/M$; it moves as if all external forces acted on the total mass there.
A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
A collision in which the objects stick together; it loses the most kinetic energy allowed by momentum conservation.
Ratio of separation speed to approach speed in a collision: 1 for elastic, 0 for perfectly inelastic.
The angle subtending an arc equal to the radius: $\theta = s/r$. A full turn is $2\pi$ rad.
The change in angular position, $\Delta\theta$, in radians.
Rate of change of angle, $\omega = d\theta/dt$, in rad/s; $\omega = 2\pi f$.
Rate of change of angular velocity, $\alpha = d\omega/dt$, in rad/s².
Revolutions per minute; $1\text{ rpm} = 2\pi/60 \approx 0.1047$ rad/s.
Resistance to angular acceleration about an axis: $I = \sum m_ir_i^2 = \int r^2\,dm$ (kg·m²).
$I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$ for an axis parallel to one through the center of mass, a distance $d$ away.
Kinetic energy of rotation, $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$.
The turning effect of a force about an axis: $\tau = rF\sin\theta$, or $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ (N·m).
The perpendicular distance from the axis to a force's line of action; $\tau = (\text{lever arm})\times F$.
Rolling in which the contact point is momentarily at rest, so $v_{\text{cm}} = R\omega$.
$L = I\omega$ for a rigid body about a fixed axis; in general $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$. Changed only by torque: $\vec\tau = d\vec L/dt$.
With zero net external torque, $L$ is constant: $I_i\omega_i = I_f\omega_f$.
A rapidly spinning wheel whose large angular momentum resists changes in direction; a torque makes it precess.
The slow rotation of a spinning object's axis caused by a torque perpendicular to its angular momentum; rate $\Omega = \tau/L$.
The state of a rigid body at rest with $\sum\vec F = 0$ and $\sum\tau = 0$.
The point where an object's total weight effectively acts; equals the center of mass in uniform gravity.
Force per unit area applied to a material, $F/A$, in pascals.
The fractional deformation of a material, such as $\Delta L/L$; dimensionless.
The ratio of tensile stress to strain for small deformations, $Y = (F/A)/(\Delta L/L)$; about $2\times10^{11}$ Pa for steel.
The largest stress a material can take and still return to its original shape when the load is removed.
The ratio of shear stress to shear strain, $S = (F/A)/(\Delta x/L)$, for a force applied parallel to a face; fluids have none.
The ratio of added pressure to fractional volume decrease, $B = -\Delta P/(\Delta V/V)$; a large $B$ means hard to compress.
Any two masses attract with $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$ along the line joining them.
$G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N·m²/kg², the constant in Newton's law of gravitation.
A dependence of the form $1/r^2$, as in gravity, Coulomb's law and the intensity of a point source.
An equatorial orbit with a 24-hour period (radius about $4.22\times10^7$ m), so the satellite stays above one point.
(1) Orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus; (2) equal areas in equal times; (3) $T^2 \propto a^3$.
Minimum launch speed to coast to infinity: $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ (11.2 km/s for Earth).
Oscillation driven by a restoring force proportional to displacement, $F = -kx$; $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$.
The maximum displacement from equilibrium in an oscillation or wave.
$\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi/T$ (rad/s); for a spring, $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$.
The angle $\phi$ in $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$ that sets where the motion starts in its cycle.
A point mass on a light string; for small swings $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$, independent of mass and amplitude.
A rigid body swinging about a pivot a distance $d$ from its center of mass; $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$.
Loss of an oscillator's energy to friction or drag, making its amplitude decay.
Large-amplitude response when a system is driven at its natural frequency.
The constant $b$ (kg/s) in a velocity-proportional damping force $F = -bv$.
The angular frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$ at which an oscillator vibrates when left alone with no damping.
Damping weaker than critical ($b < 2\sqrt{mk}$): the system still oscillates, at $\omega' = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}$, inside a decaying envelope $e^{-\gamma t}$, $\gamma = b/2m$.
Damping with $b = 2\sqrt{mk}$ ($\gamma = \omega_0$): the fastest return to equilibrium without overshooting.
Damping stronger than critical ($b > 2\sqrt{mk}$): the system returns to equilibrium without oscillating, more slowly than with critical damping.
A measure of how lightly damped an oscillator is: $Q = \omega_0/(2\gamma) = \sqrt{mk}/b$. It equals the resonant amplitude divided by the static stretch, and $\omega_0/\Delta\omega$.
A periodic external force, such as $F_0\cos\omega t$, that pushes an oscillator and feeds energy into it.
The angular frequency $\omega$ of the external force on a driven oscillator; the steady-state motion has this frequency.
The part of a driven oscillator's motion that dies away (as $e^{-\gamma t}$), leaving the steady state.
The lasting motion of a driven oscillator once transients have died out: $x = A\cos(\omega t - \delta)$ at the driving frequency.
The graph of a driven oscillator's steady-state amplitude (or absorbed power) against driving frequency; it peaks near $\omega_0$.
The width $\Delta\omega = b/m$ of a resonance, measured between the frequencies where the absorbed power is half its peak; $Q = \omega_0/\Delta\omega$.
A traveling disturbance that carries energy through a medium (or through space) without carrying matter along.
A wave that needs a material medium, such as sound or waves on a string.
A wave in which the medium moves perpendicular to the direction of travel.
A wave in which the medium moves parallel to the direction of travel, in compressions and rarefactions (e.g. sound).
The distance over which a wave repeats, crest to crest; $v = f\lambda$.
Mass per unit length of a string, $\mu = m/L$ (kg/m).
Where waves overlap, the net displacement is the sum of the individual displacements.
Overlap of waves in step, so their displacements add (path difference $m\lambda$).
Overlap of waves out of step, so their displacements cancel (path difference $(m + \tfrac12)\lambda$).
The difference in distance traveled by two waves to a point; it determines whether they interfere constructively or destructively.
A stationary oscillation pattern formed by two identical waves traveling in opposite directions.
A point in a standing wave that does not move; adjacent nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart.
A point of maximum oscillation in a standing wave, midway between nodes.
The allowed standing-wave frequencies of a system; for a string fixed at both ends, $f_n = nv/(2L)$.
The lowest standing-wave frequency of a system, $f_1$.
Power per unit area carried by a wave (W/m²); from a point source $I = P/(4\pi r^2)$.
$k = 2\pi/\lambda$ (rad/m), the spatial analog of angular frequency.
$\partial^2y/\partial x^2 = (1/v^2)\,\partial^2y/\partial t^2$, satisfied by any wave traveling at speed $v$.
The perceived highness or lowness of a sound, determined by its frequency.
Sound below about 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear.
Sound above about 20 kHz, too high for humans to hear; used in medical imaging and sonar.
$\beta = 10\log_{10}(I/I_0)$ in decibels, with $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m².
Unit of sound intensity level; +10 dB is ten times the intensity, +3 dB about twice.
The rate at which loudness throbs when two close frequencies combine: $f_{\text{beat}} = |f_1 - f_2|$.
The change in observed frequency due to relative motion of source and observer: $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$.
A cone of piled-up wavefronts from a source moving faster than the wave speed; half-angle $\sin\theta = v/v_s$.
Mass per unit volume, $\rho = m/V$ (kg/m³); water is 1000 kg/m³.
Perpendicular force per unit area, $P = F/A$, in pascals.
SI unit of pressure, $1\text{ Pa} = 1\text{ N/m}^2$; 1 atm $= 1.013\times10^5$ Pa.
Pressure above atmospheric, $P - P_{\text{atm}}$; what tire gauges read.
Total pressure including the atmosphere's contribution.
An instrument measuring atmospheric pressure, classically a mercury column ($P_{\text{atm}} = \rho gh$, 760 mm at sea level).
A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout it; basis of hydraulics, $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$.
The net upward force a fluid exerts on an immersed object, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
$F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{displaced}}\,g$.
A model fluid that is incompressible, nonviscous, and flows steadily without rotation.
The path followed by fluid elements in steady flow; streamlines never cross.
Volume passing a point per second, $Q = Av$ (m³/s).
$A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$ for an incompressible fluid: narrower sections flow faster.
Along a streamline of an ideal fluid, $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho gy$ is constant.
At equal heights, faster-moving fluid has lower pressure.
Fluid leaves a hole a depth $h$ below the open surface at $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
Internal friction in a fluid that resists flow between layers.
A measure of hotness tied to the average kinetic energy of particles; equal temperatures mean thermal equilibrium.
The state in which objects in contact no longer exchange net heat because they share the same temperature.
If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
Temperature scale with water freezing at 0°C and boiling at 100°C (1 atm).
Temperature scale with $T_F = \tfrac95T_C + 32$.
The SI absolute temperature scale, $T = T_C + 273.15$; 0 K is absolute zero.
0 K ($-273.15$°C), the lowest possible temperature.
The fractional change in length per kelvin: $\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T$.
Energy transferred because of a temperature difference (symbol $Q$, in joules).
Heat needed per kilogram per kelvin, $c$ in $Q = mc\Delta T$; 4186 J/(kg·K) for water.
Heat per kilogram absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature, $Q = mL$.
Latent heat for melting or freezing; $3.34\times10^5$ J/kg for water.
Latent heat for boiling or condensing; $2.26\times10^6$ J/kg for water.
Heat transfer through a material by molecular collisions; rate $kA\Delta T/L$.
Material property $k$ (W/(m·K)) setting how readily heat conducts through it.
Heat transfer by bulk motion of a fluid.
Heat transfer by electromagnetic waves; power $P = e\sigma AT^4$ (Stefan–Boltzmann law).
$dT/dt = -\kappa(T - T_s)$: an object approaches the surrounding temperature exponentially.
Amount of substance containing $N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ particles.
$N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}$ particles per mole.
$PV = nRT = Nk_BT$, with absolute pressure and temperature.
A gas of point particles that interact only through brief elastic collisions; real gases approach it at low pressure and high temperature.
Standard temperature and pressure: in this course 0°C (273.15 K) and 1 atm, where one mole of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L. (IUPAC now uses 1 bar = 100 kPa, giving 22.7 L.)
$v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{\overline{v^2}} = \sqrt{3k_BT/m} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$.
Made of single atoms (He, Ne, Ar); an ideal monatomic gas has $E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32nRT$.
Each quadratic degree of freedom of a molecule holds on average $\tfrac12k_BT$ of energy.
The distribution of molecular speeds in a gas at temperature $T$, peaked at $\sqrt{2k_BT/m}$ with a high-speed tail.
The total microscopic energy of a system's particles; for an ideal gas it depends only on $T$.
A graph of pressure versus volume; the area under a process curve is the work done by the gas.
$\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$, with $Q$ heat into the system and $W$ work done by it.
A property that depends only on the current state, not the path (internal energy, entropy, $P$, $V$, $T$).
At constant pressure; $W = P\Delta V$.
At constant volume; $W = 0$ and $Q = \Delta E_{\text{int}}$.
At constant temperature; for an ideal gas $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$ and $Q = W = nRT\ln(V_f/V_i)$.
With no heat exchange ($Q = 0$); for an ideal gas $PV^\gamma$ is constant.
Heat per mole per kelvin; for a monatomic ideal gas $C_V = \tfrac32R$ and $C_P = \tfrac52R$.
A process that returns a system to its initial state, so $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = 0$ and net heat equals net work.
A cyclic device that absorbs heat $Q_H$, does work $W$, and rejects heat $Q_C$ to a colder reservoir.
$e = W/Q_H = 1 - Q_C/Q_H$ for a heat engine.
No cyclic engine converts heat entirely to work; heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot; total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.
An idealized process with no friction and only infinitesimal temperature differences, which can be run backward exactly.
The reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats; its efficiency $1 - T_C/T_H$ is the maximum possible for any engine working between those two reservoir temperatures.
A device that uses work to move heat from a cold region to a warmer one.
For a refrigerator $K = Q_C/W$; for a heat pump $Q_H/W$. It can exceed 1.
A refrigerator used to deliver heat $Q_H$ to a warm space.
A state variable measuring disorder; $\Delta S = \int dQ_{\text{rev}}/T$, and $S = k_B\ln\Omega$.

references.title: Mechanics equations
references.body:
## Vectors

| | |
|---|---|
| Components | $A_x = A\cos\theta$, $A_y = A\sin\theta$ |
| Magnitude, direction | $A = \sqrt{A_x^2 + A_y^2}$, $\tan\theta = A_y/A_x$ |
| Dot product | $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\phi = A_xB_x + A_yB_y + A_zB_z$ |
| Cross product | $\lvert\vec A\times\vec B\rvert = AB\sin\phi$ (right-hand rule) |

## Kinematics

| | |
|---|---|
| Definitions | $v = \dfrac{dx}{dt}$, $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$; $\Delta x = \int v\,dt$ |
| Constant acceleration | $v = v_0 + at$; $\Delta x = v_0t + \tfrac12at^2$; $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a\Delta x$; $\Delta x = \tfrac12(v_0 + v)t$ |
| Projectile (level ground) | $R = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$, $H = \dfrac{v_0^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$, $T = \dfrac{2v_0\sin\theta}{g}$ |
| Relative velocity | $\vec v_{AC} = \vec v_{AB} + \vec v_{BC}$ |
| Circular motion | $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$, $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2r$ |

## Forces

| | |
|---|---|
| Newton's second law | $\sum\vec F = m\vec a = \dfrac{d\vec p}{dt}$ |
| Weight | $W = mg$ |
| Friction | $f_k = \mu_kn$, $f_s \le \mu_sn$ |
| Incline | $mg\sin\theta$ along, $mg\cos\theta$ into the slope |
| Spring | $F = -kx$ |
| Centripetal | $\sum F_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ |
| Atwood machine | $a = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$ |

## Energy and momentum

| | |
|---|---|
| Work | $W = Fd\cos\theta = \int\vec F\cdot d\vec\ell$ |
| Kinetic energy | $K = \tfrac12mv^2$; $W_{\text{net}} = \Delta K$ |
| Potential energy | $U_g = mgy$, $U_s = \tfrac12kx^2$, $F = -\dfrac{dU}{dx}$ |
| Energy conservation | $K_i + U_i + W_{\text{nc}} = K_f + U_f$ |
| Power | $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = Fv$ |
| Momentum, impulse | $\vec p = m\vec v$; $\vec J = \int\vec F\,dt = \Delta\vec p$ |
| Center of mass | $x_{\text{cm}} = \dfrac{\sum m_ix_i}{M} = \dfrac1M\int x\,dm$ |
| Elastic collision (target at rest) | $v_{1f} = \dfrac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i}$, $v_{2f} = \dfrac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}v_{1i}$ |
| Perfectly inelastic | $v_f = \dfrac{m_1v_1 + m_2v_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ |
| Rocket (no external force) | $\Delta v = u\ln\dfrac{m_i}{m_f}$; thrust $= u\,\lvert dm/dt\rvert$ |

## Rotation

| Linear | Rotational |
|---|---|
| $x$, $v$, $a$ | $\theta$, $\omega$, $\alpha$; $v = r\omega$, $a_t = r\alpha$ |
| $m$ | $I = \sum mr^2 = \int r^2\,dm$; $I = I_{\text{cm}} + Md^2$ |
| $F = ma$ | $\tau = rF\sin\theta = I\alpha$; $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ |
| $K = \tfrac12mv^2$ | $K = \tfrac12I\omega^2$ |
| $p = mv$ | $L = I\omega$; $\vec L = \vec r\times\vec p$; $\tau = dL/dt$ |
| $P = Fv$ | $P = \tau\omega$ |

| Shape (mass $M$) | $I$ |
|---|---|
| Hoop, radius $R$ | $MR^2$ |
| Solid disk or cylinder | $\tfrac12MR^2$ |
| Solid sphere | $\tfrac25MR^2$ |
| Thin spherical shell | $\tfrac23MR^2$ |
| Rod about center / end | $\tfrac1{12}ML^2$ / $\tfrac13ML^2$ |

Rolling from height $h$ ($I = cMR^2$): $v = \sqrt{2gh/(1 + c)}$. Static equilibrium: $\sum\vec F = 0$, $\sum\tau = 0$.

## Elasticity

| | |
|---|---|
| Tension or compression | $\dfrac{F}{A} = Y\dfrac{\Delta L}{L}$, so $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$ (steel $Y \approx 2\times10^{11}$ Pa, aluminum $7\times10^{10}$ Pa) |
| Shear | $\dfrac{F}{A} = S\dfrac{\Delta x}{L}$ |
| Bulk (volume) | $\Delta P = -B\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}$ |

## Gravitation

| | |
|---|---|
| Universal gravitation | $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2}$; $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^2}$ |
| Circular orbit | $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$, $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{GM}r^3$ |
| Potential energy | $U = -\dfrac{GMm}{r}$ |
| Escape speed | $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{R}}$ |

## Derived SI units

## Temperature

## Significant figures

references.title: Oscillations, waves, fluids, and thermodynamics
references.body:
## Oscillations

| | |
|---|---|
| SHM | $x = A\cos(\omega t + \phi)$; $\ddot x = -\omega^2x$ |
| Spring | $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ |
| Simple pendulum | $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}$ |
| Physical pendulum | $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$ |
| Maxima | $v_{\max} = A\omega$, $a_{\max} = A\omega^2$; $E = \tfrac12kA^2$ |
| Damped ($\gamma = b/2m$) | $m\ddot x + b\dot x + kx = 0$; underdamped $x = A_0e^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega' t + \phi)$, $\omega' = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}$; critical $b = 2\sqrt{mk}$ |
| Quality factor | $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0}{2\gamma} = \dfrac{\sqrt{mk}}{b} = \dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega}$, bandwidth $\Delta\omega = b/m$ |
| Driven ($F_0\cos\omega t$) | $A = \dfrac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (2\gamma\omega)^2}}$; at $\omega_0$: $A = \dfrac{F_0}{b\omega_0} = Q\dfrac{F_0}{k}$ |

## Waves and sound

| | |
|---|---|
| Wave speed | $v = f\lambda$; string: $v = \sqrt{F_T/\mu}$ |
| Traveling wave | $y = A\sin(kx - \omega t)$, $k = 2\pi/\lambda$, $\omega = 2\pi f$ |
| Power on a string | $P_{\text{avg}} = \tfrac12\mu A^2\omega^2v$ |
| String fixed at both ends; open pipe | $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{2L}$, $n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ |
| Pipe closed at one end | $f_n = \dfrac{nv}{4L}$, $n = 1, 3, 5, \ldots$ |
| Intensity | $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}$; $\beta = 10\log_{10}\dfrac{I}{I_0}$, $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m² |
| Beats | $f_{\text{beat}} = \lvert f_1 - f_2\rvert$ |
| Doppler | $f' = f\dfrac{v \pm v_o}{v \mp v_s}$ (upper signs: approaching) |

## Fluids

| | |
|---|---|
| Density, pressure | $\rho = m/V$, $P = F/A$ |
| Depth | $P = P_0 + \rho gh$; $dP/dy = -\rho g$ |
| Pascal | $F_1/A_1 = F_2/A_2$ |
| Buoyancy | $F_B = \rho_{\text{fluid}}V_{\text{disp}}g$ |
| Continuity | $A_1v_1 = A_2v_2$ |
| Bernoulli | $P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho gy$ = const |
| Torricelli | $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ |

## Heat and gases

| | |
|---|---|
| Expansion | $\Delta L = \alpha L\Delta T$ |
| Heat | $Q = mc\Delta T$; phase change $Q = mL$ |
| Conduction, radiation | $Q/t = kA\Delta T/L$; $P = e\sigma AT^4$ |
| Ideal gas | $PV = nRT = Nk_BT$ |
| Kinetic theory | $\tfrac12m\overline{v^2} = \tfrac32k_BT$; $v_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{3RT/M}$ |
| Monatomic gas | $E_{\text{int}} = \tfrac32nRT$; $C_V = \tfrac32R$, $C_P = \tfrac52R$, $\gamma = \tfrac53$ |

## Thermodynamics

| | |
|---|---|
| First law | $\Delta E_{\text{int}} = Q - W$ ($W$ by the gas) |
| Work by gas | $W = \int P\,dV$; isobaric $P\Delta V$; isothermal $nRT\ln(V_f/V_i)$ |
| Adiabatic | $PV^\gamma$ = const, $TV^{\gamma - 1}$ = const |
| Engine | $e = \dfrac{W}{Q_H} = 1 - \dfrac{Q_C}{Q_H}$; Carnot $e = 1 - \dfrac{T_C}{T_H}$ |
| Refrigerator | $K = Q_C/W$; Carnot $\dfrac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}$ |
| Entropy | $\Delta S = \int\dfrac{dQ_{\text{rev}}}{T}$; $Q/T$ at constant $T$; heating at constant $c$: $mc\ln(T_2/T_1)$ |

drills.title: Convert km/h to m/s
drills.prompt: A car travels at {v} km/h. Express this speed in m/s (3 significant figures).
drills.solution:
$${v}\,\frac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \frac{1000\text{ m}}{1\text{ km}} \times \frac{1\text{ h}}{3600\text{ s}} = \frac{{v}}{3.6}\,\frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}$$

So the speed is **{ms:sig3} m/s**.

drills.title: Convert an area from cm² to m²
drills.prompt: A solar cell has an area of {a} cm². What is its area in m²? (The conversion is exact, so give every digit.)
drills.solution:
$1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}$, so $1\text{ cm}^2 = 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$ (square the factor).

${a:dp0}\text{ cm}^2 \times 10^{-4}\,\tfrac{\text{m}^2}{\text{cm}^2} =$ **{m2:num4} m²**.

drills.title: Area with significant figures
drills.prompt: A rectangular sheet measures {l} m by {w} m. Find its area, rounded to the correct number of significant figures.
drills.solution: ${l} \times {w} = {A:num4}\text{ m}^2$. For a product, keep the fewest significant figures among the inputs: {l} has 3 and {w} has 2, so round to 2 significant figures: **{A:sig2} m²**.

drills.title: Components of a vector
drills.prompt: A force of {A} N points at {th}° measured counterclockwise from the $+x$ axis. Find its $x$ and $y$ components (include the signs), each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$F_x = F\cos\theta = {A}\cos {th}^\circ =$ **{Ax:sig3} N**

$F_y = F\sin\theta = {A}\sin {th}^\circ =$ **{Ay:sig3} N**

The signs come out of the trig functions automatically when the angle is measured from $+x$.

drills.title: Add two displacement vectors
drills.prompt: A drone flies {a} km at {t1}° (counterclockwise from east), then {b} km at {t2}°. Find the magnitude of its total displacement and its direction in degrees counterclockwise from east (magnitude to 3 significant figures, direction to the nearest 0.1°).
drills.solution:
$R_x = {a}\cos {t1}^\circ + {b}\cos {t2}^\circ = {Rx:num2}$ km

$R_y = {a}\sin {t1}^\circ + {b}\sin {t2}^\circ = {Ry:num2}$ km

$R = \sqrt{R_x^2 + R_y^2} =$ **{R:sig3} km**, at $\theta =$ **{th:num1}°** (check the quadrant from the signs of $R_x$ and $R_y$).

drills.title: Angle between two vectors
drills.prompt: For $\vec A = {a1}\hat\imath {a2:signed}\hat\jmath {a3:signed}\hat k$ and $\vec B = {b1}\hat\imath {b2:signed}\hat\jmath {b3:signed}\hat k$, find $\vec A\cdot\vec B$ and the angle between the vectors in degrees (to the nearest 0.1°).

drills.title: Average velocity and average speed
drills.prompt: A jogger runs {d1} m east in {t1} s, then turns and runs {d2} m west in {t2} s. Find her average velocity (east positive) and her average speed for the whole run, each to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
Displacement: $\Delta x = {d1} - {d2} = {dx}$ m; total time $\Delta t = {t1} + {t2} = {tt}$ s.

Average velocity $= \dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} =$ **{vavg:sig3} m/s** (east).

Distance $= {d1} + {d2}$ m, so average speed $=$ **{savg:sig3} m/s**.

drills.title: Velocity and acceleration from x(t)
drills.prompt: A particle moves along $x$ with $x(t) = {a:coef}t^3 {b:signedcoef}t^2 {c:signedcoef}t$ (meters, seconds). Find its velocity and acceleration at $t = {t}$ s (exact values).
drills.solution:
$v(t) = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = {a3}t^2 {b2:signed}t {c:signed}$, so $v({t}) =$ **{v} m/s**.

$a(t) = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = {a6}t {b2:signed}$, so $a({t}) =$ **{acc} m/s²**.

drills.title: Braking distance and time
drills.prompt: A car moving at {v0} m/s brakes with a constant acceleration of magnitude {dec} m/s². How far does it travel while stopping, and how long does it take? Give answers to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
With $v = 0$ and $a = -{dec}$ m/s²: $0 = v_0^2 - 2({dec})\Delta x$, so $\Delta x = \dfrac{{v0}^2}{2({dec})} =$ **{d:sig3} m**.

$0 = {v0} - {dec}\,t$, so $t =$ **{t:sig3} s**.

drills.title: Time and speed of a dropped object
drills.prompt: A wrench is dropped from rest from a height of {h} m. Ignoring air resistance and using $g = 9.8$ m/s², how long does it fall, and how fast is it moving at the ground? Give answers to 3 significant figures.
drills.solution:
$h = \tfrac12 g t^2 \Rightarrow t = \sqrt{2({h})/9.8} =$ **{t:sig3} s**.

$v = gt = 9.8({t:sig3}) =$ **{v:sig3} m/s** (also $v = \sqrt{2gh}$).

drills.title: Ball thrown straight up
